questions.question: The CRO of a large US bank holding company is comparing two US initiatives described in the Basel Committee report: the joint notice of proposed rulemaking by the federal banking agencies, and the cyber-security regulations of the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS). Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The NYDFS regulations were issued jointly by the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC as part of their notice of proposed rulemaking.
The federal proposal applies to financial institutions of every size, because any cyber-incident could impair safety and soundness.
The NYDFS regulations require a programme to protect consumers’ private data but leave the appointment of a CISO to each institution.
The federal proposal targets serious cyber-incidents that could affect safety and soundness, with requirements covering dependency management.

questions.solution:
CRO of a large US bank holding company comparing the federal agencies’ proposed cyber rules with the NYDFS regulations.

**Concept and theory**

The report gives two US examples of recent regulatory initiatives:

| Feature | Federal agencies’ notice of proposed rulemaking | NYDFS cyber-security regulations |
|---|---|---|
| Issuer | Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC (joint announcement) | New York State Department of Financial Services |
| Scope | Large financial institutions | Regulated institutions in New York |
| Intent | Address the type of serious cyber-incident that could impact safety and soundness | Protect consumers’ private data; help ensure safety and soundness of the financial services industry |
| Requirements | Cyber-risk governance; risk management; internal dependency management; external dependency management; incident response; assurance management of third parties; audit | A cyber-security programme; a written policy or policies approved by the board or a senior officer; a Chief Information Security Officer; controls and plans |

The comparison shows two different design choices. The federal proposal is targeted (large institutions, serious incidents) and organised around dependencies inside and outside the firm. The NYDFS rules are framed around a programme, a policy and a named accountable officer.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each option on issuer, scope and content. Only one option states the federal proposal’s intent and part of its requirement list correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Federal proposal: Fed, OCC and FDIC; large institutions; serious incidents; internal and external dependency management. NYDFS: state regulator; consumer data; board or senior officer approves the policy; CISO required.

**Reference**

LO 49.a: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience. GARP Chapter 8, Box 8.1 Case Study 1: Recent Regulatory Initiatives (US Agencies’ Notice of Proposed Rulemaking; NYDFS regulations). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not cover the US initiatives; content from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 a, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC issued the notice of proposed rulemaking; the NYDFS, a state authority, issued its own regulations. A would be correct if it referred to the federal proposal.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The federal proposal is for large financial institutions and targets serious incidents. Extending it to every size of institution drops the stated condition. B would be correct only for a rule with no size threshold.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The first half is right, but the NYDFS regulations require a Chief Information Security Officer to help protect data and systems. Making the role optional reverses the requirement. C would be correct only if the CISO were described as recommended rather than required.

d.reason: GARP Box 8.1 states that the intent of the federal proposal is to address the type of serious cyber-incident that could impact safety and soundness, with requirements on cyber-risk governance, risk management, internal and external dependency management, incident response, assurance management of third parties and audit.

questions.question:
A risk committee member at a cross-border bank that reports in GBP is comparing the initiatives presented in the Basel Committee’s case study on recent regulatory initiatives in Australia, Germany and the US. She drafts the following statements:

I. CPS 234 extends its key objective to information assets managed by related parties or third parties, and the US federal proposal includes external dependency management and assurance management of third parties.

II. Of these initiatives, only BAIT addresses outsourcing or the external procurement of IT services.

III. The NYDFS regulations require a written policy approved by the board or a senior officer, whereas CPS 234 makes the board ultimately responsible for the entity’s information security.

IV. All of the initiatives are principles-based guidance that imposes no enforceable requirements on regulated entities.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, III and IV

questions.solution:
Risk committee member comparing the Australian, German and US initiatives on third-party scope, board role and enforceability.

**Concept and theory**

The report closes Section 8.2 by noting that some jurisdictions are developing enforceable standards for cyber-resilience in the financial sector, which is the theme of its first case study. Comparing the initiatives on three axes:

| Axis | APRA CPS 234 | German BAIT | US initiatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Third parties | Objective covers assets managed by related or third parties | Outsourcing and other external procurement of IT services | Federal: external dependency management, assurance management of third parties |
| Board role | Board ultimately responsible | Not specified in the box | NYDFS: written policy approved by the board or a senior officer |
| Nature | Prudential standard with “must” requirements | Supervisory requirements refining the Banking Act | Proposed rules and state regulations |

All three extend to third parties, which mirrors the report’s introduction: the perimeter of interest is bigger and shared. They differ in where they place accountability and in their structure, but each is an example of enforceable requirements rather than voluntary guidance.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: CPS 234’s objective includes assets managed by related or third parties, and the federal proposal includes external dependency management and assurance management of third parties: accurate.

Statement II: claims only BAIT addresses outsourcing or external procurement. CPS 234 and the US proposal also address third parties: inaccurate.

Statement III: the NYDFS policy is approved by the board or a senior officer, and CPS 234 makes the board ultimately responsible: accurate.

Statement IV: calls all of them non-enforceable principles-based guidance. The report presents them as enforceable standards: inaccurate.

Accurate: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** NYDFS: policy approved by the board or a senior officer. CPS 234: the board is ultimately responsible. Box 8.1 initiatives are examples of enforceable standards, and all reach third parties.

**Reference**

LO 49.a: Define cyber-resilience and compare recent regulatory initiatives in the area of cyber-resilience. GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.2 Cyber-Resilience Standards and Guidelines and Box 8.1 Case Study 1: Recent Regulatory Initiatives (The Australian, German and US Minimum Requirements). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes only APRA and BAIT, and only in summary; the US initiatives and the enforceability framing are from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 a, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Accepting II accepts an “only” that the source does not support: third-party coverage appears in all three examples. A would be correct only if CPS 234 and the US proposal were silent on third parties.

b.reason: Statements I and III match GARP Box 8.1 directly; II and IV contradict it.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** It accepts both II (“only BAIT”) and IV (“all . . . no enforceable requirements”), and rejects the accurate I and III. C would be correct only for a set of voluntary codes with a single outsourcing provision.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It adds IV, which reverses the report’s framing. Section 8.2 introduces these initiatives precisely as jurisdictions developing enforceable standards, and CPS 234 states what an entity must do. D would be correct only if the initiatives had been described as voluntary guidance.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a regional bank in Singapore is drafting a briefing for the board risk committee that summarises the Basel Committee’s 2018 findings on cyber-governance. The committee chair has asked for one sentence that captures the overall state of regulation before the briefing moves on to individual governance areas. Which of the following sentences best describes the Basel Committee’s finding?

options.text: Most regulators have converged on prescriptive, cyber-specific regulations of broadly similar maturity, and these regulations now explicitly cover the cyber-risk management of critical business functions, interconnectedness and third-party risk.

Most regulators have issued principles-based guidance or prescriptive regulations of varying maturity that address enterprise IT risk management but rarely cover cyber-risk in critical business functions, interconnectedness or third parties.

Most regulators have issued principles-based guidance only, because prescriptive cyber regulation has been observed solely in those jurisdictions that lack an existing enterprise IT risk management framework for banks.

Most regulators have issued guidance that covers each of the main governance areas with similar depth, so that requirements on architecture and standards are now as widely established as the expectations on strategy.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Singapore bank choosing one sentence that summarises the Basel Committee’s overall finding on cyber-governance.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel Committee’s 2018 range of practices report does not set new rules; it describes what supervisors and banks are already doing. Section 8.3 (Cyber-Governance) opens with a single framing observation that governs everything else in this LO:

- **Form of the rules.** The majority of regulators have issued either principles-based guidance or prescriptive regulations, and these instruments sit at varying levels of maturity. There is no single model.
- **What they cover.** Regulatory standards and supervisory practices address enterprise IT risk management in general.
- **What they do not cover.** They do not include specific regulations or supervisory practices on the cyber-risk management of critical business functions, interconnectedness or third-party risk management.

Why does this matter? Cyber-risk is treated as a subset of IT and operational risk (the 49.a theme), so supervisors reach cyber-governance through general IT governance tools. Against that backdrop the Committee analysed five governance areas:

| No. | Governance area analysed in Section 8.3 |
|---|---|
| 1 | Cyber-security strategy |
| 2 | Management roles and responsibilities |
| 3 | Cyber-risk awareness culture |
| 4 | Architecture and standards |
| 5 | Cyber-security workforce |

These areas are not equally developed: strategy and management roles are widely addressed, while architecture and standards requirements are absent or lack coverage in most jurisdictions, and workforce supervision is at an early stage.

**Applying it to this question**

The chair wants one sentence on the overall state. Three attributes must all be right: (1) the type of instrument (guidance or regulation, varying maturity); (2) the coverage (enterprise IT risk management); (3) the gap (critical business functions, interconnectedness, third parties). Only option B gets all three right. Each other option corrupts exactly one of them.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of the gap: standards do address enterprise IT risk management but do not specifically address cyber-risk of critical business functions, interconnectedness or third parties.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3 “Cyber-Governance” (introductory paragraph and list of governance areas). Schweser compresses this to “guidance may not directly address cyber risk standards ... it addresses broader enterprise IT risk management”; GARP is more specific about the three uncovered areas. No substantive conflict; GARP used for depth.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q1 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the gap. The report says existing standards do not specifically cover critical business functions or third-party risk, and it stresses varying maturity rather than convergence. The option would be right only if the stem described a hypothetical future state in which all jurisdictions had adopted harmonised, cyber-specific rules.

b.reason: It restates the opening of Section 8.3: the majority of regulators have issued either principles-based guidance or prescriptive regulations with varying levels of maturity; these address enterprise IT risk management but do not include specific regulations or supervisory practices that cover cyber-risk management of critical business functions, interconnectedness or third-party risk management.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the finding to principles-based guidance only and invents a condition (prescriptive rules only where no IT framework exists). The report says regulators issue either form; elsewhere it notes that the EBA and emerging market economies apply granular and prescriptive requirements. The option would be right only if the question asked about a single jurisdiction that had chosen a purely principles-based model.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It asserts uniform depth across the five areas. In fact general requirements for architecture and standards are not in place, or lack coverage, in most jurisdictions, while every regulator expects a board-approved information security strategy. The option would be right if the question asked only whether the five areas were analysed by the Committee, not whether they are equally covered.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a bank that operates in several Basel Committee jurisdictions is checking a draft audit memo on supervisory expectations for cyber-security strategy. The memo contains the following statements:

I. Most regulators require regulated entities to develop a standalone cyber-security strategy, but only some expect a board-approved information security strategy.

II. Many jurisdictions expect cyber-risk to be covered by the organisation-wide risk management framework and/or the information security framework.

III. Examiners typically review an institution’s information security strategy and plans and its cyber-security implementation, including key initiatives and timelines, and may also review how it communicates with relevant stakeholders.

IV. Where cyber-risk is covered by the organisation-wide framework, that framework is expected to be monitored and reviewed by the internal audit function rather than by senior executives.

Which of the statements are consistent with the Basel Committee’s findings?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
II only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor checking four memo statements on supervisory expectations for cyber-security strategy.

**Concept and theory**

The GARP heading says it all: Cyber-Security Strategy Is Expected But Not Required. Distinguish two documents:

| Document | Regulatory status | Supervisory practice |
|---|---|---|
| Standalone cyber-security strategy | Most regulators do not require it | Very few supervisors require or evaluate it |
| Information security strategy, policy and procedures | All regulators expect it, board-approved, under the remit of effective oversight of technology | Most supervisors review it |

Many jurisdictions (for example Australia, Brazil and jurisdictions across Europe) expect cyber-risk to be covered by the organisation-wide risk management framework and/or the information security framework, which is monitored and reviewed by senior executives.

What do examiners look at? Typically the institution’s information security strategy, its information security plans and its cyber-security implementation, including key cyber-security initiatives and timelines. They may also review its practices for communicating with relevant stakeholders.

The logic: cyber-risk sits inside the wider technology and risk governance structure, so supervisors check that wider structure rather than demanding a separate cyber document.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the two-document distinction and the actors.

- I: reverses both halves. Most regulators do not require a standalone cyber strategy, and all (not some) expect a board-approved information security strategy. False.
- II: matches the “many jurisdictions” finding. True.
- III: matches the list of what examiners typically review. True.
- IV: the framework is monitored and reviewed by senior executives, not by internal audit. False.

True set: II and III only, which is option D.

**Fragile fact.** “All” expect a board-approved information security strategy; “most do not require” a standalone cyber-security strategy. The framework covering cyber is reviewed by senior executives.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Security Strategy Is Expected But Not Required”. Schweser (Cybersecurity Strategy) says regulators “require” broader information security strategy and policies and omits “board-approved”; GARP says “expect” and specifies board approval. GARP wording used; no conflict on the facts tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q2 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It includes statement I, which flips “most do not require” to “most require” and “all expect” to “only some expect”. Statement I would be true only in a stem that described an information security strategy as optional and a cyber strategy as mandatory, which is the reverse of the report.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It includes statement IV, which gives the monitoring and review of the framework to internal audit. GARP assigns that to senior executives (Schweser: senior management). IV would be correct only if the stem asked who provides independent assurance over the framework, which is the third line’s job rather than ongoing monitoring.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts II but rejects III, treating supervisory review as confined to the strategy document itself. GARP says examiners typically review the information security strategy and the plans and cyber-security implementation, including key initiatives and timelines, and may review stakeholder communication. C would be right only if the stem asked what the board approves, which is the strategy, policy and procedures rather than the implementation record.

d.reason: GARP states that many jurisdictions expect cyber-risk to be covered by the organisation-wide risk management and/or information security framework (II), and that examiners typically review the information security strategy, plans and cyber-security implementation, including key initiatives and timelines, and may review stakeholder communication practices (III).

questions.question:
A risk consultant at an advisory firm is comparing how the authorities in three jurisdictions enforce cyber-security strategy requirements on banks. The consultant’s notes are summarised below.

| Jurisdiction | Banks supervised | Observed practice |
|---|---|---|
| X | 42 | The authority sets cyber-security strategy requirements that apply across banking, insurance and securities firms, and every firm must comply. |
| Y | 310 | Each bank designs its own cyber-security strategy under principles-based risk management, and the supervisor reviews it within its assessment of the bank’s overall risk management. |
| Z | 185 | The supervisor examines whether each bank has an IT strategy and the accompanying security provisions. |

Based on the Basel Committee’s findings, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: X’s practice is common in emerging market economies with relatively homogeneous banking systems, and Z’s practice is the approach described as prevalent in Europe.
X’s practice is common in developed economies with relatively fragmented banking systems, and Y’s practice is the approach described as prevalent in Europe.
Y’s practice is consistent with the findings only where the authority has first set sector-wide strategy requirements, since a review presupposes a regulatory template.
Z’s practice is a variant of X’s practice, because examining a bank’s IT strategy means that the authority itself prescribes the bank’s cyber-security strategy.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant matching three jurisdictions’ practices for enforcing cyber-security strategy requirements to the Basel approaches.

**Concept and theory**

Section 8.3 identifies three non-mutually exclusive regulatory approaches that jurisdictions use to enforce cyber-security strategy requirements:

| No. | Approach | Where it is typical |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The regulator or authority sets cyber-security strategy requirements, either sector-specific or across multiple industries, with which institutions must comply | Common in emerging market economies with relative homogeneity in their banking systems |
| 2 | Institutions establish their own cyber-security strategies in line with principles-based risk management; regulators review them as part of assessing overall risk management practices | Principles-based regimes generally |
| 3 | The supervisor examines whether entities have an IT strategy and the accompanying security provisions | Prevalent in Europe |

Why would homogeneity favour approach 1? When banks have similar business models and technology, one set of authority-written requirements fits them all, so a top-down template is efficient. In diverse systems a principles-based approach (2) lets each bank fit its strategy to its own risk profile. Approach 3 reflects the European habit of reaching cyber through IT governance.

**Applying it to this question**

- X: authority-written requirements covering banking, insurance and securities, that is “across multiple industries”. This is approach 1, associated with emerging markets with relatively homogeneous banking systems.
- Y: bank-designed strategy reviewed within overall risk management. Approach 2.
- Z: examination of the IT strategy and accompanying security provisions. Approach 3, prevalent in Europe.

The “Banks supervised” column is irrelevant: the report does not link the approach to the number of supervised banks.

**Fragile fact.** Authority-set requirements (sector-specific or cross-sector) go with emerging markets with homogeneous banking systems; the IT strategy plus security provisions examination is the European approach.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Security Strategy Is Expected But Not Required” (numbered list of three approaches). Schweser lists the same three approaches with the same associations. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q3 of 16.

a.reason: GARP describes approach 1 as “a common approach in emerging market economies with relative homogeneity in their banking systems” and approach 3 as “prevalent in Europe”. Both halves of A match.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attaches the opposite context to approach 1 (developed, fragmented) and moves the “prevalent in Europe” label from approach 3 to approach 2. It would be right only if the report had said that institution-led strategies are the European norm, which it does not.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It adds a precondition that does not exist. Approach 2 stands alone: institutions write their own strategies under principles-based risk management and supervisors review them. The approaches are non-mutually exclusive, but none depends on another. C would be right only if the stem described a regime that explicitly made the review conditional on a prior template.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It merges approach 3 into approach 1. Examining whether a bank has an IT strategy and security provisions is a review of the bank’s own document; it does not mean that the authority writes the cyber-security strategy. D would describe approach 1 correctly only if Z’s authority itself issued the strategy requirements.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a global systemically important bank headquartered in the EU is comparing how jurisdictions treat management roles and responsibilities in cyber-governance. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: In the US, the EU and Japan, binding rules require all banks, regardless of systemic importance, to adopt a single cyber-governance structure designed by senior management and approved by the supervisor.
Emerging market economies tend to rely on high-level principles for management roles, while the EBA leaves cyber-security requirements to national discretion without issuing granular requirements.

In the US, the EU and Japan, high-level guidelines encourage G-SIBs and D-SIBs to implement well-defined, risk-sensitive frameworks under board initiatives, while the EBA applies granular, prescriptive requirements.

In the US, the EU and Japan, high-level guidelines encourage G-SIBs and D-SIBs to implement management frameworks under initiatives taken by the chief information officer, with the board limited to approving the IT budget.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at an EU G-SIB comparing how jurisdictions treat management roles and responsibilities in cyber-governance.

**Concept and theory**

Under “Management Roles and Responsibilities: Recognition of the Importance of the Board of Directors and Senior Management”, GARP reports:

- Some jurisdictions have issued specific guidance and requirements on the cyber-governance roles of the board (BoD) and senior management. Most such guidance prioritises those roles; some prioritise them even more in overseeing overall business technology risks. Other jurisdictions treat cyber-governance as a risk to be handled within existing risk management frameworks.
- Almost all jurisdictions emphasise the importance of management roles and responsibilities for cyber-governance and key controls.
- **US, EU and Japan:** high-level guidelines encourage G-SIBs and D-SIBs to implement well defined, risk-sensitive management frameworks under initiatives taken by the BoD.
- **EBA:** implements granular and prescriptive requirements, ensuring consistent cyber-security regulation and supervision across the European banking sector.
- **Emerging market economies:** similarly implement more granular and prescriptive requirements.

The pattern: accountability starts at the top (board initiative), the form of the instrument varies (high-level guidelines in the US, EU and Japan versus granular rules from the EBA and in emerging markets), and the scope of the high-level guidelines is systemically important banks.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each option on three dimensions: instrument (high-level guidelines vs granular rules), scope (G-SIBs and D-SIBs), and actor (board initiatives). Only C has all three right and also attributes granular and prescriptive requirements to the EBA.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: frameworks are implemented “under initiatives taken by the BoD”. Granular and prescriptive: EBA and emerging markets; high-level guidelines: US, EU and Japan, aimed at G-SIBs and D-SIBs.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Management Roles and Responsibilities: Recognition of the Importance of the Board of Directors and Senior Management”. Schweser says the US, EU and Japan “encourage banks” to implement frameworks through board initiatives and omits both the G-SIB/D-SIB scope and the emerging market point; GARP is more precise and is used here. This is a compression, not a factual conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q4 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It turns high-level guidelines for G-SIBs and D-SIBs into binding rules for all banks with a single structure approved by the supervisor. It would be right only for a hypothetical jurisdiction that imposed a uniform, mandatory governance template.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the characterisation of both actors: emerging market economies and the EBA are the ones that implement more granular and prescriptive requirements. B would be right if the stem asked about the US, EU and Japan high-level guidelines, which are the less granular instrument.

c.reason: GARP: “In the US, EU and Japan, high-level guidelines encourage global systemically important banks (G-SIBs) and domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs) to implement well defined, risk-sensitive management frameworks under initiatives taken by the BoD. In addition, the EBA implements granular and prescriptive requirements.”

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It keeps the right instrument and scope but moves the initiative from the board to the CIO and confines the board to budget approval. GARP places the initiative with the BoD. D would describe an IT-led governance model that the report treats as inadequate.

questions.loText: Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-8 b Q5
questions.question: The newly appointed head of operational risk at a bank in Brazil tells the board: “Our supervisor has adopted the three lines of defence (3LD) model for cyber-risk, so we must now restructure exactly as the supervisor prescribes, with responsibilities allocated across the lines in the supervisor’s format.” Which of the following responses best reflects the Basel Committee’s findings?

options.text: The proposal is correct, because most regulators both require 3LD at regulated entities and prescribe precisely how cyber responsibilities are distributed across the lines.
The proposal is unnecessary, because most regulators have rejected 3LD as a lens for assessing cyber-security risk and controls at regulated entities.
The proposal is unnecessary, because regulators expect the third line to define the responsibilities of the first and second lines on the bank’s behalf.
The proposal misreads the supervisor: most regulators use 3LD to assess cyber risk and controls, but banks define the responsibilities themselves, with no gaps.

questions.solution:
Head of operational risk at a Brazilian bank claims the supervisor’s adoption of 3LD obliges the bank to restructure in the supervisor’s prescribed format.

**Concept and theory**

The **three lines of defence (3LD)** model allocates risk responsibilities:

| Line | Who | Role |
|---|---|---|
| First | Business units and operations (including IT operations) | Own and manage the risk |
| Second | Risk management and compliance (CRO function) | Oversee and challenge |
| Third | Internal audit (with external audit) | Independent assurance |

GARP’s sub-section “Variety of Supervisory Approaches Regarding the Second and Third Lines of Defence (3LD)” makes four points that must be kept apart:

1. The majority of regulators have adopted the 3LD model to assess cyber-security risk and controls (a supervisory lens).
2. However, most regulators do not require implementation of 3LD at regulated entities and do not prescribe precisely how responsibilities should be distributed across the lines.
3. The expectation is for banks themselves to clearly define responsibilities and leave no gaps between the lines.
4. As a result, supervisory practices for assessing 3LD implementation vary widely (developed in Q12).

Why this design? Supervisors want accountability to be clear, but the right split of duties depends on each bank’s size and structure, so they assess the outcome (clear responsibilities, no gaps) rather than impose a template.

**Applying it to this question**

The head of operational risk makes an inference error: from “the supervisor uses 3LD” to “the supervisor prescribes our 3LD structure”. Point 1 is true, but points 2 and 3 break the inference. The correct response accepts the lens and rejects the prescription, placing the design duty on the bank. That is D.

**Fragile fact.** Two verbs, two answers: regulators use 3LD to assess (majority yes) but do not require or prescribe it (most no). The bank defines responsibilities and must leave no gaps.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Variety of Supervisory Approaches Regarding the Second and Third Lines of Defence (3LD)”. Schweser: regulatory standards “often include” 3LD for cyber-risk “but have not required institutions to adopt this model”; consistent with GARP. The line descriptions in the table follow the Schweser Professor’s Note, which is consistent with GARP’s usage. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q5 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns “do not require” and “do not prescribe” into “require” and “prescribe precisely”. A would be right only in a jurisdiction that had issued a mandatory 3LD rule with a prescribed allocation, which the report says is not the norm.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It flips the first finding: the majority of regulators have adopted 3LD as an assessment model; they have not rejected it. B would be right only if the stem asked whether most regulators mandate 3LD at banks, where the answer is indeed no, but not because they reject the model.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives the job of defining first and second line responsibilities to the third line. The report places that duty on the bank itself (management and the board), while internal audit provides independent assurance. C would describe the third line’s role correctly only if it read “assess whether” rather than “define”.

d.reason: GARP: “The majority of regulators have adopted the 3LD risk management model to assess cyber-security risk and controls. However, most regulators do not require the implementation of 3LD at regulated entities and do not prescribe precisely how responsibilities should be distributed across the lines, as the expectation is rather for banks themselves to clearly define responsibilities and leave no gaps between the lines.”

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-8 b Q6
questions.question: The CEO of a large, globally active bank headquartered in the UK is reviewing a dispute. The CISO, who reports to the CRO, wants to apply risk-based security controls through a plan-do-check-act cycle so that a new GBP digital payments product can launch on schedule. The CRO has blocked the approach on compliance grounds. Which of the following statements best describes the view in the Basel Committee’s case study on the role of the CISO?

options.text: The reporting line is the emerging good practice among global banks, since placing the CISO under the CRO ensures that compliance considerations take precedence over technological innovation.
The reporting line is common but not ideal, since the CRO’s compliance emphasis can conflict with the CISO’s risk-based approach; some global banks now have the CISO report to the CEO or board.
The reporting line is common but not ideal, so the case study recommends moving the CISO to report to the chief information officer, whose priorities are aligned with security protection.
The reporting line is rare among large banks, since most CISOs at globally active banks already have an independent reporting line to the board of directors through the audit committee.

questions.solution:
UK G-SIB CEO resolving a dispute between a CISO who reports to the CRO and the CRO, who blocks risk-based controls on compliance grounds.

**Concept and theory**

Box 8.2 (Case Study 2) addresses the roles and responsibilities of the **chief information security** **officer (CISO)** in cyber-governance. Its argument runs in steps:

1. **Structure.** A widespread practice among large, globally active banks is a governance structure based on 3LD, in which the CISO is the executive officer responsible for the bank’s cyber-security management.
2. **Purpose.** The CISO acts as a circuit breaker, balancing the firm’s risk appetite with security protection considerations long before digital services or products are introduced or expanded.
3. **Current reporting.** In most cases the CISO reports to the CRO or to the CIO, with no independent reporting line to the CEO or board.
4. **Problem.** CROs typically place more emphasis on compliance than on risk management. When the CISO tries to implement risk-based cyber and IT controls that accommodate innovation through the plan-do-check-act (PDCA) cycle, the CRO may prioritise compliance over the benefits of innovation. The two roles have inherently conflicting priorities, so placing the CISO under the CRO is “not ideal”.
5. **Response.** Some global banks are restructuring the role so that the CISO reports directly to the CEO or board.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem reproduces the case study’s conflict almost exactly: a CISO under the CRO, risk-based controls through PDCA to support an innovation, and a CRO blocking on compliance grounds. The case study’s verdict is that the line is common but not ideal, and the observed remedy is a direct line to the CEO or board. The GBP product detail is context only.

**Fragile fact.** Most CISOs report to the CRO or CIO (no independent line); the CRO line is not ideal; the trend is a direct line to the CEO or board.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Box 8.2 “Case Study 2: Roles and Responsibilities of Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) in Cyber-Governance”. Schweser does not cover this case study; the content is from GARP only. No conflict, but this is a GARP-only point that a condensed source omits.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q6 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It presents the CRO line as the emerging good practice and treats compliance precedence as desirable. The case study says emerging trends indicate the opposite. A would be right only if the question asked for the CRO’s view in the dispute, not the case study’s.

b.reason: It matches each element of Box 8.2: the CRO line is common (“in most cases”), it is “not ideal” because of conflicting priorities and the CRO’s compliance emphasis, and “some global banks are restructuring the CISO role by having the CISO report directly to the CEO or BoD”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** The CIO is the other common reporting line named in the case study (“reports to the CRO or to the CIO”), not the remedy. The remedy is a line to the CEO or board, which is independent of both. C would be right only if the question asked which other line is commonly observed today.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses “in most cases the CISO reports to the CRO or CIO, with no independent reporting line to the CEO or BoD”. It also confuses the CISO with the chief audit executive, whose line runs to the audit committee. D would be right only for a bank that had already completed the restructuring the case study describes.

questions.question:
A working group of HR and operational risk staff at a bank in South Korea is designing a cyber-risk awareness programme. It has listed the following candidate practices:

I. Cyber-security awareness training during each phase of the employment process, from recruitment to termination.

II. Awareness and risk culture expectations that extend to staff and management at all levels, including the board and third-party employees.

III. Awareness requirements confined to IT staff, because a common risk culture across the banking industry is not seen as necessary for sector cyber-resilience.

IV. Non-disclosure clauses within staff agreements.

Which of the practices are consistent with regulatory guidance and requirements observed by the Basel Committee?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
HR and risk working group at a Korean bank selecting practices for a cyber-risk awareness programme.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s “Cyber-Risk Awareness Culture” sub-section starts from a premise: an awareness of cyber-risk by staff at individual banks and a common risk culture across the banking industry are prerequisites for maintaining cyber-resilience in the sector. People are both the first line of detection and a source of insider threat, so culture is a governance tool.

Observed regulatory practices:

| Practice | Detail in GARP |
|---|---|
| Guidance on awareness and culture | For staff and management at all levels, including BoDs and third-party employees (most jurisdictions) |
| Awareness and staffing requirements | Increasing cyber-security awareness and cyber-related staffing at regulated entities |
| Lifecycle training | In some jurisdictions, training during each phase of employment, from recruitment to termination |
| Non-disclosure clauses | Regulated entities may be required to include them within staff agreements |
| Insider threat checks | Screening of new employees; periodic reverification of existing employees (Q14) |
| Common risk culture | Encouraged by the majority of regulators, sufficient to ensure effective cyber-risk management |

**Applying it to this question**

- I: lifecycle training is required in some jurisdictions. Consistent.
- II: guidance covers all levels, including BoDs and third-party employees. Consistent.
- III: confines awareness to IT staff and denies the need for an industry-wide culture. This contradicts both the “all levels” guidance and the “prerequisite” premise. Inconsistent.
- IV: non-disclosure clauses within staff agreements may be required. Consistent.

Consistent set: I, II and IV, which is option C.

**Fragile fact.** Scope of awareness: all levels, including the board and third-party employees; training runs from recruitment to termination.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Risk Awareness Culture”. Schweser (Awareness) says management and the board are responsible for ensuring training and that new employees sign non-disclosure agreements; GARP refers to non-disclosure clauses within staff agreements generally and does not limit them to new joiners. GARP used; the difference is one of compression.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q7 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It rejects IV, typically because the reader files non-disclosure agreements under third-party confidentiality (the outsourcing contracts of LO 49.e) rather than staff agreements. GARP places non-disclosure clauses within staff agreements as an awareness and insider-threat measure. A would be right only if IV referred to confidentiality clauses in service provider contracts.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts III, which reverses the report: awareness must extend to all levels and an industry-wide common risk culture is a prerequisite. B would be right only if III read “extended to all staff, including the board and third-party employees”.

c.reason: Each of I, II and IV is stated in GARP’s “Cyber-Risk Awareness Culture” sub-section, and III contradicts it.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It rejects I, treating awareness training as an induction event. Some jurisdictions require training at each phase from recruitment to termination. D would be right only if the stem asked what all jurisdictions require, since lifecycle training is a “some jurisdictions” practice.

questions.question: An IT examiner at a banking supervisor is benchmarking other jurisdictions before drafting guidance on cyber-security architecture. Which of the following statements best describes the range of practice reported by the Basel Committee?

options.text: In most jurisdictions general requirements for architecture and standards are absent or lack coverage; the US FFIEC handbook has supervisors confirm that network diagrams are current, securely stored and reflect defence in depth.

In most jurisdictions general requirements for architecture and standards are firmly in place; the US FFIEC handbook directs banks to submit their network architecture diagrams to the supervisor for formal annual approval.

In most jurisdictions general requirements for architecture and standards are absent or lack coverage; in Saudi Arabia, cyber-security architecture practices must be certified annually by an external auditor rather than being self-assessed.

In most jurisdictions general requirements for architecture and standards are absent or lack coverage, and no jurisdiction has yet issued substantial supervisory guidance or control considerations for cyber-security architecture.

questions.solution:
IT examiner benchmarking jurisdictions before drafting guidance on cyber-security architecture.

**Concept and theory**

**Cyber-security architecture** is the design of networks and systems so that security controls are layered and consistent (“defence in depth”: several independent layers, so that the failure of one control does not expose the asset). GARP’s “Architecture and Standards” sub-section is short but precise:

- For most jurisdictions, general regulatory requirements for architecture and standards are not in place, or there is a lack of coverage.
- Only a small number of countries specifically highlight control considerations and substantial supervisory guidance for cyber-security architecture.
- **US:** the FFIEC IT Examination Handbook specifies that, when discussing network architecture, supervisors should confirm that the diagrams are current, securely stored and reflective of a defence-in-depth security architecture.
- **Saudi Arabia:** practices covering cyber-security architecture are subject to a periodic self-assessment.

This is the least developed of the five governance areas, which is why it is a favourite target for “most jurisdictions” polarity traps.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options open with a statement on prevalence, then add a jurisdictional example. Prevalence: absent or lacking coverage in most jurisdictions, so B fails at once. Then test the example: A’s FFIEC description matches GARP; C swaps the Saudi practice; D denies that any country has substantial guidance.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and object: under the FFIEC handbook it is the supervisor who confirms that network architecture diagrams are current, securely stored and defence-in-depth; Saudi Arabia uses periodic self-assessment.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Architecture and Standards”. Schweser compresses the FFIEC point to “U.S. regulations require supervisors to ensure content is current and properly stored” and omits the reference to network diagrams and defence in depth; it also describes the Saudi self-assessments as “around cybersecurity” rather than specifically architecture. GARP’s fuller wording is used; this looks like condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q8 of 16.

a.reason: Both halves match GARP: general requirements for architecture and standards are not in place or lack coverage for most jurisdictions, and the FFIEC handbook directs supervisors to confirm that network architecture diagrams are current, securely stored and reflective of defence in depth.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says requirements are firmly in place in most jurisdictions and turns the FFIEC examiner check into an annual approval by the supervisor. B would be right only for a jurisdiction-specific question about a regime with detailed architecture rules, which the report says are rare.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It replaces Saudi Arabia’s periodic self-assessment with external certification, borrowing an assurance mechanism from elsewhere in the chapter (independent audit reports used for third parties under LO 49.e). C would be right only if the report had described an external audit requirement for Saudi architecture practices.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** “No jurisdiction” overstates the gap. A small number of countries do highlight control considerations and provide substantial supervisory guidance, the US being the example. D would be right if “no jurisdiction” were replaced with “only a small number of countries”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is mapping how jurisdictions regulate the roles and responsibilities of IT and information security staff. The consultant has identified four regulatory approaches.

| Code | Approach to IT and information security staff roles and responsibilities |
|---|---|
| P | Regulations issued specifically to address IT staff’s roles and responsibilities |
| Q | Requirements embedded in the jurisdiction’s global governance framework |
| R | Requirements encompassed by those for the board of directors and senior management |
| S | Requirements included in the national cyber-security strategy |

Which of the following pairings is consistent with the Basel Committee’s findings?

options.text: Switzerland: S; South Africa: Q
Argentina: R; Mexico: P
Switzerland: Q; South Africa: S
United States: P; Japan: R

questions.solution:
Risk consultant mapping jurisdictions to four ways of regulating the roles and responsibilities of IT and information security staff.

**Concept and theory**

Under “Cyber-Security Workforce”, GARP notes that jurisdictions diverge in how they regulate the roles and responsibilities of IT and information security staff. Four patterns are reported:

| Code | Pattern | Jurisdictions named |
|---|---|---|
| P | Regulations specifically addressing IT staff’s roles and responsibilities | Argentina, Australia, the EU, Japan, Saudi Arabia |
| Q | Regulations embedded in the jurisdiction’s global governance framework | Switzerland |
| R | Requirements encompassed by those for the BoD and senior management | Mexico, the US, Saudi Arabia |
| S | Included in the national cyber-security strategy | South Africa |

Why the divergence? Some regimes write role-level rules for IT staff (P). Others treat IT roles as a by-product of top-level accountability (R): if the board and senior management are responsible for cyber-governance, they must define IT and security roles. Switzerland folds the matter into its general governance framework (Q), and South Africa handles it at national policy level (S).

**Applying it to this question**

Check each pairing against the table:

- A: Switzerland is Q (not S); South Africa is S (not Q). Both swapped.
- B: Argentina is P (not R); Mexico is R (not P). Both swapped.
- C: Switzerland Q, South Africa S. Both correct.
- D: the US is R (not P); Japan is P (not R). Both swapped.

**Fragile fact.** US and Mexico: IT staff roles sit inside board and senior management requirements; Switzerland: global governance framework; South Africa: national cyber-security strategy.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Security Workforce”. Conflict noted: GARP lists Saudi Arabia under both P and R, whereas Schweser lists Saudi Arabia only under P and names only the US and Mexico under R. The question avoids Saudi Arabia for this reason. On the four jurisdictions used, GARP and Schweser agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q9 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It exchanges the two single-country patterns (Q and S). A would be right if the jurisdictions were reversed: Switzerland: Q; South Africa: S.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It exchanges the specific-regulation pattern (P) with the board-level pattern (R) for Argentina and Mexico. B would be right as “Argentina: P; Mexico: R”.

c.reason: GARP: “Sometimes regulations are embedded in a jurisdiction’s global governance framework, such as those issued in Switzerland ... In South Africa, such regulations are included in the national cyber-security strategy.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It makes the same P and R exchange for the US and Japan. A US reader may expect detailed IT staff rules, but GARP places the US among jurisdictions whose IT and security role requirements are encompassed by BoD and senior management requirements. D would be right as “United States: R; Japan: P”.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a banking group with subsidiaries in three North American jurisdictions is preparing a report on how each home supervisor treats cyber-security strategy. The group’s balance sheet data are shown below.

| Subsidiary | Reporting currency | Total assets (bn) |
|---|---|---|
| United States | USD | 214.6 |
| Canada | CAD | 97.3 |
| Mexico | MXN | 1250.0 |

Which of the following statements should the CCO include in the report as accurate?

options.text: Canada’s self-assessment guidance seeks to determine whether a bank has a cyber-security strategy aligned with its business strategy and implementation plan, while the US FFIEC handbook does not specifically address one.

The US FFIEC IT Examination Handbook seeks to determine whether a bank has a cybersecurity strategy aligned with its business strategy and implementation plan, while Canada’s guidance does not specifically address one.

Mexico’s supervisors operate practices focused on evaluating banks’ cyber-security strategies, although Mexico has issued no regulation that directs its banks to develop IT security strategies of any kind.

All three supervisors require a standalone, board-approved cyber-security strategy, since a standalone cyber-security strategy is the common supervisory expectation across Basel Committee jurisdictions.

questions.solution:
CCO of a North American banking group reporting how the US, Canadian and Mexican supervisors treat cyber-security strategy.

**Concept and theory**

The headline finding (Q2) is that a cyber-security strategy is expected but not required. GARP adds that “a variety of approaches can also be observed within regions”, and gives three North American examples:

| Jurisdiction | Practice on cyber-security strategy |
|---|---|
| US | The FFIEC IT Examination Handbook does not specifically address the development of a cyber-security strategy |
| Canada | Self-assessment guidance attempts to determine whether a regulated institution has established a cyber-security strategy aligned with its business strategy and implementation plan |
| Mexico | No supervisory practices focused on cyber-security strategy, but regulations direct banks to develop IT security strategies |

The lesson is that even neighbouring jurisdictions sit at different points: Canada looks for a cyber-specific strategy, the US relies on its general IT examination framework, and Mexico regulates at the level of IT security strategy.

**Applying it to this question**

The balance sheet table (assets in USD, CAD and MXN) is irrelevant: the treatment of strategy depends on the supervisor, not on size or currency. Match each option to the three-row table:

- A: Canada checks alignment with business strategy; FFIEC does not specifically address it. Correct.
- B: swaps the US and Canada.
- C: reverses both halves of the Mexico finding.
- D: claims a standalone cyber strategy is required everywhere.

**Fragile fact.** Canada checks for a cyber strategy aligned with business strategy; the US FFIEC handbook does not specifically address one; Mexico regulates IT security strategies but has no cyber-strategy supervisory practice.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Security Strategy Is Expected But Not Required”. Conflict noted: Schweser says “neither U.S. nor Mexican regulations specifically focus on the development of cybersecurity strategies”, which blurs GARP’s distinction that Mexico has no supervisory practices on cyber strategy while its regulations do direct banks to develop IT security strategies. Resolved from GARP. This looks like condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q10 of 16.

a.reason: GARP: “while the FFIEC IT Examination Handbook in the US does not specifically address the development of a cyber-security strategy, Canada’s self assessment guidance attempts to determine whether a regulated financial institution has established a cyber-security strategy aligned with the institution’s business strategy and implementation plan.”

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes Canada’s practice to the US handbook and the US position to Canada. B would be right if the jurisdiction names were exchanged back.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says Mexico has no supervisory practices focused on cyber-security strategy but has issued regulations directing banks to develop IT security strategies. C reverses both. It would be right as “Mexico has no supervisory practices focused on cyber-security strategy, but its regulations direct banks to develop IT security strategies.”

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It asserts a universal standalone cyber-security strategy requirement. The common expectation is a board-approved information security strategy; most regulators do not require a standalone cyber-security strategy. D would be right if “standalone, board-approved cyber-security strategy” were replaced with “board-approved information security strategy”.

questions.question:
A board member at a bank in the Gulf region notes that the local authority compels banks to formulate their own cyber-security strategies while it develops its own supervisory practices for implementing cyber-security strategy. The CRO prepares the following comments for the board:

I. The authority is combining two of the three observed approaches, which is consistent with the Basel Committee’s description of the approaches as non-mutually exclusive.

II. Under the institution-led approach, the regulator reviews a bank’s cyber-security strategy as part of its assessment of the bank’s overall risk management practices.

III. Because the authority sets cyber-security strategy requirements, the Basel findings imply that the jurisdiction must have a homogeneous banking system.

IV. The approach described as prevalent in Europe would instead involve examining whether banks have an IT strategy and the accompanying security provisions.

Which of the CRO’s comments are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
CRO preparing board comments on an authority that compels banks to write their own cyber strategies while developing its own supervisory practices.

**Concept and theory**

The three approaches to enforcing cyber-security strategy requirements (Q3) are described in GARP as non-mutually exclusive. A jurisdiction can use more than one at once. GARP’s footnote gives the example: the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) applied the first two approaches by compelling financial institutions to formulate their own cyber-security strategies while it developed supervisory practices for implementing cyber-security strategy.

Recall the content of each approach:

1. Authority-set requirements (sector-specific or cross-sector); common in emerging markets with relatively homogeneous banking systems.
2. Institution-designed strategies under principles-based risk management; the regulator reviews them as part of its assessment of overall risk management practices.
3. Examination of whether entities have an IT strategy and accompanying security provisions; prevalent in Europe.

Note the qualifiers “common” and “prevalent”. They describe where an approach is typically found; they are not necessary conditions.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: the authority is combining approaches 1 and 2, as SAMA did; this is possible because the approaches are non-mutually exclusive. Accurate.
- II: describes approach 2 correctly. Accurate.
- III: turns “common in” into “must have”. An association is not a necessary condition. Inaccurate.
- IV: describes approach 3 correctly. Accurate.

Accurate set: I, II and IV, which is option D.

**Fragile fact.** The three approaches are non-mutually exclusive; SAMA combined approaches 1 and 2. “Common in” and “prevalent in” describe typical settings, not requirements.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Security Strategy Is Expected But Not Required” (three approaches and footnote 11 on SAMA). Schweser lists the three approaches but omits “non-mutually exclusive” and the SAMA footnote; those points are from GARP only. No factual conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q11 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It omits IV, often because the reader thinks the European approach looks for a cyber-specific strategy. GARP says it looks for an IT strategy and accompanying security provisions. A would be right if IV had said “cyber-security strategy” instead of “IT strategy”.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It accepts III, which upgrades a typical association (“common approach in emerging market economies with relative homogeneity”) into a necessary condition. B would be right only if the report had said the approach is used only where banking systems are homogeneous.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It rejects I, treating the approaches as alternatives so that combining two is inconsistent with the findings. GARP explicitly calls them non-mutually exclusive, and SAMA combined the first two. C would be right only if the report described the approaches as mutually exclusive.

d.reason: GARP describes the three approaches as “non-mutually exclusive” (I), describes approach 2 as regulators reviewing institutions’ strategies “as part of their assessment of an institution’s overall risk management practices” (II), and describes approach 3, “prevalent in Europe”, as examining whether entities have “an IT strategy and the accompanying security provisions” (IV).

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the annual cyber inspection plan of a banking supervisor in Australia. The plan allocates the supervisor’s specialist hours across the lines of defence at the banks it supervises as follows.

| Line of defence | Planned hours | Share (%) |
|---|---|---|
| First line (business and IT operations) | 1080 | 45 |
| Second line (risk and compliance) | 960 | 40 |
| Third line (internal audit) | 360 | 15 |
| Total | 2400 | 100 |

The plan sets no expectation on the reporting line from the chief audit executive to the audit committee. Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the Basel Committee’s findings?

options.text: The allocation is atypical across jurisdictions, since supervisors usually concentrate on the third line because internal audit provides the independent assurance in the model.
The allocation is typical across jurisdictions, and the relatively light coverage of the third line could hamper the effectiveness of the 3LD checks and balances model.
The allocation is typical across jurisdictions, and the gap is minor because most jurisdictions have set specific expectations on the reporting line from the chief audit executive.
The allocation is typical across jurisdictions, and it shows that supervisory practices for assessing the degree of 3LD implementation have largely converged.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant interpreting an Australian supervisor’s allocation of cyber inspection hours across the three lines of defence.

**Concept and theory**

Because most regulators do not prescribe how 3LD should be implemented (Q5), supervisory practices for assessing the degree of 3LD implementation vary widely. Two further findings concern the third line:

- There appears to be a greater supervisory focus on the first and second lines than on the third line across jurisdictions, which could hamper the effectiveness of the 3LD checks and balances model.
- Only a few jurisdictions have formulated specific expectations on the independent reporting line from the chief audit executive (CAE) to the audit committee of the BoD.

Why does under-supervision of the third line matter? The model works as checks and balances: the third line gives the board independent assurance that the first two lines are working. If supervisors rarely test internal audit, and few set expectations on the CAE’s independent line to the audit committee, the independence of that assurance is not verified, and a weakness in the top layer can go unnoticed.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the table. The intermediate figures:

Lines 1 and 2 share = 45% + 40% = 85%, Line 3 share $= \frac{360}{2400} =$ 15%.

So the plan puts 85% of hours on lines 1 and 2 and 15% on line 3. This matches the observed pattern (greater focus on lines 1 and 2). The absence of a CAE reporting-line expectation is also typical, since only a few jurisdictions have one. The conclusion must therefore be “typical” plus “could hamper checks and balances”. The total of 2,400 hours is not needed.

**Fragile fact.** Supervisory focus: lines 1 and 2 more than line 3, which could hamper the checks and balances. CAE to audit committee expectations exist in only a few jurisdictions.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Variety of Supervisory Approaches Regarding the Second and Third Lines of Defence (3LD)”. Schweser: “since regulatory supervision tends to focus on the first and second lines of defense, this could reduce the effectiveness of the model. Only a few jurisdictions have guidance about the independent reporting of the chief audit executive and the audit committee.” Consistent. Schweser omits “vary widely”; that point is from GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q12 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says supervisors usually concentrate on the third line. The report finds the opposite. A would be right only if the question asked where supervisory focus should increase to strengthen the model.

b.reason: GARP: “there appears to be a greater supervisory focus on the first and second lines of defence than on the third line across jurisdictions, which could hamper the effectiveness of the 3LD checks and balances model.”

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns “only a few jurisdictions” into “most jurisdictions” for the CAE reporting-line expectation, and so dismisses the gap. C would be right only if CAE-line expectations were widespread, which would partly offset light third-line inspection.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It claims convergence. GARP says supervisory practices for assessing 3LD implementation “vary widely”. D would be right if “largely converged” were replaced with “vary widely”.

questions.question: A supervisor at an emerging market central bank is drafting a principles-based cyber-security framework modelled on the approach of the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) described in the Basel Committee’s case study on CISOs. Which of the following provisions is consistent with that model?

options.text: Banks must have a cyber-security function independent of IT, with separate budgets and staff evaluations, reporting directly to the CEO or managing director or to senior management of the control function.

Banks must place the cyber-security function within the IT function under the chief information officer, so that security budgets and staff evaluations are fully aligned with IT project budgets and delivery goals.
Banks must complete a single self-assessment against the framework at the licensing stage, after which the supervisor relies on incident reports instead of on-site and off-site review of compliance.
Banks must have the CISO report to the chief audit executive, so that the third line of defence directly manages day-to-day cyber-security operations and chairs the cyber-security committee.

Emerging market supervisor drafting a cyber-security framework modelled on SAMA’s approach in the CISO case study.

**Concept and theory**

The second half of Box 8.2 describes how the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) builds roles and responsibilities into a principles-based cyber-security framework with which financial institutions are mandated to comply:

| Element | What SAMA requires |
|---|---|
| CISO responsibilities | Defined across the cyber-security committee, security strategy, security architecture, risk-based cyber-security solutions, operational security, etc, so that controls apply throughout the institution |
| Independent cyber function | A cyber-security function independent from the IT function, with separate budgets and staff evaluations |
| Reporting line | The cyber-security function reports directly to the CEO or managing director, or to senior management of the control function |
| Assurance | Periodic self-assessments against the framework, subject to SAMA review on-site and off-site to determine compliance and cyber-security maturity |

The IT function builds and runs systems under delivery and budget pressure; if security sits inside it, security budgets and staff appraisals can be subordinated to delivery goals. The stem asks which provision fits the SAMA model. questions.question: An operational risk manager at a mid-sized commercial bank in China is preparing a paper for the risk committee on people-related cyber-risk practices that regulators have adopted. Which of the following statements should the manager include as accurate?

options.text: Regulators in some jurisdictions assess each bank’s cyber-risk appetite, considering factors such as the bank’s liquidity position, its capital ratio and its external credit rating.
Some jurisdictions view cyber-security as a critical business function, because a cyber-attack could cause serious reputational damage to an institution, though not its insolvency.
To mitigate insider threats, some jurisdictions require screening and background verification of new employees and mandatory reverification of existing employees at regular intervals.
Regulators that assess whether staff understand their responsibilities and are suitable for their roles limit the assessment to permanent employees, excluding contractors and third-party vendors.

questions.solution:
Operational risk manager at a Chinese bank selecting accurate statements on people-related cyber-risk practices for the risk committee.

**Concept and theory**

The second half of GARP’s “Cyber-Risk Awareness Culture” sub-section turns from training to people controls and to how regulators view cyber-risk in the bank’s overall risk profile:

- **Insider threat controls.** To mitigate insider threats, some jurisdictions require new employees to complete a screening and background verification process, while existing employees undergo a mandatory reverification process at regular intervals. A one-time check at hiring cannot catch a change in an employee’s circumstances, so periodic reverification closes the gap.
- **Suitability and responsibilities.** In some jurisdictions, regulators assess whether banks have robust processes and controls so that their employees, contractors and third-party vendors understand their responsibilities, are suitable for their roles and have the requisite skills, to reduce the risk of theft, fraud or misuse of facilities.
- **Cyber-risk appetite.** In some jurisdictions, regulators assess each bank’s cyber-risk appetite, considering the bank’s business model, core business strategy and key technologies.
- **Critical business function.** Some jurisdictions view cyber-security as a critical business function, because a cyber-attack could lead to the insolvency of individual entities or even to widespread disruption of the entire sector.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option takes one of these four points and changes something. Check the deciding detail: A changes the appetite factors; B caps the impact below insolvency; C keeps both halves of the insider-threat control (new hires screened, existing staff reverified periodically); D narrows the population to permanent staff. Only C is unaltered.

**Fragile fact.** New employees: screening and background checks; existing employees: periodic reverification. Appetite factors: business model, core strategy, key technologies.

**Reference**

LO 49.b: “Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.3, “Cyber-Risk Awareness Culture”. Schweser mentions screening and background checks for new employees and periodic reverification for existing employees, consistent with GARP. Schweser omits the cyber-risk appetite assessment, the critical business function view and the contractor and vendor population; those points are from GARP only. No factual conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-8 b, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It replaces the cyber-risk appetite factors (business model, core business strategy, key technologies) with financial-strength measures that belong to prudential capital and liquidity assessment. A would be right if the factors were “business model, core business strategy and key technologies”.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It denies the very reason the report gives for treating cyber-security as a critical business function: an attack could lead to insolvency of individual entities or wider disruption of the sector. B would be right if “though not its insolvency” were replaced with “or even its insolvency”.

c.reason: GARP: “To mitigate insider threats, some jurisdictions require new employees to complete a screening and background verification process, while existing employees undergo a mandatory reverification process at regular intervals.”

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops contractors and third-party vendors from the population assessed. GARP names employees, contractors and third-party vendors. D would be right if the population were widened to include contractors and vendors.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a bank in Singapore is reviewing the Basel Committee’s case study on frameworks for professional training in cyber-security and certification programmes. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The Bank of England’s CBEST scheme accredits individual penetration testers, and it has replaced the certifications offered to individuals by the Council for Registered Ethical Security Testers.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore requires financial institutions to have a comprehensive technology risk and cyber-security training programme for the board, so that it can exercise its oversight function.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Professional Development Programme is a stand-alone scheme, separate from its Cybersecurity Fortification Initiative, that seeks to increase the supply of qualified professionals.
Japan’s Center for Financial Industry Information Systems serves as a model for jurisdictions moving from risk-based, incentive-compatible regulation towards more prescriptive regulatory models.

questions.solution:

Box 8.3 (Case Study 3) describes four frameworks through which public authorities develop cybersecurity skills. It belongs to this LO because workforce competence, including the board’s competence to oversee cyber-risk, is one of the five governance areas.

| Framework | Key features in GARP |
|---|---|
| FISC (Japan) | Public-private partnership founded in 1984; exchanges staff between supervisors, banks and IT security vendors; produced the FISC Guidelines used by FSA and BoJ examiners; a model for jurisdictions moving from prescriptive to more risk-based and incentive-compatible regulation. Korea’s FSI (2015) has the same structure. |
| Bank of England | CBEST accreditation for suppliers of threat intelligence and penetration testing services, in addition to CREST accreditation for individuals (CCTIM, CCSAM, CCSAS). |
| MAS (Singapore) | Requires financial institutions to have a comprehensive technology risk and cyber-security training programme for the BoD, which may include periodic briefings by in-house or external specialists, so that the board can competently exercise its oversight function and appraise the cyber-resilience programme. |
