questions.question: A senior analyst in the group ML/FT risk management function of a Dubai-headquartered bank is preparing guidance after a branch reported suspicious activity on a corporate account. Which of the following statements in the draft guidance is least accurate?

options.text: The group function should evaluate the potential risks posed by activity reported by the branch and, where appropriate, assess the group-wide risk of that customer or category.
The group function should have procedures to ascertain whether other branches or subsidiaries hold accounts for the same customer, including any related or affiliated parties.
The head office should be able to require all branches and subsidiaries to search their files against specified lists of suspected individuals or organisations and report matches.
Branches and subsidiaries should refer all requests from local law enforcement agencies and FIUs to the home supervisor rather than respond to them under their own domestic laws.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst in a Dubai bank’s group ML/FT risk function identifying the least accurate statement in post-STR guidance.

**Concept and theory**

Once a branch reports suspicious activity, the question becomes whether the risk is local or group-wide. The guidance gives the group’s overall ML/FT risk management function the following tasks and tools:

| Task or tool | Content |
|---|---|
| Evaluate | Evaluate potential risks posed by activity reported by branches and subsidiaries and, where appropriate, assess the group-wide risks of a customer or category |
| Find linked accounts | Procedures to ascertain whether other branches or subsidiaries hold accounts for the same customer, including related or affiliated parties |
| Escalate | Policies for higher-risk or potentially suspicious global relationships, including escalation and restricting or closing accounts |
| Respond to authorities | The bank and its branches and subsidiaries should, in accordance with their respective domestic laws, be responsive to requests from law enforcement agencies, supervisory authorities or FIUs |
| Search | The head office should be able to require all branches and subsidiaries to search files against specified lists or requests and report matches |

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C each restate one row. D instructs offices to send all local law enforcement and FIU requests to the home supervisor rather than respond themselves, which contradicts the duty of each office to respond in accordance with its own domestic laws.

**Fragile fact.** Each office responds to law enforcement, supervisor and FIU requests under its own domestic law; the head office can order group-wide file searches.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Group-Wide Information-Sharing (paragraphs 79 to 80). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser does not reproduce these paragraphs.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q15 of 18.

a.reason: **True statement.** Accurate restatement of paragraph 79 on evaluating activity reported by branches and subsidiaries. It would be the answer if the stem asked for the most accurate statement.

b.reason: **True statement.** Accurate restatement of paragraph 79 on ascertaining whether other offices hold accounts for the same customer, including related or affiliated parties. A reader who forgets the “related or affiliated parties” extension may doubt it, but it is in the source.

c.reason: **True statement.** Accurate restatement of paragraph 80 on the head office’s power to require all branches and subsidiaries to search their files and report matches. A reader who thinks subsidiaries are outside head-office instructions (scope error) would wrongly select it.

d.reason: D is the least accurate statement, built by role misassignment. GARP paragraph 80: “a bank and its branches and subsidiaries should, in accordance with their respective domestic laws, be responsive to requests from law enforcement agencies, supervisory authorities or FIUs for information about customers”.

questions.question: The head of onboarding at the Singapore subsidiary of a European banking group receives customers referred by a sister bank in the same group. The sister bank is subject to the same AML/CFT standards as the subsidiary, and the application of those standards is supervised at group level. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with the Basel Committee guidance?

options.text: Rely on the sister bank’s CDD without obtaining the customer information, because group-level supervision makes collecting that information unnecessary.
Place no more reliance on the sister bank than on an unaffiliated introducer, because membership of the same group is irrelevant to reliance decisions.
Consider placing a higher level of reliance on the sister bank, while still obtaining the customer information from it in case reporting to an FIU is needed.
Place a higher level of reliance on the sister bank even if it became subject to less strict local standards, because group membership alone is sufficient.

questions.solution:
Head of onboarding at a group’s Singapore subsidiary deciding how far to rely on a sister bank introducer.

**Concept and theory**

Q4 covered the general reliance rule: never rely on an introducer subject to less strict standards. Within a group, the guidance goes further. A bank “may rely on an introducer that is part of the same financial group and could consider placing a higher level of reliance on the information provided by this introducer”, subject to two conditions and one obligation:

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| Condition 1 | The introducer is subject to the same standards as the bank |
| Condition 2 | The application of these requirements is supervised at group level |
| Obligation | The bank still obtains the customer information from the referring bank, because it may be required to be reported to FIUs if a transaction involving the referred customer is found to be suspicious |

The logic is that common standards plus group-level supervision justify more trust, but the bank still needs the data itself in order to meet its own reporting duties.

**Applying it to this question**

The sister bank is in the same group, under the same standards, and supervised at group level, so both conditions hold. The subsidiary may consider a higher level of reliance, but must still obtain the customer information.

**Fragile fact.** Same group plus same standards plus group-level supervision allows higher reliance, but the bank still obtains the customer information for possible FIU reporting.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraph 69). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not mention the same-group higher-reliance treatment or the obligation to obtain customer information; content is taken from GARP. No conflict in direction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q16 of 18.

a.reason: **Dropped term.** It drops the obligation to obtain the customer information. Group-level supervision does not remove the need to hold data that may have to be reported to FIUs. It would be correct only if the stem asked about repeating the CDD procedures, which higher reliance can reduce.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It denies any benefit from group membership. The guidance says the bank could consider placing a higher level of reliance on a same-group introducer that meets the conditions. It would be correct if the sister bank were not supervised at group level.

c.reason: GARP paragraph 69 permits a higher level of reliance on a same-group introducer subject to the same standards with group-level supervision, and adds that the bank “should ensure, however, that it obtains customer information from the referring bank . . . as this information may be required to be reported to FIUs”.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops Condition 1. If the sister bank became subject to less strict standards, the general rule in paragraph 69 would bar reliance altogether. It would be correct only if “less strict” were replaced by “the same”.

questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 c Q17
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a CAD-reporting banking group is reviewing how the group manages accounts that its branch in Country M has flagged as representing heightened risk. Which of the following best describes the practice the group should follow for such accounts?

options.text: Integrate information on the customer, its beneficial owners and the funds involved, and complement local monitoring with robust information-sharing with the head office.
Integrate information on the customer and its beneficial owners, leaving the funds involved to the local office, because tracing funds is a host-country matter.
Replace local monitoring with head-office monitoring for such accounts, because local offices should not maintain their own monitoring of heightened-risk accounts.
Share information on such accounts with other branches only, because sharing with the head office is reserved for accounts that are already the subject of a filed STR.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a CAD-reporting group reviewing how accounts flagged as heightened risk by a foreign branch should be managed.

**Concept and theory**

Two complementary layers manage accounts that may represent heightened risk:

1. **Local monitoring.** Regardless of location, each office should establish and maintain effective monitoring policies and procedures appropriate to the risks in the jurisdiction and in the bank.
2. **Information-sharing.** Local monitoring should be complemented by a robust process of information-sharing with the head office and, if appropriate, with other branches and subsidiaries, regarding accounts and activity that may represent heightened risk.

To manage the ML/FT risk from such accounts, the bank should integrate the information based not only on the customer but also on its knowledge of both the beneficial owners of the customer and the funds involved. Each of the three elements answers a different question: who holds the account, who ultimately controls it, and where the money comes from and goes.

**Applying it to this question**

The Country M branch has flagged heightened-risk accounts. The correct practice integrates all three information elements and keeps both layers: local monitoring continues, and is complemented by sharing with the head office.

**Fragile fact.** Integrate three elements: customer, beneficial owners and funds; and local monitoring is complemented, not replaced, by sharing with the head office.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. GARP Chapter 10, Section 10.3, Consolidated AML/CFT Policies and Procedures (paragraphs 72 to 73). No GARP vs Schweser conflict; Schweser’s key concepts list the same three elements (“beneficial owners of the customer (if one exists)”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q17 of 18.

a.reason: GARP paragraph 72 requires local monitoring “complemented by a robust process of information-sharing with the head office”, and paragraph 73 requires the bank to “integrate this information based not only on the customer but also on its knowledge of both the beneficial owners of the customer and the funds involved”.

b.reason: **Dropped term.** It drops the funds involved from the integration, leaving them to the local office. Paragraph 73 lists the funds involved as one of the three elements to integrate at group level. It would be correct only if the stem had asked about customer identification alone.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It removes local monitoring. Paragraph 72 says each office, regardless of location, should maintain effective monitoring; sharing complements it rather than replacing it. It would be correct only if “replace” were changed to “complement”.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It excludes the head office and adds an STR precondition that does not exist. Sharing on heightened-risk accounts is with the head office and, if appropriate, other offices, and does not wait for an STR. Sharing with other branches is permitted only as an addition (“if appropriate”) to sharing with the head office, and no STR precondition exists; D would be correct only if the stem asked which additional offices may receive the information and the STR clause were removed.

questions.reading: ORR-10: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.topic: Sound Management of Risks related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-10 c Q18
questions.question: A newly appointed bank supervisor in a host country is preparing the supervisory plan for the local subsidiary of a foreign banking group. Which of the following statements most accurately describes the supervisor’s expected role in a cross-border context?

options.text: Supervisors should apply the home jurisdiction’s requirements in all cases, because the group-wide AML/CFT policies are set by the head office.
Supervisors should ensure the stricter of the two jurisdictions’ requirements is applied and verify group-wide policy compliance during on-site inspections.
Supervisors should carry out the group audit of AML/CFT procedures themselves, rather than ensure that the group has its own group audit in place.
Supervisors should be classified as “third parties” in countries that restrict disclosure of customer information to third parties, to protect confidentiality.

questions.solution:
Newly appointed host-country supervisor preparing the supervisory plan for the local subsidiary of a foreign banking group.

**Concept and theory**

Banks implement group-wide AML/CFT; supervisors check it. The Schweser notes for this LO list the supervisors’ expected role. Supervisors should comply with FATF Recommendation 26 and apply the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision to AML/CFT supervision, set out supervisory expectations for banks’ policies, and adopt a risk-based approach. In the cross-border context the relevant duties are:

| Duty | Content |
|---|---|
| Stricter standard | Make sure the stricter of the two jurisdictions’ requirements is applied |
| On-site verification | Verify a bank’s compliance with group-wide AML/CFT policies and procedures during on-site inspections |
| Home-host cooperation | Extend full cooperation and assistance to home-country supervisors assessing a bank’s overseas compliance with group-wide policies |
| Group audit | Ensure there is a group audit and determine the scope and frequency of audits of the group’s AML/CFT procedures |
| Confidentiality | Ensure the confidentiality of customer information provided to supervisors, and make sure supervisors are not classified as “third parties” where disclosure to third parties is restricted |

The last point matters because if supervisors were treated as third parties, bank secrecy rules could block them from seeing the customer information they need.

**Applying it to this question**

The host supervisor is planning supervision of a foreign group’s subsidiary. Option B combines two listed duties: ensuring the stricter standard and verifying group-wide compliance on site. Each other option corrupts one duty.

**Fragile fact.** Supervisors must not be classified as third parties; they ensure a group audit exists (and set its scope and frequency) rather than perform it.

**Reference**

LO 51.c: Explain practices for managing ML/FT risks in a group-wide and cross-border context. Schweser notes, LO 51.c, Role of Supervisors. This content is from the condensed Schweser source only: the GARP chapter as printed reproduces the guidance for banks and banking groups (Sections 10.1 to 10.3) but not the part addressed to supervisors, so the wording may compress the original Basel framing. GARP does state the bank-level counterpart, that offices apply the higher standard of the two (paragraph 64), consistent with this answer.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-10 c, where it is Q18 of 18.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It replaces “the stricter of the two” with “the home jurisdiction’s in all cases”. The home rule applies only when it is the stricter one. It would be correct only if the home jurisdiction’s requirements were stricter than the host’s.

b.reason: The Schweser notes for LO 51.c list among supervisors’ duties: “Make sure the stricter of the two jurisdictions’ requirements is applied” and “Verify a bank’s compliance with group-wide AML/CFT policies and procedures during on-site inspections.”

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It has the supervisor perform the group audit. The supervisor’s role is to ensure that there is a group audit and to determine its scope and frequency; the audit itself is performed by the bank’s audit function (internal audit as third line, possibly supported by external auditors). It would be correct if “carry out” were replaced by “ensure there is”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says supervisors should be classified as third parties. The duty is the reverse: make sure supervisors are not classified as third parties where disclosure to third parties is restricted, so that secrecy rules do not block supervisory access. Confidentiality is protected separately, by supervisors keeping the information confidential.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q1
questions.question:
The head of financial crime compliance at a UK building society is preparing a briefing note for newly hired analysts on how financial crime is defined and where it sits in the Basel operational risk taxonomy. A draft contains the following statements:

I. Under the FCA Handbook definition, financial crime includes offences involving handling the proceeds of crime and the financing of terrorism, as well as fraud or dishonesty and market misconduct.

II. Under the FCA Handbook definition, an act committed abroad counts as an offence only if it is also an offence in the jurisdiction where it took place.

III. Internal fraud and external fraud are the first two Basel event types, whereas money laundering and terrorism financing relate to the Clients, Products, and Business Practices event type.

IV. Money laundering and terrorism financing are classified in the Basel external fraud event type, because they are carried out by parties outside the bank.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Head of financial crime compliance at a UK building society auditing four statements on the FCA definition of financial crime and its Basel mapping.

**Concept and theory**

Financial crime is an umbrella term. The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Handbook defines it as any kind of criminal conduct relating to money or to financial services or markets, including any offence involving: (a) fraud or dishonesty; (b) misconduct in, or misuse of information relating to, a financial market; (c) handling the proceeds of crime; or (d) the financing of terrorism. The Handbook adds a jurisdictional rule: “offence” includes an act or omission that would be an offence if it had taken place in the United Kingdom. The test is therefore anchored on UK law, not on the law of the place where the act happened.

GARP reads the four limbs as follows: limbs (a) and (b) cover internal and external fraud, limb (c) is money laundering and limb (d) is terrorism financing. The definitions matter for control design because each family of risk sits in a different place in the Basel operational risk taxonomy and is owned by different control frameworks.

| Risk | FCA limb | Basel event type |
|---|---|---|
| Internal fraud | (a), (b) | Event type 1: Internal fraud |
| External fraud | (a), (b) | Event type 2: External fraud |
| Money laundering | (c) | Clients, Products, and Business Practices |
| Terrorism financing | (d) | Clients, Products, and Business Practices |

The logic of the CPBP mapping is that it is a breach, for any organisation, to participate in or be involved in handling the proceeds of crime or funds aimed at financing terrorism. The loss to the bank comes from its own failure in dealing with clients, not from being defrauded by an outsider.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I lists the four FCA limbs correctly: true. Statement II reverses the jurisdictional anchor: the FCA test asks whether the act would be an offence if it had taken place in the UK, not whether it is an offence where it occurred: false. Statement III restates GARP’s mapping exactly: true.

Statement IV places money laundering and terrorism financing in external fraud, which contradicts GARP’s CPBP mapping: false. Only I and III survive.

**Fragile fact.** Money laundering and terrorism financing map to Basel CPBP, not to external fraud; and the FCA “offence” test asks whether the act would be an offence if done in the UK.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Context and Scope: Definition of Financial Crime; Definition of Internal Fraud. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says only that internal and external fraud, money laundering and terrorism financing are covered by the Basel definition of operational risk; GARP is more specific and maps money laundering and terrorism financing to CPBP. Resolved from GARP; Schweser’s wording is a compression, not a contradiction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q1 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts Statement II, which changes the condition in the FCA definition from “would be an offence if it had taken place in the UK” to “is an offence where it took place”. It would be correct only if the stem asked about a definition anchored on the law of the place of the act, which is not the FCA’s wording.

b.reason: GARP states that financial crime covers internal and external fraud (points a and b) alongside money laundering (point c) and terrorism financing (point d), that internal and external fraud are the first two Basel event types, and that money laundering and terrorism financing relate to the CPBP category.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts Statement IV, which attributes money laundering and terrorism financing to the neighbouring external fraud event type because the actors are outside the bank. GARP maps them to CPBP. Option C would only be right if the question asked about a case where a third party defrauds the bank of its own assets, which is external fraud.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It includes Statement III correctly but also accepts Statement II, the jurisdictional reversal. It would be correct only if the FCA definition anchored the offence on the foreign jurisdiction.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q2
questions.question:
An operational risk analyst at a Singapore private bank is classifying four recent incidents into the Basel internal fraud subcategories before they are entered in the loss database.

| Event | Description | Loss (SGD m) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A relationship manager knowingly executes a transaction type that is outside his authorised mandate; the trade closes without loss | 0.00 |
| 2 | A back-office clerk embezzles funds from dormant client accounts | 0.40 |
| 3 | An employee files a discrimination claim against her line manager | 0.15 |
| 4 | A trader intentionally mismarks illiquid positions to hide losses | 1.20 |

Which of the following classifications is most accurate?

options.text: Event 1 is not an internal fraud event, because no monetary loss was suffered by the bank.
Event 3 is an internal fraud event, because it involves at least one internal party.
Events 2 and 4 both belong to the “theft and fraud” subcategory of internal fraud.
Events 1 and 4 both belong to the “unauthorized activities” subcategory of internal fraud.

questions.solution:
Operational risk analyst at a Singapore private bank classifying four incidents into the Basel internal fraud subcategories.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel Committee defines internal fraud as losses due to acts of a type intended to defraud, misappropriate property or circumvent regulations, the law or company policy, excluding diversity and discrimination events, which involve at least one internal party. Three features drive classification:

- **Actor**: at least one internal party must be involved.
- **Intent**: the act is intended to defraud, misappropriate or circumvent rules.
- **Exclusion**: diversity and discrimination events are carved out (they belong elsewhere in the taxonomy).

GARP describes two subcategories. “Unauthorized activities” are any intentional violation of the law or of internal policies by an employee, and they do not necessarily result in a monetary loss for the firm. Basel examples include the intentional non-reporting of transactions, the mismarking of trading positions and the execution of unauthorized transaction types; GARP adds the sharing of passwords, disclosure of confidential information and mis-selling to vulnerable clients. Today these are more often called misconduct, as in limb (b) of the FCA definition. “Theft and fraud” covers the more common misappropriation of assets: extortion, embezzlement, malicious destruction of assets, bribery and tax evasion.

| Subcategory | Essence and examples |
|---|---|
| Unauthorized activities | Intentional breach of law or policy; loss not required; non-reporting, mismarking, unauthorized transaction types |
| Theft and fraud | Misappropriation of assets; embezzlement, extortion, bribery, tax evasion, malicious destruction |

**Applying it to this question**

Event 1 is the execution of an unauthorized transaction type, done knowingly: unauthorized activities, and the zero loss does not matter. Event 2 is embezzlement: theft and fraud. Event 3 is a discrimination event, which the Basel definition expressly excludes from internal fraud. Event 4 is intentional mismarking of positions: unauthorized activities. So Events 1 and 4 share the unauthorized activities subcategory. The loss column is an irrelevant input for classification.

**Fragile fact.** Unauthorized activities need intent, not a loss; discrimination events are excluded from internal fraud even though an employee is involved.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Context and Scope: Definition of Internal Fraud. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists smuggling and forgery among internal theft and fraud examples and omits malicious destruction of assets and mis-selling; GARP’s lists are used. No conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q2 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It adds a condition (a monetary loss) that the source explicitly removes for unauthorized activities. It would be correct only for a taxonomy that recorded events solely when a loss crystallised, which is not how GARP describes the subcategory.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It applies the “at least one internal party” condition but drops the exclusion of diversity and discrimination events. It would be correct only if the event were, for example, an employee bribing a supplier, which does involve intent to defraud.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It places mismarking (Event 4) in the neighbouring theft and fraud subcategory. Event 2 is theft and fraud, but Event 4 is unauthorized activities. It would be correct if Event 4 were a trader stealing client securities.

d.reason: GARP lists “the mismarking of trading positions or the execution of unauthorized transaction types” as Basel examples of unauthorized activities, and notes that these “do not necessarily result in money loss for the firm”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian credit union is reviewing how the operational risk team maps external events to the Basel external fraud subcategories. The team’s mapping guide is being updated after a year in which CAD 2.3 million of losses were recorded. Which of the following statements in the guide is most accurate?

options.text: A hacking attack by an outside group that damages systems and steals client data is classified as “systems security”.
A cheque forged by an outside party with no employee involvement is classified as “unauthorized activities”.
A fraud is classified as external whenever the loss arises on a client account, even if an employee took part.
Theft of information by outsiders is classified as “theft and fraud”, leaving “systems security” for hacking damage only.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Canadian credit union reviewing the mapping of events to Basel external fraud subcategories.

**Concept and theory**

The Basel Committee defines external fraud as losses due to acts of a type intended to defraud, misappropriate property or circumvent the law, by a third party. The definition mirrors internal fraud except for the actor: the perpetrator is outside the firm. Two consequences follow in GARP:

- The “unauthorized activity” subcategory does not apply, because only an employee can breach the firm’s internal authorities.
- The two subcategories are “theft and fraud” and “systems security”. Systems security includes hacking damage and theft of information.

GARP notes that the digitalisation of financial services has given systems security particular prominence, and that the management of cyber and information risk (information security risk management, ISRM) has become a specialised branch of operational risk management.

| Feature | Internal fraud | External fraud |
|---|---|---|
| Actor | At least one internal party | Third party |
| Subcategory 1 | Unauthorized activities | Theft and fraud |
| Subcategory 2 | Theft and fraud | Systems security |

**Applying it to this question**

A hacking attack by outsiders that damages systems and steals client data combines both named elements of systems security: hacking damage and theft of information. The CAD 2.3 million loss figure is irrelevant to classification.

**Fragile fact.** Systems security covers both hacking damage and theft of information; unauthorized activity exists only on the internal fraud side.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Context and Scope: Definition of External Fraud. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser adds cybersecurity breaches as an example of systems security).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q3 of 20.

a.reason: GARP: the other subcategory of external fraud “is systems security, which includes hacking damage and theft of information”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It borrows the unauthorized activities subcategory from internal fraud. GARP states that this subcategory does not apply to external fraud. An outside forgery is external theft and fraud. The option would be right only if the forger were an employee intentionally breaching internal policy.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the decisive condition of the internal fraud definition: if at least one internal party is involved, the event is internal fraud, whichever account bears the loss. The option would be right only if no employee had taken part.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves theft of information into the theft and fraud subcategory, although GARP names it as part of systems security. It would be right only for theft of physical assets, such as a robbery.

questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q4
questions.question:
A compliance officer at the EU subsidiary of a Brazilian bank is training staff on the activities that the EU Directive of 20 May 2015 regards as money laundering. She presents four cases:

I. A gallery owner accepts BRL 900,000 in cash for a painting, knowing at the time of receipt that the funds derive from criminal activity, and keeps the funds.

II. An adviser counsels a client on how to route transfers so as to disguise the illicit origin of the client’s proceeds, without ever handling the funds personally.

III. A fundraiser collects donations from sympathisers, knowing that part of the money will be used to carry out an act considered terrorist by the authorities.

IV. A buyer acquires property that, unknown to him when he receives it, is later found to derive from criminal activity.

Which of the cases would be regarded as money laundering under the Directive’s list of activities?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I and II only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Compliance officer at the EU subsidiary of a Brazilian bank testing four cases against the EU Directive list of money laundering activities.

**Concept and theory**

The European Directive of 20 May 2015 applies to all financial institutions, credit institutions and other professions exposed to the risk, and defines money laundering and terrorism financing in its Article 1. The activities regarded as money laundering are:

(a) the conversion or transfer of property, knowing it is derived from criminal activity, to conceal or disguise its illicit origin or to help a person evade the legal consequences;

(b) the concealment or disguise of the true nature, source, location, disposition, movement, rights or ownership of property, knowing it is derived from criminal activity;

(c) the acquisition, possession or use of property, knowing, at the time of receipt, that it was derived from criminal activity;

(d) participation in, association to commit, attempts to commit, and aiding, abetting, facilitating and counselling the commission of any of (a) to (c).

GARP summarises: organising, facilitating or concealing laundering activity (using or converting funds to conceal their illicit origin) is money laundering. Two features recur: the property derives from crime, and the person knows it. Terrorism financing is different in kind. Using the IMF definition, it is the provision or collection of funds, by any means, directly or indirectly, with the intention or knowledge that they will be used, in full or in part, to carry out an act considered terrorist. The funds need not be criminal in origin; what matters is their intended use.

**Applying it to this question**

Case I is acquisition and possession with knowledge at the time of receipt: limb (c), money laundering. Case II is counselling the conversion or transfer of criminal proceeds: limb (d), money laundering, even though the adviser never touches the funds. Case III is the collection of funds for a terrorist act: terrorism financing, not an activity on the money laundering list. Case IV fails the knowledge requirement of limb (c), because the buyer did not know at receipt. So I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Limb (c) needs knowledge at the time of receipt; terrorism financing turns on the intended use of the funds, not on their origin.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Context and Scope: Definition of Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Terrorism Financing (TF). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes terrorism financing as “providing or using” funds, while GARP (citing the IMF) says “provision or collection”; GARP’s wording is used. GARP’s text cites the Directive as EU 2015/949 while its footnote link reads 2015/849, an apparent typographical difference that does not affect the content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q4 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops limb (d), which extends money laundering to aiding, facilitating and counselling. It would be correct only if the list were limited to persons who personally handle the property.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It treats terrorism financing (Case III) as money laundering and omits Case II. Terrorism financing is defined separately, by intended use of funds rather than their criminal origin. B would be right if the question asked which cases are terrorism financing or money laundering, and Case II were removed.

c.reason: Cases I and II match limbs (c) and (d) of the Directive’s list; Cases III and IV do not.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts Case IV by dropping the requirement that the person know, at the time of receipt, that the property derived from crime. It would be correct only if the buyer had known the origin when receiving the property.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q5
questions.question: A member of the risk committee at an Australian asset manager with AUD 40 billion under management is reviewing the draft risk appetite statement, which says that the firm has “zero tolerance for internal fraud”. Which interpretation of this wording is most consistent with how firms generally use it?

options.text: Every perpetrator of internal fraud who is caught will be sanctioned; it does not claim that fraud cannot occur.
Prevention controls are designed so that internal fraud cannot materialise, leaving no residual fraud risk.
Sanctions apply only where the fraud caused a monetary loss, since the appetite is expressed in loss terms.
The stance covers employees only; contractors working close to the firm fall outside the fraud framework.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at an Australian asset manager interpreting “zero tolerance for internal fraud” in a risk appetite statement.

**Concept and theory**

Most firms, if not all, state in their risk appetite statements that they have “zero tolerance” for internal fraud. GARP is explicit about what this means: every perpetrator of fraud who is caught will be sanctioned. It does not mean that the prevention mechanism is such that the risk cannot materialise. The statement is a commitment about consequences, which supports the deterrents component of the framework, not a promise that residual risk is nil.

GARP also notes how fraud management has been organised. Historically, internal and external fraud in banks were the responsibility of internal audit; some banks, such as ING, had a subdivision of internal audit called “inspection” dedicated to detecting, monitoring and reporting fraud, and former police officers and forensic specialists often work in fraud risk departments. The control framework then has four components. Its first, selection, screens employees, contractors and third parties that will operate within or close to the firm.

**Applying it to this question**

The decisive phrase is the firm’s commitment. A reading that turns zero tolerance into “no fraud can happen” overstates it; a reading that ties sanctions to monetary loss contradicts it; and a reading that excludes contractors conflicts with the framework, which screens contractors and third parties. The AUD 40 billion figure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Zero tolerance is about sanctioning every perpetrator caught, not about eliminating the possibility of fraud.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: Internal Fraud Management. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: if offenders are caught, they will be punished or sanctioned).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q5 of 20.

a.reason: GARP: zero tolerance means “that every perpetrator of fraud who is caught will be sanctioned, not that the fraud risk prevention mechanism is such that the risk cannot materialize”.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It turns a commitment to sanction into a promise that fraud cannot occur, which GARP expressly rejects. It would be right only if the question asked what zero tolerance is commonly misread as.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It adds a monetary loss condition. Zero tolerance applies to every perpetrator caught, and unauthorized activities are internal fraud even without loss. It would be right only for a loss-based appetite metric, not for the zero tolerance statement.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the framework to employees. The selection component explicitly covers “employees, contractors, and third parties that will operate within or close to the firm”. It would be right only if contractors had no access to the firm’s operations.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q6
questions.question:
A senior risk consultant is helping a London commodity trading firm restructure its measures against internal fraud. The firm has assigned five proposed controls to the components of its internal fraud framework as follows:

| No. | Proposed control | Component assigned by the firm |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Due diligence on contractors before system access | Selection |
| 2 | Delegation of authorities by role | Prevention |
| 3 | Daily reconciliations of trading positions | Prevention |
| 4 | Legal pursuits against perpetrators | Deterrents |
| 5 | Tone and culture, alignment of values | Deterrents |

Which of the assignments are consistent with the standard internal fraud control framework?

options.text: 1 and 2 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1, 4 and 5 only
1, 2 and 4 only

questions.solution:
Senior risk consultant checking a London commodity trader’s assignment of five anti-fraud controls to the four framework components.

**Concept and theory**

GARP presents a framework of controls for internal fraud (Figure 11.1), inspired by a trading company that wanted to refresh and restructure its anti-fraud measures. It has four components, which follow the life cycle of a fraud: who is let in, what they are allowed to do, how quickly misconduct is spotted, and what happens afterwards.

| Component | Purpose | Typical controls (Figure 11.1) |
|---|---|---|
| Selection | Screen employees, contractors and third parties operating within or close to the firm | Screening at onboarding; due diligence on employees and third parties; tone and culture, alignment of values |
| Prevention | Clearly delimit the rights, authority and access of each function | Segregation of duties; access rights and authorizations; delegation of authorities |
| Detection | Shorten time to detection; also deters | Team supervision; monitoring for abnormal patterns and behaviours; reconciliations |
| Deterrents | Announced sanctions and actions after fraud | Sanctions and disciplinary actions; legal pursuits |

GARP calls delimiting rights, authority and access “the cornerstone of fraud risk management”. Tone from the top, culture and alignment of values reside in selection: hiring people who share the firm’s values and ethical standards makes people management much easier.

**Applying it to this question**

Row 1, due diligence on contractors: selection, correct. Row 2, delegation of authorities: prevention, correct. Row 3, reconciliations: detection, so “prevention” is wrong. Row 4, legal pursuits: deterrents, correct. Row 5, tone and culture: selection, so “deterrents” is wrong. Consistent rows: 1, 2 and 4.

**Fragile fact.** Reconciliations are detective, not preventive; tone and culture sit in selection, not in deterrents.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: Internal Fraud Management, Figure 11.1 (Controls for internal fraud management: case study at a trading firm). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser omits tone and culture from selection; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q6 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It identifies two correct rows but leaves out Row 4, which is also correct. It would be the answer only if legal pursuits sat outside the deterrents component.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts reconciliations as prevention. Reconciliations reveal discrepancies after the event and belong to the neighbouring detection component. It would be right if Row 3 were “segregation of duties”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It accepts tone and culture as a deterrent. GARP places tone, culture and alignment of values in selection, as part of who is brought into the firm. It would be right if Row 5 read “sanctions and disciplinary actions”.

d.reason: Figure 11.1 places due diligence in selection, delegation of authorities in prevention and legal pursuits in deterrents; it places reconciliations in detection and tone and culture in selection.

questions.question: The CRO of a Tokyo securities firm is reviewing a cost proposal. It would cut team supervision and daily reconciliations in the cash equities back office, saving JPY 180 million a year, and use part of the saving to publicise tougher disciplinary sanctions for fraud. Which of the following best describes the likely effect on internal fraud risk?

options.text: Neutral, because only announced sanctions deter fraud, while detective controls act only after a fraud has already occurred.
Adverse, because detective controls also deter: incentives to commit fraud fall when the risk of being caught is high.
Favourable, because publicised sanctions are prevention controls that delimit the rights and access of each function.
Adverse, because team supervision is a selection control, and weaker selection admits staff with misaligned values.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Tokyo securities firm assessing a proposal to cut supervision and reconciliations and fund publicised sanctions instead.

**Concept and theory**

The four components of the internal fraud framework are not independent. GARP makes two points about detection:

- **Time to detection limits impact.** Like many operational risk incidents, especially those developing quickly or repeating over time, the sooner a fraud is detected, the smaller its impact.
- **Detection deters.** Detective controls are particularly important in internal fraud management and also act as a deterrent: incentives to fraud are much lower if the risk of being caught is high. Team supervision and other means of monitoring are effective controls, and managers should be alert to signs of resentment, disengagement or other suspicious behaviour.

Deterrents proper are the announced sanctions and actions following any act of fraud. They act as disincentives by tipping the risk and reward balance of the potential fraudster’s decision. A useful way to see the interaction: the expected cost to a fraudster is roughly the probability of being caught multiplied by the sanction. Raising the sanction while cutting the probability of detection need not lower the incentive, and it lengthens the time to detection, which increases the impact.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal removes two detective controls (team supervision, reconciliations) and adds to the deterrents component. Because detection itself deters, the firm loses deterrence from the higher chance of being caught, and also loses speed of detection. The JPY 180 million saving is irrelevant to the direction of the effect.

**Fragile fact.** Detection has a double role: it limits impact through time to detection and it deters by raising the risk of being caught.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: Internal Fraud Management, items 3 (Detection) and 4 (Deterrents). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: when detection is strong, the risk of being caught is high and the incentive to commit fraud is low). The “probability times sanction” framing is a teaching device, not a formula in either source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q7 of 20.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns the deterrent effect solely to the sanctions component and denies it to detection, which GARP explicitly gives a deterrent role. It would be right only for a control that has no effect on the chance of being caught, such as a change in the wording of a policy.

b.reason: GARP: detective controls “also act as a deterrent: Incentives to fraud are much lower if the risk of being caught is high”. Weakening them raises internal fraud risk even if sanctions are publicised.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes to sanctions the defining property of prevention, delimiting the rights, authority and access of each function. Publicised sanctions are deterrents. It would be right if the saving were spent on segregation of duties or access controls.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It reaches the right direction for the wrong reason, placing team supervision in selection. Team supervision is a detective control; selection concerns screening at onboarding and alignment of values. It would be right if the proposal cut pre-hire screening.

questions.question:
A fraud analyst at an Australian retail bank is classifying two external fraud cases for the quarterly fraud report.

- Case X: a small business customer overstates its receivables and the value of its collateral in a loan application to obtain an AUD 3 million facility.
- Case Y: a criminal group uses a stolen identity to open a credit card in the name of an existing customer and draws AUD 25,000 on it.

Which of the following classifications is most accurate?

options.text: X is third-party fraud, as an external firm gains; Y is first-party fraud, as the victim is the account holder.
X is a credit risk event rather than fraud, because misstating values in a loan application involves no theft.
X is first-party fraud, committed by the customer for its own benefit; Y is third-party fraud by an external actor.
X and Y are both first-party fraud, because each of them involves an account or facility held by a customer.

questions.solution:
Fraud analyst at an Australian retail bank classifying a loan misrepresentation and an identity theft as first-party or third-party fraud.

**Concept and theory**

External fraud management shifts the focus from employees to external bad actors: professional criminals, and also customers and business partners who may commit fraud. External fraud includes bank robbery, cheque kiting, fraudulent wire transfers, credit card fraud and identity theft. Most institutions also categorise misrepresentation of income, assets and collateral values in loan applications as fraudulent.

GARP notes that external fraud is sometimes subdivided to distinguish who commits it and who is harmed:

| Type | Perpetrator and motive | Who is affected |
|---|---|---|
| First-party fraud | Customer or business partner, for their own benefit | The bank |
| Third-party fraud | An external actor other than the customer | The customer as well as the bank |

**Applying it to this question**

In Case X the borrower itself misstates receivables and collateral to obtain a larger facility: the customer is the perpetrator and the beneficiary, which is first-party fraud, and GARP confirms that loan application misrepresentation is treated as fraud. In Case Y a criminal group impersonates an existing customer: the customer is a victim alongside the bank, which is third-party fraud. The AUD amounts are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** First-party means the customer or partner defrauds for its own benefit; third-party means an outsider whose fraud can hit the customer as well as the bank.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: External Fraud Management. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes third-party fraud only as “other external parties committing fraud”; GARP adds that it may affect the customer as well as the bank. GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q8 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses both labels, treating the borrowing firm as a “third party” and the impersonated customer as the first-party perpetrator. It would be right only if X were a fraud by an outsider against the borrower and Y a fraud by the account holder.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows fraud to theft. GARP states that most institutions categorise misrepresentation of income, assets and collateral values in loan applications as fraudulent. B would be right only for an honest error in a loan application, with no intent.

c.reason: GARP distinguishes “fraud committed by the customer or business partner for their own benefit, as opposed to an external actor who carries out fraud that may impact the customer as well as the bank”.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It uses the location of the account as the test, rather than who commits the fraud and who benefits. It would be right only if the customer in Case Y had opened the card and drawn the funds itself.

questions.question: The head of operational risk at a Chinese commercial bank with CNY 1.1 trillion of assets is presenting to new analysts on how external fraud is managed compared with internal fraud. Which of the following statements is least accurate?

options.text: External fraud management shares many components with internal fraud management, with the focus shifted to external bad actors.
Company security monitors and secures physical structures such as branches and ATMs, and partners with local law enforcement after incidents.
Retail banks generally keep teams dedicated to deposit or cheque fraud and to card fraud, often working with specialised law enforcement.
Because the range of perpetrators is narrow, external fraud can generally be handled by one generalist team without dedicated specialists.

questions.solution:
Head of operational risk at a Chinese commercial bank presenting how external fraud management differs from internal fraud management; least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes external fraud management as sharing many of the same components as internal fraud management, with an obvious shift of focus toward external bad actors: professional criminals as well as potential fraud by customers and business partners. Because the set of fraud types and actors is broad (robbery, cheque kiting, fraudulent wire transfers, card fraud, identity theft, loan application misrepresentation), external fraud generally requires special teams:

- company security monitors and secures the bank’s physical structures against robbery, including ATMs, and partners with local law enforcement after incidents;
- retail banks generally have teams dedicated to deposit and cheque fraud and to credit and debit card fraud, often working with specialised law enforcement to discover and catch perpetrators.

**Applying it to this question**

Options A, B and C restate GARP. Option D claims the range of perpetrators is narrow and that one generalist team suffices, which is the reverse of GARP’s reasoning: the breadth of fraud types and actors is precisely why special teams are needed. The CNY asset figure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** External fraud spans a broad set of types and actors, which is why GARP says it generally needs special teams.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: External Fraud Management. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q9 of 20.

a.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP: management of external fraud “shares many of the same components as internal fraud management but with an obvious shift of focus toward external bad actors”. A would be the answer only if it claimed that external fraud uses an entirely different framework.

b.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP names company security, physical structures, ATMs and partnership with local law enforcement. B would be the answer if it assigned ATM security to the internal audit inspection unit, a role misassignment.

c.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP names dedicated deposit or cheque fraud and card fraud teams working with specialised law enforcement. C would be the answer if it said these teams worked without external partners.

d.reason: It is the least accurate statement. GARP: “External fraud, therefore, generally requires special teams to manage this broad set of fraud type and actors.”

questions.question:
The money laundering risk officer at a Frankfurt bank is reviewing an investigation file that reconstructs a scheme in three steps:

- Step 1: proceeds of drug sales were paid in as many cash deposits of under EUR 9,000 each into the account of a cash-intensive business, supported by false invoices.
- Step 2: the funds were moved through several foreign accounts in varying amounts and patterns, mixed with further deposits and withdrawals.
- Step 3: the funds were paid out as dividends to accomplices and as salaries to fictitious employees.

Which of the following statements about the scheme is most accurate?

options.text: Step 1 is placement, and splitting the cash into many small deposits is meant to stay below the AML reporting threshold.
Step 2 is integration, because the funds pass through foreign accounts before they re-enter the legitimate economy.
Step 3 is layering, because paying fake dividends and fake salaries obscures the audit trail of the original funds.
Step 1 is integration, because false invoicing gives the cash a legitimate commercial appearance in the accounts.

questions.solution:
Money laundering risk officer at a Frankfurt bank labelling the three steps of a reconstructed laundering scheme.

**Concept and theory**

Criminals typically use two or three phases to turn the proceeds of crime into apparently legitimate funds. GARP names them placement, layering and integration (or extraction).

| Phase |  | Aim | Techniques named in GARP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Placement |  | Disguise the origins of the funds as they enter the system | Cash transfer to businesses, false invoicing, trusts and offshore companies, smurfing, foreign bank accounts |
| Layering |  | Make tracking as hard as possible and circumvent AML controls | Combining placement and extraction strategies with varying amounts and patterns |
| Integration traction) | (ex- | Get the money out to use without attracting law enforcement or tax authorities | Fake payments to employees, fake loans, dividends to accomplices |

Smurfing is making a series of small transactions instead of a single large one, to remain below the AML reporting threshold for bank accounts or credit cards.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1 combines three placement techniques: small cash deposits under a threshold (smurfing), cash paid into a business, and false invoicing. Step 2 moves funds through varying amounts and patterns across accounts: layering. Step 3 pays out fake dividends and salaries: integration. The EUR 9,000 figure signals the below-threshold design.

**Fragile fact.** False invoicing and smurfing are placement; fake salaries, fake loans and dividends to accomplices are integration (extraction).

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: AML Risk Management. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes layering as “a series of complex transactions using multiple accounts” and adds asset purchases to integration; GARP’s framing (combining placement and extraction strategies) is used. Likely a framing compression rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q10 of 20.

a.reason: GARP lists smurfing, “making a series of small transactions instead of a single large transaction in order to remain below the AML reporting threshold”, as a placement technique, together with cash transfer to businesses and false invoicing.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It gives Step 2 the label of the neighbouring phase. Moving funds in varying amounts and patterns to defeat tracking is layering; integration is getting the money out to use. B would be right if Step 2 described fake loans or dividends paid to accomplices.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It labels fake dividends and fake salaries as layering. GARP names exactly these as integration (extraction) techniques. C would be right if Step 3 described further transfers between accounts.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It labels false invoicing as integration. GARP lists false invoicing among placement techniques. D would be right if Step 1 described paying out funds to accomplices.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q11
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US regional bank with USD 60 billion of deposits is reviewing the AML training module given to branch staff. The module includes the following statements on the phases of money laundering:

I. Smurfing replaces a single large transaction with a series of small ones, to remain below the AML reporting threshold for bank accounts or credit cards.

II. Layering combines placement and extraction strategies with varying amounts and patterns, to make transactions as hard as possible to track.

III. Integration, also called extraction, gets the money out to use without attracting the attention of law enforcement or the tax authorities.

IV. Every laundering scheme must pass through all three phases, in strict sequence, before the criminal proceeds can be used as legitimate funds.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a US regional bank auditing four training statements on the phases of money laundering.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens its AML section with the observation that criminals typically use two or three phases to disguise the proceeds of their criminal activity into legitimate sources of funds. The three phases are placement, layering and integration (or extraction).

- **Placement** covers all techniques aimed at disguising the origins of funds, including smurfing: a series of small transactions instead of a single large one, to remain below the AML reporting threshold for bank accounts or credit cards.
- **Layering** is essentially the use of a combination of placement and extraction strategies with varying amounts and patterns, to make tracking as hard as possible and circumvent AML controls.
- **Integration or extraction** is getting the money out to use, without attracting attention from law enforcement or the tax authorities, through fake payments to employees, fake loans, or dividends to accomplices.

The phrase “two or three phases” is a deliberate qualifier: the phases are a typical pattern, not a mandatory sequence that every scheme must complete.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches GARP’s description of smurfing, including the threshold for bank accounts or credit cards: true. Statement II reproduces GARP’s definition of layering: true. Statement III reproduces the definition of integration or extraction: true. Statement IV turns a typical pattern into a rule (every scheme, all three phases, strict sequence), contradicting “typically use two or three phases”: false.

**Fragile fact.** GARP says criminals typically use two or three phases; layering mixes placement and extraction strategies rather than being a separate set of techniques.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Financial Crime Risk Management: AML Risk Management. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser presents the three phases as a fixed sequence (“first step”, “second phase”, “last phase”) and omits “two or three”; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q11 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It rejects Statement III, which is GARP’s own definition of integration or extraction. It would be right only if III had attributed the aim of avoiding law enforcement to layering.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It accepts Statement IV, which claims every scheme must complete all three phases in strict order, and drops the true Statements I and III. It would be right only if GARP said criminals always use three phases.

c.reason: Statements I, II and III restate GARP; IV is an absolute claim that GARP’s “two or three phases” rules out.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It accepts all four statements, including the absolute claim in IV. It would be right if IV read “criminals typically use two or three phases”.

questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q12
questions.question: A risk consultant is validating the AML control inventory of a Canadian bank, which has assigned each control to one of the four steps of its AML control framework. Which of the following assignments is correct?

options.text: Ongoing reconciliation of customer records with OFAC and PEP lists is a selection control, as it screens customers.
Staff information and training is a prevention control, alongside the risk-based approach and allocation of responsibilities.
Escalation of a case to the financial intelligence unit is a detection control, as it follows a transaction alert.
Ethos and values is a deterrent control, as it discourages staff from helping clients to launder criminal funds.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant validating a Canadian bank’s assignment of AML controls to the four steps of its AML control framework.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Figure 11.2 presents the key risk mitigation measures for AML risk in banks, based on regulatory guidance. It reproduces the structure used for internal fraud, highlighting the similarities in how different fraud risks are organised.

| Step | Controls (Figure 11.2) |
|---|---|
| Selection | Customer due diligence (KYC); verification of the identity and origins of funds; ethos and values |
| Prevention | Risk-based approach on risk driving factors; staff information and training; allocation of responsibilities |
| Detection | Transaction monitoring system; alerts on abnormal behaviours or transactions; reconciliation with external lists (OFAC, PEP) |
| Deterrents | Escalation to the relevant financial intelligence unit (FIU); legal pursuits; closure of accounts |

The logic follows the life of a client relationship: who is accepted (selection), how risk is managed by design (prevention), how suspicious activity is spotted (detection), and what consequences follow (deterrents).

**Applying it to this question**

Ongoing reconciliation with OFAC and PEP lists is detection. Staff information and training, together with the risk-based approach and allocation of responsibilities, is prevention. Escalation to the FIU is a deterrent, an action taken once suspicion is established. Ethos and values sit in selection. Only the assignment in option B is correct.

**Fragile fact.** OFAC and PEP reconciliation is detection; escalation to the FIU is a deterrent; training is prevention.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management, Figure 11.2 (Control framework for AML risks, based on regulatory guidance). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser places the money laundering risk officer under detection and describes “tight risk controls with proper employee training” under prevention; consistent with Figure 11.2 on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q12 of 20.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves reconciliation with external lists into selection. In Figure 11.2 it is a detection control alongside transaction monitoring and alerts. It would be right if the control were initial customer due diligence (KYC) at account opening.

b.reason: Figure 11.2 lists “risk-based approach on risk driving factors”, “staff information and training” and “allocation of responsibilities” together in the prevention step.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It treats escalation to the FIU as detection because it follows an alert. Escalation is the consequence, and Figure 11.2 places it in deterrents. It would be right if the control were the alert itself.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It places ethos and values in deterrents. Figure 11.2 places it in selection, mirroring tone and culture in the internal fraud framework. It would be right if the control were closure of accounts or legal pursuits.

questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q13
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a UK bank with GBP 85 billion of assets is comparing the bank’s internal fraud framework with its AML control framework. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: The AML framework reproduces the four-step structure used for internal fraud: selection, prevention, detection and deterrents.
Legal pursuits appear in the deterrents step of both frameworks, as announced consequences that discourage wrongdoing.
Selection and profiling are key risk mitigation mechanisms in AML as well as in the management of internal fraud.
The AML deterrents step is limited to disciplinary action against staff, since the bank cannot act against its customers.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member comparing a UK bank’s internal fraud framework with its AML framework; statement that is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP deliberately builds the AML framework (Figure 11.2) on the same four-step structure as the internal fraud framework (Figure 11.1): selection, prevention, detection and deterrents. It notes that selection and profiling are key risk mitigation mechanisms in AML and in third-party risk management, as well as in internal fraud.

| Step | Internal fraud (Figure 11.1) | AML (Figure 11.2) |
|---|---|---|
| Selection | Screening, due diligence, tone and culture | KYC, identity and origin of funds, ethos and values |
| Prevention | Segregation of duties, access rights, delegation | Risk-based approach, training, allocation of responsibilities |
| Detection | Supervision, monitoring, reconciliations | Transaction monitoring, alerts, list reconciliation |
| Deterrents | Sanctions and disciplinary actions, legal pursuits | Escalation to FIU, legal pursuits, closure of accounts |

The deterrents differ because the target differs. Internal fraud deterrents act on employees (disciplinary actions). AML deterrents act on customers and the wider system: escalation to the financial intelligence unit, legal pursuits and closure of accounts.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C restate the parallel structure. D confines AML deterrents to staff discipline and claims the bank cannot act against customers, whereas Figure 11.2 names closure of accounts and escalation to the FIU, both aimed at customers. D is the incorrect statement. The GBP asset figure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** AML deterrents are aimed at customers: FIU escalation, legal pursuits and account closure; staff disciplinary action belongs to the internal fraud framework.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, Internal Fraud Management (Figure 11.1) and AML Risk Management (Figure 11.2). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: deterrents include lawsuits, closing customer accounts and referral to financial intelligence agencies).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q13 of 20.

a.reason: **Correct statement.** GARP: Figure 11.2 “reproduces the structure presented for internal fraud”. A would be the answer if it said the AML framework had three steps or omitted deterrents.

b.reason: **Correct statement.** Legal pursuits appear in the deterrents column of both figures. B would be the answer if it placed legal pursuits in detection in either framework.

c.reason: **Correct statement.** GARP: “Selection and profiling are also key risk-mitigation mechanisms in AML and in third-party risk management.” C would be the answer if it limited selection to employees.

d.reason: It is NOT correct. Figure 11.2’s deterrents are “escalation to relevant financial intelligence unit (FIU)”, “legal pursuits” and “closure of accounts”.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q14
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian commercial bank is reviewing the onboarding file of a new client who wishes to open an account and deposit BRL 12 million from the sale of a family business. The onboarding team plans to verify the client’s identity documents and the origin of the funds before accepting the deposit. Which of the following best describes these steps?

options.text: They are customer selection, arguably the most important AML step, and they let the bank demonstrate due diligence before entering the business.
They are detection, as verifying the origin of funds is a form of transaction monitoring that is carried out after the deposit is accepted.
They are prevention, and verifying the origin of funds is required only for customers who are already classified as high risk or as PEPs.
They are customer selection, but identity checks alone demonstrate due diligence, so verifying the origin of significant funds is optional.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank assessing identity and origin-of-funds checks on a BRL 12 million deposit by a new client.

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls the profiling and selection of customers “the first, and arguably the most important step of AML controls”. It has two parts:

- **Know your customer (KYC)**: verification of the identity documents of customers applying to open an account.
- **Origin of funds**: verification of the origins of the funds, for the deposit of any significant amount, which is essential for banks to demonstrate the effectiveness of their due diligence before entering business transactions. It should ensure that the funds are not linked to any criminal activity.

The timing matters: both checks are done before the bank enters the relationship or accepts the funds. That is why they are selection, the step that keeps criminal money from being placed in the first place, rather than detection, which works on activity already in the system.

**Applying it to this question**

The client is new, is opening an account, and is depositing a significant amount. The planned checks are KYC and verification of the origin of funds, done before acceptance. Both are selection controls, and the origin-of-funds check is required because the deposit is significant, not because of a prior high-risk rating.

**Fragile fact.** Origin-of-funds checks are triggered by any significant deposit and done before the business starts; they are selection, not detection.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management (text following Figure 11.2). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser calls KYC “one of the most critical steps”; GARP calls selection “arguably the most important step”. Same point, different emphasis; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q14 of 20.

a.reason: GARP: selection is “the first, and arguably the most important step”; origin-of-funds verification “for the deposit of any significant amount is essential for banks to demonstrate the effectiveness of their due diligence before entering business transactions”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns the checks to detection and moves them after acceptance. Transaction monitoring is detection, but KYC and origin-of-funds verification are selection controls performed before the business starts. B would be right if the stem described alerts on an existing client’s unusual transfers.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows origin-of-funds verification to clients already rated high risk or PEPs. GARP requires it for the deposit of any significant amount. C would be right if the deposit were small and the policy applied enhanced checks only to high-risk clients.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops one of the two elements of selection. GARP treats origin-of-funds verification as essential to demonstrate due diligence. D would be right only for a small deposit where the identity check is the operative control.
