questions.question: A supervisor at a national banking regulator is reviewing the AML policy of a Singapore bank to assess whether it follows the risk-based approach recommended by regulators and industry guidance. Which of the following policy statements is most consistent with that approach?

options.text: All customers receive the same depth of AML controls, because a risk-based approach requires consistent treatment of every client.
Customers rated low risk receive the tightest controls, because they are the least likely to draw attention from routine monitoring.
Customers are rated low, medium or high risk on factors such as country, industry and traceability of funds, which also drive monitoring.
Customers are rated by risk factors only at onboarding; once assigned, these factors play no further role in ongoing monitoring.

questions.solution:
Banking supervisor reviewing whether a Singapore bank’s AML policy follows the risk-based approach.

**Concept and theory**

Regulators and industry guidance recommend a risk-based approach to AML risk, which GARP calls good risk management practice in general: the higher the risks, the tighter the controls, and vice versa. In practice:

- customers, both retail and business, are typically categorised as low, medium or high risk;
- the categorisation uses risk factors such as country of operation, industry, history with the bank, corporate structure, location of the subsidiaries, third parties and clients, traceability of funds, and volume and frequency of transactions;
- these risk factors are used as the main monitoring criteria, so they continue to drive controls after onboarding.

In Figure 11.2, “risk-based approach on risk driving factors” sits in the prevention step: it is a design choice that allocates control effort where risk is greatest.

**Applying it to this question**

The test has two parts: proportionality (more risk, tighter controls) and continuity (the factors drive ongoing monitoring). Only C satisfies both: it categorises customers into three tiers on named factors and uses those factors for monitoring.

**Fragile fact.** Higher risk means tighter controls, and the same risk factors are the main monitoring criteria, not only onboarding inputs.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management (risk-based approach paragraph and Figure 11.2). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s factor list (occupation, volume and frequency, history with the bank, documentation, PEP status) merges GARP’s general risk factors with its retail-specific monitoring list; GARP’s separation is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q15 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It replaces proportional controls with uniform controls, dropping the condition that controls scale with risk. It would describe a rules-based minimum standard, not a risk-based approach.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction: GARP says the higher the risks, the tighter the controls. B would be right if it said high-risk customers receive the tightest controls.

c.reason: GARP: customers “are typically categorized as low, medium, or high risk, depending on risk factors such as country of operation, industry, . . . traceability of funds, volume and frequency of transactions. These risk factors are used as the main monitoring criteria.”

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It confines the risk factors to onboarding. GARP states they are used as the main monitoring criteria. D would be right only for a one-off onboarding score, not for the monitoring role GARP describes.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Dublin retail bank is selecting inputs for the specific AML monitoring of retail clients. The data team has offered the following inputs:

| No. | Input | Data source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | PEP status | External PEP list |
| 2 | Occupation | Onboarding form |
| 3 | Credit bureau score (EUR loans only) | Credit bureau |
| 4 | Volume and types of transactions | Core banking system |
| 5 | Annual profitability of the relationship | Finance system |
| 6 | Documentation supporting the origin of funds | Client file |

Which set contains only inputs that AML guidance identifies for the specific monitoring of retail clients?

options.text: 1, 2 and 3 only
1, 2, 4 and 6 only
2, 4, 5 and 6 only
3, 4 and 6 only

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst at a Dublin retail bank selecting inputs for the specific AML monitoring of retail clients from a list with irrelevant items.

**Concept and theory**

Within the risk-based approach, GARP distinguishes the general risk factors used to categorise all customers (country of operation, industry, history with the bank, corporate structure, location of subsidiaries, third parties and clients, traceability of funds, volume and frequency of transactions) from the specific monitoring of retail clients, which includes:

| No. | Specific monitoring of retail clients |
|---|---|
| 1 | PEP lists (politically exposed persons) |
| 2 | Occupation |
| 3 | Volume and types of transactions |
| 4 | History with the bank |
| 5 | Documentation supporting the origins of funds |

Each item helps judge whether a client’s activity is consistent with who the client is and where the money comes from. A PEP status calls for enhanced due diligence; occupation sets the expected level of income; documentation on origins of funds links the money to a legitimate source.

**Applying it to this question**

Inputs 1 (PEP status), 2 (occupation), 4 (volume and types of transactions) and 6 (documentation supporting origin of funds) are named by GARP. Input 3 (credit bureau score) measures creditworthiness, a credit risk input, and is not on the AML list. Input 5 (relationship profitability) measures commercial value to the bank and is also absent. The only set free of irrelevant inputs is 1, 2, 4 and 6.

**Fragile fact.** Retail AML monitoring uses PEP lists, occupation, volume and types of transactions, history with the bank and origin-of-funds documentation; creditworthiness and profitability are not AML inputs.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management (risk-based approach paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser places these factors under prevention as determinants of the risk classification, without separating retail monitoring; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q16 of 20.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It includes the credit bureau score, a credit risk measure from a neighbouring discipline, and omits transaction volumes and documentation of funds. It would be right if Input 3 were “history with the bank”.

b.reason: GARP: “Specific monitoring of retail clients include PEP lists (politically exposed persons), occupation, volume and types of transactions, history with the bank, and documentation supporting the origins of funds.”

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It includes relationship profitability, which says nothing about AML risk, and drops PEP status, the one item that triggers enhanced due diligence. It would be right if Input 5 were PEP status.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It includes the credit bureau score and drops PEP status and occupation. It would be right if Input 3 were occupation and the set also included PEP status.

questions.question: The newly appointed chief compliance officer of an Irish payment institution handling EUR 6 billion of payments a year is reviewing the governance of its AML programme. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A dedicated MLRO accountable for AML is mandatory for most institutions in most jurisdictions, with written policies, training and systematic reviews.
Appointing an MLRO is voluntary good practice, so AML accountability may instead be spread across business lines with no single named owner.
Once an MLRO is in place, customer data and monitoring systems need to be reviewed only when alerts arise, as accountability replaces review.
Under UK guidance, a bank that cannot demonstrate effective AML controls is exposed to fines only once it is shown to hold the proceeds of crime.

questions.solution:
New chief compliance officer at an Irish payment institution reviewing AML governance: MLRO, policies, training, reviews and regulatory consequences.

**Concept and theory**

GARP stresses that governance is important in AML. A dedicated MLRO (money laundering risk officer) accountable for the management of AML is mandatory for most institutions in most jurisdictions. Around that role sit three supporting elements:

- the maintenance of written policies;
- employee training;
- systematic reviews to ensure that customer data and monitoring systems are up to date.

The stakes are regulatory. UK regulatory guidelines state that banks unable to demonstrate effective AML and CTF controls expose themselves to regulatory fines, restrictions of business, and possibly more severe prosecution if it is established that they are holding the proceeds of crime. The trigger for fines is the inability to demonstrate effective controls; holding criminal proceeds raises the stakes further, to prosecution.

**Applying it to this question**

Option A states GARP’s governance requirements fully. B treats the MLRO as optional, C replaces systematic reviews with reactive reviews, and D makes holding proceeds of crime a precondition for fines, when it is in fact the condition for possible prosecution. The EUR payment volume is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Fines follow from failing to demonstrate effective controls; proof of holding criminal proceeds is what can escalate the matter to prosecution.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management (governance paragraph); Context and Scope: Definition of AML and TF (UK regulatory guidelines). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says risk overview “is often delegated to a dedicated money laundering risk officer”; GARP says a dedicated MLRO is mandatory for most institutions in most jurisdictions. Conflict resolved from GARP; it looks like a compression in Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q17 of 20.

a.reason: GARP: “a dedicated MLRO . . . accountable for the management of AML is mandatory for most institutions in most jurisdictions, together with the maintenance of written policies, employee training, and systematic reviews to ensure that customer data and monitoring systems are up to date.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns “mandatory” into “voluntary” and removes the single accountable owner. It would be right only in a jurisdiction that does not require an MLRO, which GARP treats as the exception.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It replaces systematic reviews with reviews triggered only by alerts, dropping the condition that reviews keep data and systems up to date. It would be right only if the stem asked about investigating a specific alert.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It moves the “holding proceeds of crime” condition from prosecution to fines. Fines and restrictions of business follow from failure to demonstrate effective controls alone. D would be right if it said “more severe prosecution” instead of “fines”.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a São Paulo asset manager, which executes trades for its clients through a New York broker, is drafting the firm’s sanctions screening procedure for the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) list. Which of the following statements should the procedure contain?

options.text: The list binds only banks incorporated in the United States, so a non-US firm dealing with US parties indirectly need not screen against it.
The list covers only parties linked to targeted countries, so terrorists and narcotics traffickers not tied to a country fall outside it.
The list is fixed at the time of designation, so screening each client once at onboarding is enough to meet the requirement in full.
The list, published by an office of the US Treasury, covers parties linked to targeted countries and also non-country-specific designations.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a São Paulo asset manager trading through a New York broker, drafting an OFAC sanctions screening procedure.

**Concept and theory**

Sanctions screening is a detection control in Figure 11.2 (“reconciliation with external lists (OFAC, PEP)”). GARP describes the US list:

- **Publisher**: the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), part of the US Treasury Department.
- **Content**: individuals and companies owned or controlled by, or acting for or on behalf of, targeted countries; and individuals, groups and entities, such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers, designated under programs that are not country-specific.
- **Who must comply**: every company that does business with or in the United States, directly or indirectly, must ensure that its clients are not on the list.
- **Maintenance**: the list is refreshed regularly.

Because the list changes, screening is not a one-off onboarding step; it is an ongoing reconciliation of client records against the current list. Automation is particularly useful for checking whether customers or related businesses are sanctioned or are PEPs.

**Applying it to this question**

The firm is not a US bank, but it does business with the United States indirectly through a New York broker, so it is within the “directly or indirectly” reach. Option D correctly states the publisher and both parts of the list’s content.

**Fragile fact.** OFAC reach is “with or in the United States, directly or indirectly”; the list includes non-country-specific designations and is refreshed regularly.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management (OFAC paragraph) and Figure 11.2. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says all companies doing business “in or with” the United States must screen, without “directly or indirectly” and without the refresh point; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q18 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the obligation to US-incorporated banks. GARP extends it to every company that does business with or in the United States, directly or indirectly. A would be right only for a firm with no direct or indirect US business.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the non-country-specific programs, under which terrorists and narcotics traffickers are designated. B would be right only for the country-based part of the list.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** It treats the list as fixed and onboarding screening as complete. GARP says the list is refreshed regularly, which is why reconciliation with external lists sits in detection. C would be right only for a static list, which OFAC’s is not.

d.reason: GARP: OFAC, “part of the US Treasury Department, publishes a sanction list of individuals and companies owned, controlled by, or acting for or on behalf of targeted countries. It also lists individuals, groups, and entities, such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers designated under programs, that are not country-specific.”

questions.loText: Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 a Q19
questions.question: A member of the risk committee at a Japanese online bank is assessing a proposal to adopt a RegTech solution for AML compliance. Which of the following statements best describes what such solutions are used for?

options.text: They remove the need for regulators to review the quality of KYC controls at digital banks, as machine learning eliminates human error.
They are used mainly to set the bank’s AML risk appetite, while customer profiling and due diligence remain manual processes.
They use machine learning to automate customer profiling, speed up due diligence by scanning, and flag unexplained behaviour early.
They help with transaction monitoring but cannot verify whether customers or their related businesses are sanctioned or are PEPs.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at a Japanese online bank assessing what RegTech solutions are used for in AML compliance.

**Concept and theory**

RegTech companies use data analytics to provide compliance services, AML in particular, and have flourished in recent years. GARP lists what they do:

- use machine learning to automate the profiling of customers (selection);
- speed up the due diligence process through automated scanning, and document and validate identities and photos (selection);
- use advanced analytics to detect anomalies or unexplained changes in the behaviour of a customer, individual or corporate, and raise alerts early (detection);
- automate AML checks, which is particularly useful to verify whether customers or related businesses are sanctioned or are PEPs (detection).

Automation does not remove oversight. In the UK, fully digital challenger banks are heavy users of automated controls using artificial intelligence, but they are under regulatory scrutiny on the quality of those controls (Box 11.1).

**Applying it to this question**

Option C reproduces the uses GARP names: automated profiling, faster due diligence through scanning, and early alerts on unexplained behaviour. The other options either overclaim (A), mislocate the technology (B) or deny a use GARP highlights (D).

**Fragile fact.** Automation is “particularly useful” for sanctions and PEP checks, but heavy reliance on it draws, rather than removes, regulatory scrutiny.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management (RegTech paragraph); Box 11.1. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q19 of 20.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It claims automation ends regulatory review and eliminates error. GARP states that challenger banks relying on AI controls are under regulatory scrutiny on the quality of those controls. A would be right only if regulators had stopped reviewing automated KYC, which GARP contradicts.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves RegTech from profiling and due diligence to setting risk appetite, a governance task the source does not assign to it. It would be right if it said profiling and due diligence are automated.

c.reason: GARP: RegTech companies “use machine-learning techniques to automate the profiling of customers, speed up the due diligence process through automated scanning . . . Advanced analytics like machine learning can help facilitate the detection of anomalies or unexplained changes in the behavior of a customer . . . and raise alerts early.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It denies the use GARP calls “particularly useful”: verifying whether customers or related businesses are sanctioned or are PEPs. D would be right if “cannot” read “can”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a fast-growing UK digital bank, with GBP 4 billion of deposits, on the findings of the FCA’s 2022 review of financial crime controls at challenger banks. The consultant’s draft summary contains the following statements:

I. The FCA saw a risk that information gathered at fast digital account opening may be insufficient to identify higher-risk customers.

II. The weaknesses that increased financial crime risk were found at the onboarding stage only, not during the customer’s tenure with the bank.

III. The FCA found weaknesses in customer due diligence and inconsistent application of enhanced due diligence, for example for PEPs.

IV. The FCA found inconsistent or inadequate rationale for ignoring monitoring alerts, and asked banks to adjust oversight to keep up with growth.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Risk consultant auditing four statements summarising the FCA’s 2022 review of financial crime controls at UK challenger banks.

**Concept and theory**

Challenger banks are fully digital and promote the ability to open accounts very quickly to attract customers. In 2022 the FCA published the latest update of its report on their financial crime controls (Box 11.1). Its findings are mapped below onto the AML framework; the step and implication columns are an interpretive teaching aid, not part of the FCA text:

| FCA finding | Framework step | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| Information at fast account opening may be insufficient to identify higher-risk customers | Selection | Strengthen customer risk assessment |
| Good practice: innovative technology to identify and verify customers quickly | Selection | Technology helps when well designed |
| Weaknesses at onboarding and during the customer’s tenure | Selection and detection | Controls needed throughout the relationship |
| Weaknesses in CDD; inconsistent EDD, for example for PEPs | Selection and prevention | Proper customer risk assessment |
| Inconsistent or inadequate rationale for ignoring alerts | Detection | Better alert management |
| Risk-based approach with continuous monitoring of controls; adjust oversight to growth | Prevention and governance | Controls must keep pace with growth |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is the FCA’s core concern: true. Statement II restricts the weaknesses to onboarding, but the FCA found weaknesses “at the customer onboarding stage as well as during the customer’s tenure”: false. Statement III matches the CDD and EDD finding: true. Statement IV matches the alert-handling finding and the recommendation to adjust oversight and control frameworks to growth: true. So I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** The FCA found weaknesses both at onboarding and during the customer’s tenure; fast digital onboarding is a risk to information quality, while innovative technology was noted as good practice.

**Reference**

LO 52.a: “Describe elements of a control framework to manage financial fraud risk and money laundering risk.” GARP Chapter 11, AML Risk Management, Box 11.1 (Financial Crime Controls at UK Challenger Banks). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser only notes that regulators have scrutinised the effectiveness and quality of challenger banks’ controls and does not list the FCA findings; content is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 a, where it is Q20 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It omits Statement IV, which reports both the alert-handling weakness and the recommendation to adjust oversight to growth. It would be right only if IV misdescribed the alerts finding.

b.reason: Box 11.1 records all three findings in Statements I, III and IV, and states that weaknesses increased financial crime risk at onboarding as well as during the customer’s tenure, which falsifies II.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts Statement II, which drops “during the customer’s tenure”, and rejects the core finding in Statement I. It would be right only if the FCA had found the weaknesses at onboarding alone and had not raised the information concern.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It accepts all four, including the narrowed Statement II. It would be right if II read “at the onboarding stage as well as during the customer’s tenure”.

questions.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 b Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore commercial bank is preparing a one-paragraph briefing note on the 2022 enforcement action against USAA Federal Savings Bank (USAA FSB) for the bank’s financial crime committee. Which of the following summaries of the enforcement action is most accurate?

options.text: USAA FSB incurred USD 140 million of fines under two separate consent orders, reached with FinCEN and the Federal Reserve, for a willful failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program.
USAA FSB incurred USD 140 million of fines under two separate consent orders, reached with FinCEN and the OCC, for a willful failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program.
USAA FSB incurred USD 140 million of fines under two separate consent orders, reached with FinCEN and the OCC, for an inadvertent failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program.
USAA FSB incurred USD 140 million of fines under a single joint consent order, reached with FinCEN and the OCC, for a willful failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Singapore bank summarising the 2022 enforcement action against USAA FSB.

**Concept and theory**

USAA Federal Savings Bank (USAA FSB) provides the banking services of the USAA group, which mainly serves US military members (a Schweser background note). In the United States, anti-money laundering (AML) obligations for banks are set by the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), and two federal bodies enforced them in this case:

- **FinCEN**, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network;
- **the OCC**, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which Schweser describes as the national banking regulator.

As general background (not set out in the source), a consent order records the outcome when a regulator and a bank settle an enforcement matter, with the bank agreeing to the order’s terms. GARP’s account of the case is precise on four facts, each of which an examiner can corrupt:

| Element | GARP’s account (Box 11.2) |
|---|---|
| Amount and date | USD 140 million, reported in March 2022 |
| Instrument | Two separate consent orders |
| Counterparties | FinCEN and the OCC |
| Characterisation | A “willful” failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program |

The word “willful” matters: it signals that regulators did not regard the failure as an innocent oversight. That fits the rest of the case, in which the bank admitted that for more than five years its program did not meet the minimum requirements of the BSA.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share the amount (USD 140 million) and the subject (a failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program). They differ in exactly one of three slots: the number of consent orders, the identity of the second regulator, and the character of the failure. Option B is the only one that gets all three slots right: two separate orders, FinCEN and the OCC, willful failure.

**Fragile fact.** Two separate consent orders, with FinCEN and the OCC (not the Federal Reserve), and the failure was “willful”.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the bank was fined by US federal regulators “including” FinCEN and the OCC and does not mention two separate consent orders; GARP is more specific and is used here. Schweser also adds that the compliance program failed to keep pace with account growth; this point is Schweser-only and is not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The second regulator is replaced by the Federal Reserve, a neighbouring US banking authority. The Federal Reserve appears elsewhere in the syllabus (for example the outsourcing guidance of the next reading), which makes the swap tempting, but in this case the orders were with FinCEN and the OCC. A would be correct only if the stem described an enforcement action reached with FinCEN and the Federal Reserve.

b.reason: Box 11.2 states that USAA FSB “incurred a fine of \$140 million from two separate consent orders reached with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)”, and that the fines were levied because of the bank’s “willful” failure to implement and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program. Every element of B matches.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** “Willful” is reversed to “inadvertent”. The regulators specifically characterised the failure as willful, which is the opposite of inadvertent. C would be correct only for a case in which the regulator accepted that the breach was unintentional.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The two separate consent orders are collapsed into a single joint order. The total of USD 140 million came from two separate orders, one with each regulator. D would be correct only if the stem stated that FinCEN and the OCC issued one joint order.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.
questions.reading: ORR-11: Financial Crime and Fraud
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 b Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US savings bank is benchmarking the bank’s BSA/AML program against the findings in the USAA FSB consent orders. She drafts the following statements for her working papers:

I. USAA FSB admitted that its failure to implement and maintain an adequate AML program ran from January 2016 through April 2021.

II. USAA FSB admitted that its AML program met the minimum requirements of the BSA but fell short of supervisory expectations for a bank of its size.

III. The deficiencies cited by the OCC included suspicious activity identification, evaluation and reporting, as well as third-party risk management.

IV. FinCEN’s consent order found that the bank’s BSA/AML compliance department was significantly understaffed.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a US savings bank checking four statements on USAA FSB’s admitted failures and cited deficiencies.

**Concept and theory**

A regulatory finding is more than “the bank was weak”. In USAA FSB’s case the consent orders recorded three layers of fact:

1. **An admission and a period.** From January 2016 through April 2021, USAA FSB admitted that it failed to implement and maintain an AML program that met the minimum requirements of the BSA. Five years of failure is the backbone of the “accumulated failings” lesson.
2. **The OCC’s list of deficiencies.** The OCC consent order cited “inadequate internal controls and risk management practices; suspicious activity identification, evaluation, and reporting; staffing; training; and third-party risk management, among others”.
3. **FinCEN’s addition.** FinCEN’s consent order added that the BSA/AML compliance department was “significantly understaffed”, with the shortage filled by third-party contractors.

The distinction between “minimum requirements” and “best practice” is the key trap. A bank that meets the BSA minimum but falls short of good practice has a supervisory issue; a bank that fails the minimum has a legal breach. USAA FSB was in the second category.

**Applying it to this question**

- Statement I: matches the admitted period, January 2016 through April 2021. **Correct.**
- Statement II: claims the program met the BSA minimum. GARP says the bank admitted it failed to meet the minimum. **Incorrect.**
- Statement III: suspicious activity identification, evaluation and reporting, and third-party risk management are both on the OCC’s list. **Correct.**
- Statement IV: the “significantly understaffed” finding is FinCEN’s. **Correct.**

The correct set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** USAA FSB failed the BSA minimum requirements (January 2016 to April 2021); “significantly understaffed” is FinCEN’s wording, while the OCC listed staffing among its deficiencies.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser summarises the period as “at least five years (between 2016 and 2021)” and does not reproduce the OCC’s list of deficiencies; GARP’s fuller account is used. No conflict on substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** A accepts I and III but rejects IV. The likely reasoning is that staffing appears in the OCC’s list, so the reader concludes that the understaffing finding was the OCC’s and that a FinCEN finding on staffing is invented. In fact both regulators addressed staffing, and the phrase “significantly understaffed” comes from FinCEN’s order. A would be correct only if IV attributed a finding to FinCEN that FinCEN never made.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B accepts II, which reverses “failed to meet the minimum requirements” into “met the minimum requirements”, and it also drops two true statements, I and III. B would be correct only for a bank whose program cleared the BSA minimum and whose findings were limited to staffing.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C includes the reversed statement II and omits the true FinCEN finding in IV. C would be correct only if the admission had been about falling short of best practice and FinCEN had made no staffing finding.

d.reason: Box 11.2 records the admission for January 2016 through April 2021 (I), the OCC’s list including suspicious activity identification, evaluation and reporting and third-party risk management (III), and FinCEN’s statement that the compliance department was significantly understaffed (IV). Statement II contradicts the admission that the program did not meet the minimum requirements of the BSA.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of an Australian retail bank faces a sharp rise in AML case work with a tight regulatory deadline and plans to supplement her team with third-party contractors. Before approving the plan, the board asks what the USAA FSB case shows about the use of contractors. Which of the following statements best reflects the regulatory finding on this point?

options.text: Supplementing scarce staff with contractors is not unusual in banking; the failing was that USAA FSB did not train them or ensure they had satisfactory qualifications and expertise.
Supplementing scarce staff with contractors is not permitted for BSA/AML work; the failing was that USAA FSB engaged contractors for that work in the first place.
Supplementing scarce staff with contractors is not unusual in banking; the failing was that the OCC, which had approved them, did not train them or check their qualifications.
Supplementing scarce staff with contractors is not unusual in banking; the failing was that USAA FSB used them during AML remediation work rather than in business as usual.

questions.solution:
Australian bank’s chief compliance officer planning to use contractors; what the USAA FSB case shows about contractors.

**Concept and theory**

AML work is labour-intensive: every alert raised by a monitoring system has to be reviewed by a person who can judge whether the activity is suspicious and, if it is, escalate it and file a report. When the work spikes, banks often bring in third-party contractors. GARP’s case commentary makes three linked points:

1. **The root cause was understaffing.** FinCEN found USAA FSB’s BSA/AML compliance department “significantly understaffed”, with the shortage supplemented by third-party contractors.
2. **Using contractors is not itself the problem.** GARP notes that the practice “is not unusual in banking, especially when institutions face large spikes in workload accompanied with tight deadlines, which is common in AML remediation programs.”
3. **The failing was competence assurance.** Regulators stated that the bank “failed to properly train or otherwise ensure these contractors possessed satisfactory qualifications and expertise”, which “only made the problem worse”.

The lesson is a third-party risk management one: outsourcing capacity does not outsource accountability. The bank remains responsible for ensuring that whoever reviews alerts is trained and qualified, which is why third-party risk management was also on the OCC’s list of deficiencies.

**Applying it to this question**

The CCO’s situation (a spike in case work and a tight deadline) is exactly the circumstance in which GARP says contractor use is common. The board’s question is therefore not “may we use contractors?” but “what went wrong when USAA FSB did?”. The deciding fact is the regulators’ statement that USAA FSB did not train the contractors or ensure their qualifications and expertise.

**Fragile fact.** The finding was not “used contractors” but “failed to train or ensure the qualifications and expertise of” contractors brought in because of understaffing.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the bank “failed to adequately train these contractors in AML compliance matters” and omits GARP’s comment that the practice is not unusual; GARP is used for that point. No conflict on substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: It combines both halves of GARP’s account: the practice is not unusual in banking, and the failing was the absence of training and of checks on qualifications and expertise.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** B turns “not unusual” into “not permitted” and makes the mere engagement of contractors the breach. GARP describes the practice as common and locates the failing in training and qualifications. B would be correct only if a rule prohibited contractors from performing BSA/AML reviews.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** C identifies the right failing (no training, no check on qualifications) but assigns it to the wrong actor: the OCC. The regulators’ statement is that the bank failed to train its contractors or ensure their qualifications and expertise; nothing in the case suggests the OCC approved or was responsible for them. The bank, not its supervisor, is accountable for the people it engages. C would be correct only in a regime where the supervisor itself approved and trained a bank’s contractors.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D takes a circumstance that GARP mentions as typical (AML remediation programs) and turns it into the failing. GARP cites remediation programs as an example of when contractor use is common, not as an improper setting. D would be correct only if the regulators had objected to the timing or setting of contractor use rather than to their training.

questions.question:
A senior risk consultant is reviewing the AML remediation plan of a Brazilian bank whose compliance department, like that of USAA FSB, is short of permanent staff and relies on agency contractors to review monitoring alerts. The plan lists four actions with their estimated costs.

| Action | Description | Cost (BRL m) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Raise alert thresholds to halve the monthly alert volume | 1.5 |
| 2 | Commission a review of all client files for the past five years | 18.0 |
| 3 | Verify contractor qualifications and deliver AML training before contractors review alerts | 2.4 |
| 4 | Appoint a dedicated money laundering risk officer accountable for AML | 0.9 |

Which action most directly addresses the contractor-related finding in the USAA FSB case?

options.text: Action 1
Action 2
Action 3
Action 4

questions.solution:
Consultant choosing which remediation action at a Brazilian bank addresses the USAA contractor finding.

**Concept and theory**

The USAA FSB findings are a bundle of distinct failures, and each has its own remedy. Matching the remedy to the finding is the practical skill this LO tests.

| Finding or lesson (GARP Chapter 11) | Matching remedy |
|---|---|
| Contractors not trained, qualifications and expertise not ensured | Verify qualifications; deliver AML training before contractors review alerts |
| Monitoring system too sensitive, unmanageable alerts | Recalibrate (parametrize) the system and run a false positive and false negative feedback loop |
| After regulatory findings: lookback | Review all client files for a specified period, verify, file reports, close accounts |
| Governance (control framework, LO 52.a) | Dedicated money laundering risk officer accountable for AML |

A remedy can be sensible in general and still fail to address the specific finding in question.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem fixes the finding: the bank relies on agency contractors to review alerts, as USAA FSB did. The regulators’ complaint at USAA FSB was that the bank “failed to properly train or otherwise ensure these contractors possessed satisfactory qualifications and expertise”. The only action aimed at that complaint is Action 3. The cost column is irrelevant: the question asks which action addresses the finding, not which is cheapest.

**Fragile fact.** Match remedy to finding: contractor finding means train and qualify; alert finding means parametrize and feed back; post-sanction means lookback.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”; the MLRO point in option D is from the section “AML Risk Management” (LO 52.a) and is used only as a distractor. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q4 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Action 1 answers a different USAA finding, the over-sensitive monitoring system that created an unmanageable number of alerts. It would be the right answer if the stem asked which action addresses the alert backlog (and even then GARP’s lesson is proper parametrization with a feedback loop, not simply halving volume).

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Action 2 is a lookback, the costly remediation program that GARP says typically follows regulatory findings and sanctions. It deals with the legacy of past failures across all client files, not with the competence of the contractors now reviewing alerts. It would be correct if the stem asked what remediation a regulator would typically require after sanctions.

c.reason: Action 3 (verify contractor qualifications and deliver AML training before contractors review alerts) is the direct mirror of the regulators’ statement in Box 11.2.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Action 4 is an element of the general AML control framework (governance, LO 52.a): GARP says a dedicated money laundering risk officer is mandatory in most jurisdictions. It is sound practice but does not address contractor training or qualifications. It would be correct if the stem asked which action strengthens AML governance and accountability.

questions.question: The head of model validation at a Japanese bank is preparing a report on what went wrong with the transaction monitoring system that USAA FSB implemented in the first quarter of 2021. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.text: FinCEN found the system insufficiently sensitive, so it missed suspicious activity; by the end of 2021 about 90,000 suspicious transactions had gone unreported.
FinCEN found the system too sensitive; the resulting backlog delayed the detection of suspicious activity but not its reporting, because alerts were already logged.
FinCEN found the system too sensitive; by the end of 2021 the backlog stood at about 6,900 unreviewed alerts and about 90,000 unreviewed cases.
FinCEN found the system too sensitive; by the end of 2021 the backlog stood at about 90,000 unreviewed alerts and about 6,900 unreviewed cases.

questions.solution:
Head of model validation at a Japanese bank describing what went wrong with USAA FSB’s 2021 monitoring system.

**Concept and theory**

A transaction monitoring system screens account activity against rules or models and raises an alert when activity looks abnormal. An analyst reviews each alert; alerts that merit further work are grouped into cases, which are investigated and, where warranted, end in a suspicious activity report to the authorities. The chain is therefore:

transactions → alerts → cases → suspicious activity reports

(This alert, case and report chain is general background to make the figures readable; it is not set out in the source.) Because many alerts are closed without becoming cases, a backlog will normally contain far more unreviewed alerts than unreviewed cases.

USAA FSB implemented a new transaction monitoring system in the first quarter of 2021. FinCEN described it as “too sensitive” and said it “creates an unmanageable number of alerts and cases”. As of the end of 2021, the backlog was about **90,000 unreviewed alerts** and **6,900 unreviewed** **cases**, and the backlogs “lead to unreasonable delays in the detection and reporting of potentially suspicious activity”.

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts decide this question: the direction of the problem (too sensitive, not too insensitive), the consequence (delays in both detection and reporting), and the allocation of the two figures (90,000 alerts, 6,900 cases). Only D gets all three right.

**Fragile fact.** Too sensitive; about 90,000 unreviewed alerts and 6,900 unreviewed cases at end-2021; delays in detection and reporting.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser gives “close to 90,000 unreviewed alerts and nearly 7,000 unreviewed cases” and dates the system to 2021; GARP gives 6,900 and the first quarter of 2021. This is rounding, not a version difference; GARP’s figures are used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A reverses “too sensitive” into “insufficiently sensitive” and turns 90,000 unreviewed alerts into 90,000 unreported suspicious transactions. The problem was too many alerts, not too few. A would be correct for a system whose thresholds were so loose that it missed suspicious activity.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B accepts the delay in detection but drops reporting. FinCEN said the backlogs led to unreasonable delays in the detection and reporting of potentially suspicious activity: an alert that has not been reviewed cannot be reported, however well it is logged. B would be correct only if review were not a precondition for reporting.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** C swaps the two figures, giving 6,900 alerts and 90,000 cases. (The general background in part a also suggests that more unreviewed cases than alerts would be unusual, but the deciding fact is the source’s own figures.) C would be correct only if the two figures in the source were reversed.

d.reason: It reproduces FinCEN’s characterisation (too sensitive) and the end-2021 backlog exactly as Box 11.2 reports it: around 90,000 unreviewed alerts and 6,900 unreviewed cases.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a Chinese commercial bank is choosing between two configurations of a new transaction monitoring system. The vendor recommends Configuration X because “it catches more”. Pilot results are shown below.

| Configuration | Alerts generated per month | Alerts reviewable per month | Annual licence (CNY m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 40 000 | 9000 | 3.2 |
| Y | 8500 | 9000 | 2.6 |

Which assessment of Configuration X is most consistent with the lessons of the USAA FSB case?

options.text: It is preferable, because higher sensitivity maximises detection and any backlog can be cleared later through a lookback.
It would recreate USAA FSB’s failure, because alerts beyond review capacity build a backlog that delays detection and reporting.
It is acceptable if contractors review the surplus alerts, because USAA FSB’s regulators objected to the alert count rather than to the reviewers.
It is acceptable, because regulators impose fines only once a backlog has been shown to conceal an actual money laundering case.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank’s CRO choosing a monitoring configuration whose alerts exceed review capacity.

**Concept and theory**

A monitoring control has two halves: the system that raises alerts and the people who review them. An alert is only a potential control. It becomes a real control when someone reviews it, decides whether the activity is suspicious and, if so, reports it. A system that raises more alerts than the institution can review therefore does not add detection; it adds a queue.

This is the central operational lesson of USAA FSB’s 2021 system. FinCEN described the system as “too sensitive”, creating “an unmanageable number of alerts and cases”. The backlog (around 90,000 unreviewed alerts and 6,900 unreviewed cases by the end of 2021) led to “unreasonable delays in the detection and reporting of potentially suspicious activity”. GARP’s wider lesson is that detection systems need proper parametrization and a feedback loop on false positives and false negatives, so that the volume of alerts is meaningful and manageable.

**Applying it to this question**

Compare alerts generated with alerts reviewable each month:

Configuration X: 40,000 − 9,000 = 31,000 unreviewed alerts added each month

Configuration Y: 8,500 − 9,000 = −500 (spare capacity of 500 alerts each month)

Configuration X builds a backlog of 31,000 alerts every month, the USAA FSB pattern. The licence cost is irrelevant to the question: the issue is whether the control can operate, not what it costs. The vendor’s claim that X “catches more” confuses alerts raised with suspicious activity detected and reported.

**Fragile fact.** More alerts is not more detection: an unreviewed alert delays detection and reporting, and at USAA FSB the system was too sensitive.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”; GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2) for the parametrization and feedback-loop lesson. Schweser frames the same lesson as ensuring that alerts “do not create a large number of false positives or false negatives, and that the number of alerts is manageable”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A treats more sensitivity as unambiguously better, which reverses the case’s lesson: at USAA FSB, excess sensitivity was the problem. It also misuses the lookback, which GARP describes as a costly remediation program imposed after regulatory findings, not a planned way to clear a backlog. A would be correct only if review capacity were unlimited.

b.reason: It states the USAA FSB mechanism: alerts beyond review capacity build a backlog, and the backlog delays both the detection and the reporting of potentially suspicious activity (Box 11.2).

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C treats the alert count as the regulators’ only concern and treats contractors as a free fix. The USAA FSB regulators objected both to the unmanageable alert volume and to the use of contractors who were not trained or qualified. C would be correct only if the stem specified that the contractors were trained and qualified and that their capacity covered the full surplus.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D adds a condition that the case explicitly rejects: that fines require a demonstrated laundering case. GARP states that the USAA FSB fines were due to a lack of control over AML risk, not demonstrated AML cases. D would be correct only in a regime where penalties were limited to proven laundering.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-11 b Q7
questions.question: At a meeting of the risk committee of a German bank, a board member argues: “We have never had a money laundering incident, so our exposure to AML enforcement action is low.” The chief risk officer responds by citing the USAA FSB case. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The USAA FSB fines were due to a lack of control over AML risk rather than demonstrated AML cases, so a weak control environment alone can warrant fines.
The USAA FSB fines were due to a laundering case traced through its alert backlog rather than to control design, so a proven incident remains the usual trigger.
The USAA FSB fines were due to a lack of control over AML risk rather than demonstrated AML cases, but outside the United States fines still require a proven case.
The USAA FSB fines were due to a lack of control over AML risk rather than demonstrated AML cases, but fines follow only once customers have suffered losses.

questions.solution:
German bank’s CRO rebutting a board member who equates no incidents with low AML enforcement risk.

**Concept and theory**

A common intuition is that regulators punish banks for what went wrong: a laundering scheme uncovered, money lost. The USAA FSB case contradicts that intuition. GARP introduces the case by saying that USAA FSB was required to pay USD 140 million “for failure to address persistent weaknesses in its AML risk management program”, and that “the fines were due to a lack of control over AML risk, not because of demonstrated AML cases.” It then draws the general lesson: “A weak control environment is sufficient to warrant fines by regulators, and not only in the United States.”

Why would regulators fine a bank that has no proven case? Because the purpose of AML regulation is to keep criminals and terrorists out of the financial system. A bank that cannot demonstrate that its controls are designed and operating effectively is exposed whether or not a case has yet surfaced; indeed, weak monitoring makes it less likely that a case would be detected. The regulatory standard is therefore the control environment, not the incident record.

**Applying it to this question**

The board member’s argument assumes that enforcement exposure depends on incidents. The deciding fact is GARP’s statement that USAA FSB was fined for lack of control over AML risk, not for demonstrated cases, so a weak control environment alone can warrant fines. Option A states exactly that. The bank’s clean incident record is not evidence of effective controls.

**Fragile fact.** The fine was for the control environment, not for an incident: no demonstrated AML case was needed, in the United States or elsewhere.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser states the same point (fines “not imposed because of known thefts or AML cases” but because of a lack of adequate controls and an ineffective program). No conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: It reproduces both halves of GARP’s statement: lack of control, not demonstrated cases, and a weak control environment is sufficient to warrant fines.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B invents a demonstrated case (a laundering scheme traced through the backlog) and makes a proven incident the trigger. GARP says the fines were not because of demonstrated AML cases. B would be correct for a bank fined after a specific laundering scheme was found.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C accepts the US lesson but confines it geographically. GARP adds “and not only in the United States”, noting that banks in the EU, the UK and Asia have been fined for being unable to demonstrate that their AML controls are properly designed and operate effectively. C would be correct only if non-US regulators required a proven case before fining.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D adds an unsupported trigger: customer losses. Nothing in the case links the fine to losses suffered by customers; the basis was the inadequacy of the AML program itself. D would be correct only under a regime that fined banks solely for consumer harm.

questions.question: A senior examiner at a Canadian supervisory authority is training new examiners. She describes four hypothetical banks and asks which one most closely mirrors the basis on which USAA FSB was penalised.

options.text: Bank P: its AML controls were documented and tested as effective, but law enforcement later uncovered a CAD 900 million layering scheme run through one client’s accounts.
Bank Q: its AML controls were otherwise effective, but one suspicious activity report was filed two days late during a single overnight outage of its monitoring system.
Bank R: no laundering case has been proven, but for several years it has been unable to demonstrate that its AML controls are properly designed and operate effectively.
Bank S: no laundering case has been proven, but a business customer defrauded it by misstating collateral values in a loan application to obtain a larger facility.

questions.solution:
Canadian examiner asking which of four hypothetical banks mirrors the basis of the USAA FSB penalty.

**Concept and theory**

The basis of a penalty is the fact pattern the regulator relied on. In USAA FSB’s case GARP identifies it precisely:

- **No demonstrated case.** The fines were due to a lack of control over AML risk, not demonstrated AML cases.
- **Persistence.** The bank failed to address persistent weaknesses in its AML risk management program, over a period that ran from January 2016 through April 2021.
- **Demonstration of controls.** The international parallel is banks fined “for being unable to demonstrate that their AML controls have been properly designed and operate effectively”.

The three features distinguish the USAA pattern from three neighbours: a single incident at a well-controlled bank, a one-off operational lapse, and a fraud loss that is not an AML matter at all.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each bank against the three features:

| Bank | No proven case | Persistent weakness | Cannot demonstrate effective AML controls |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | No | No | No (tested as effective) |
| Q | Yes | No (single lapse) | No (otherwise effective) |
| R | Yes | Yes (several years) | Yes |
| S | Yes | Not stated | Not an AML control failure |

Only Bank R has all three features.

**Fragile fact.** The USAA basis has three features at once: no proven case, persistent multi-year weakness, inability to demonstrate effective AML controls.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2); GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure” for the January 2016 to April 2021 period. The external fraud example in option D is from the section “External Fraud Management” (LO 52.a). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Bank P has the opposite profile: effective, tested controls and a proven laundering scheme. Its exposure arises from an incident, which the case says was not the basis of the USAA FSB fines. A would be correct if the question asked which bank’s situation is driven by a demonstrated AML case.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Bank Q has a single, short operational lapse at an otherwise effective program. The USAA FSB basis was persistent weakness across the whole program over several years, leading to unreasonable delays in detection and reporting. B would be correct only if the case had involved an isolated late filing.

c.reason: Bank R combines no proven laundering case with a multi-year inability to demonstrate that its AML controls are properly designed and operate effectively, which is GARP’s description of the USAA FSB basis and of the international cases that parallel it.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Bank S describes external fraud by a customer (misrepresentation of collateral values in a loan application), which GARP classifies under external fraud management (LO 52.a), not AML control failure. D would be correct if the question asked for an example of first-party external fraud.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK building society is presenting the USAA FSB case to newly hired analysts and wants a single slide on what the case teaches about responding to regulatory findings. Which of the following statements best describes that lesson?

options.text: Heavy regulatory fines do not come out of the blue: they result from years of accumulated failings and procrastination in making the changes that regulators require.
Heavy regulatory fines usually come without warning, so the main lesson is to hold provisions for them rather than to reorder the remediation of findings.
Heavy regulatory fines result from years of accumulated failings, although most firms implement the required changes early, so the main lesson concerns technology choice.
Heavy regulatory fines result from years of accumulated failings, but completing the required changes just before the regulator’s deadline reliably avoids them.

questions.solution:
UK building society analyst summarising the USAA FSB lesson on responding to regulatory findings.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes Box 11.2 with its headline lesson: “Ignore regulatory findings at one’s own peril.” The reasoning has three steps:

1. **Fines are not sudden.** “Heavy regulatory fines do not come out of the blue: They result from years of accumulated failings and procrastination about implementing the necessary changes and improvements required by regulators.”
2. **Why firms procrastinate.** “Transformations are effortful, change is uncomfortable”, so most firms postpone implementing changes in response to regulatory findings until the last minute.
3. **Why that fails.** Leaving change to the last minute “is often too late, as in the case of USAA”.

In USAA FSB’s case the failings ran from January 2016 through April 2021. The lesson for any institution is that a regulatory finding starts a clock: the longer it stays open, the more the accumulated failings resemble the pattern that precedes heavy penalties.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide needs the lesson in GARP’s terms. Three options start from the same true premise (fines come from accumulated failings) and then corrupt one element. Only A keeps both elements: fines are not sudden, and they follow procrastination in making required changes.

**Fragile fact.** Most firms postpone change until the last minute, and that is often too late; fines follow years of accumulated failings.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”, closing paragraphs. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not state this lesson. Moreover, its module quiz on the case treats “previously flagged deficiencies have not been satisfactorily addressed” as an inferior reason for the fine, whereas GARP introduces the case as a “failure to address persistent weaknesses” and draws this lesson. GARP is used; the question tests the lesson as GARP states it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: It is a direct statement of GARP’s lesson in Box 11.2: heavy fines do not come out of the blue; they follow years of accumulated failings and procrastination about implementing changes required by regulators.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses “do not come out of the blue” into “usually come without warning” and draws the wrong action from it (provisioning rather than remediation). B would be correct only if fines were unrelated to the bank’s record of findings.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C keeps the accumulated-failings premise but reverses GARP’s observation on firm behaviour: GARP says most firms postpone changes until the last minute, not that they implement them early. It then shifts the lesson to technology choice. C would be correct only if firms typically remediated findings promptly.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D treats last-minute completion as a reliable defence. GARP says the opposite: postponing until the last minute is often too late, as at USAA FSB. D would be correct only if regulators assessed nothing but formal closure before the deadline.

A risk consultant is reviewing the regulatory findings tracker of an Australian bank with total assets of AUD 48 billion. The regulator has set 31 December 2026 as the final date for closing all three findings.

| Finding | Year raised | Status | Planned closure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transaction monitoring calibration | 2022 | Open, deferred three times | Q4 2026 |
| AML training coverage of staff | 2023 | Open, deferred twice | Q4 2026 |
| Contractor qualification checks | 2024 | Open | Q4 2026 |

Which assessment is most consistent with the lessons of the USAA FSB case?

options.text: The open findings pose mainly reputational risk, because none of them has yet produced a demonstrated money laundering case at the bank.
The open findings are acceptable, because every planned closure falls before the regulator’s final date of 31 December 2026.
The open findings can be given lower priority, because fines are triggered by newly raised findings rather than by older open ones.
The repeatedly deferred findings show the accumulated failings that precede heavy fines, so remediation should be brought forward.

questions.solution:
Consultant assessing an Australian bank’s repeatedly deferred regulatory findings against the USAA FSB lesson.

**Concept and theory**

The USAA FSB case teaches that the timeline of a bank’s response to findings is itself a risk indicator. GARP’s commentary:

- heavy regulatory fines “result from years of accumulated failings and procrastination about implementing the necessary changes and improvements required by regulators”;
- most firms “postpone implementing changes in response to regulatory findings until the last minute, and often this is too late, as in the case of USAA”;
- the fines in the case were due to a lack of control over AML risk, not demonstrated AML cases.

So a findings tracker that shows the same items deferred again and again, all bunched up against the final date, is a warning sign, not a comfort.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the tracker as a timeline. The calibration finding was raised in 2022 and has been deferred three times; the training finding was raised in 2023 and deferred twice; all three findings are now scheduled for the last quarter before the deadline. That is the pattern GARP describes: years of accumulated failings and procrastination, with everything left to the last minute. The findings also mirror USAA FSB’s own deficiencies (monitoring calibration, training, contractor qualifications). The total assets figure (AUD 48 billion) is irrelevant to the assessment.

**Fragile fact.** Age and repeated deferral of a finding raise the enforcement risk; last-minute closure is “often too late”.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, Box 11.2 “USAA to Pay \$140 Million of Fines in AML Management Failure”, closing paragraphs; GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2) for the “not demonstrated AML cases” point. GARP vs Schweser: as noted for Q9, Schweser does not state the procrastination lesson; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A assumes that without a demonstrated laundering case the exposure is mainly reputational. GARP states that the USAA FSB fines (USD 140 million) were due to a lack of control over AML risk, not demonstrated AML cases. A would be correct only in a regime that fined banks solely for proven laundering.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B treats closure before the deadline as sufficient. GARP warns that postponing changes until the last minute is often too late, as in the USAA case. B would be correct only if the findings had been remediated promptly and the planned dates had not slipped.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses the lesson by treating older open findings as less dangerous than new ones. GARP says fines result from years of accumulated failings: the age and repeated deferral of a finding increase, not decrease, the risk. C would be correct only if regulators disregarded findings once they had been open for some time.

d.reason: It recognises the repeatedly deferred findings as the accumulated failings that precede heavy fines, and draws GARP’s conclusion that remediation should be brought forward rather than left to the last minute.

questions.question: A policy analyst at a US banking regulator is writing a note on whether the USAA FSB case is an isolated US phenomenon. Which of the following statements about the international context of the case is most accurate?

options.text: Fines for weak AML control environments are largely confined to the United States; Asia-Pacific fines of USD 5.1 billion in 2020 related only to proven laundering cases.
Banks in the EU, the UK and Asia have also been fined for being unable to demonstrate effective AML controls; Asia-Pacific fines reached USD 5.1 billion in 2020, a seven-fold rise on 2019.
Banks in the EU, the UK and Asia have also been fined for being unable to demonstrate effective AML controls; Asia-Pacific fines reached USD 5.1 billion in 2020, a seven-fold fall on 2019.
Banks in the EU, the UK and Asia have also been fined for being unable to demonstrate effective AML controls; the FATF imposed fines of USD 5.1 billion on Asia-Pacific banks in 2020.

questions.solution:
US policy analyst assessing whether the USAA FSB case is an isolated US phenomenon.

**Concept and theory**

GARP uses the USAA FSB case to make a point about AML enforcement in general, not only about one bank. Immediately after stating that a weak control environment is sufficient to warrant fines “and not only in the United States”, it adds:

- Banks in the EU, the UK and Asia have been fined, sometimes heavily, “for being unable to demonstrate that their AML controls have been properly designed and operate effectively”.
- In 2020, authorities based in the Asia-Pacific region issued fines totalling **USD 5.1 billion** for breaches of AML laws and related misconduct, which “corresponds to a seven-fold increase from 2019”.

Two features of this context are easy to corrupt: the direction of the change (a sharp rise, not a fall) and the actor (national and regional authorities in the Asia-Pacific region issue the fines). The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), mentioned in GARP’s footnotes, is described there as an independent inter-governmental body that develops and promotes policies against money laundering and terrorist financing, and whose Recommendations are recognised as the global AML and counter-terrorist financing standard. Nothing in the source describes it as imposing fines; it is a standard setter.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst’s question is whether the USAA pattern (fines for an inability to demonstrate effective controls) is unique to the United States. GARP says it is not, and supports the point with the Asia-Pacific figure. Three options carry the correct premise about the EU, the UK and Asia; they differ in the direction of the change and the identity of the fining body. Only B has the rise and the right actor.

**Fragile fact.** Asia-Pacific authorities, 2020, USD 5.1 billion, seven-fold increase on 2019; the FATF sets standards, it does not fine.

**Reference**

LO 52.b: “Summarize the regulatory findings and describe the lessons learned from the USAA case study.” GARP Chapter 11, Case Study: Financial Crime and Fraud, section “Case Study” (text introducing and following Box 11.2); the FATF description is from the footnote to the section “AML Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says only that the USAA FSB case is one of a growing number of cases globally and omits the Asia-Pacific figure; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-11 b, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A confines the pattern to the United States and attributes the Asia-Pacific fines to proven laundering cases. GARP says the pattern is “not only in the United States” and that non-US banks were fined for being unable to demonstrate effective controls; the Asia-Pacific figure covers breaches of AML laws and related misconduct. A would be correct only if non-US fines required proof of laundering.

b.reason: It matches GARP’s text: banks in the EU, the UK and Asia fined for being unable to demonstrate effective AML controls, and Asia-Pacific authorities’ fines of USD 5.1 billion in 2020, a seven-fold increase from 2019.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses “seven-fold increase” into “seven-fold fall”. C would be correct only if Asia-Pacific fines in 2019 had been about seven times their 2020 level.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D gives the right figure and year but the wrong actor. The fines were issued by authorities based in the Asia-Pacific region; the source describes the FATF as a body that develops and promotes policies and standards, not as an authority that fines banks. D would be correct only if the stem described the FATF as an enforcement authority.
