questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q13
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a regional bank is dealing with a billing disagreement with its domestic mortgage subservicer. The subservicer has threatened to stop servicing the bank’s loans until the disagreement is settled. Which of the following best describes what the dispute resolution provision of the agreement should have contained?

options.text: Express choice-of-law and jurisdictional terms, so that any disagreement is adjudicated under the laws of a single, specific jurisdiction.
Suspension of all services until the dispute is resolved, so that neither party is prejudiced by continuing to perform during the disagreement.
Referral of every disagreement to litigation in the institution’s home courts, so that each dispute ends with an enforceable judgment.
A process to expedite problem resolution that also addresses the continuation of the arrangement between the parties during the dispute resolution period.

questions.solution:
CCO facing a billing dispute in which the domestic subservicer threatens to stop servicing.

**Concept and theory**

In an outsourcing relationship a disagreement can do more damage than the amount in dispute, because the provider controls a service the institution depends on. The **dispute resolution** provision addresses both the disagreement and the service. GARP: agreements should include a dispute resolution process in order to (1) expedite problem resolution and (2) address the continuation of the arrangement between the parties during the dispute resolution period. The second purpose is the distinctive one: the clause is designed so that a billing or performance dispute does not interrupt the outsourced activity.

It is distinct from the foreign-based service provider provision, which concerns which law and jurisdiction govern disputes with a provider located abroad.

**Applying it to this question**

The subservicer is domestic, so choice of law across borders is not the issue. The threat to stop servicing is exactly the risk the second limb of the provision addresses. The right description must combine speed of resolution with continuation of the arrangement.

**Fragile fact.** Dispute resolution has two jobs: expedite resolution and keep the arrangement running during the dispute; choice of law is a different provision.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Dispute resolution”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says “resolve disputes quickly and minimize disruption during a dispute”; GARP’s “continuation of the arrangement” is used. Consistent in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q13 of 22.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Express choice-of-law and jurisdictional terms under a single jurisdiction belong to the foreign-based service providers provision. A would be right if the provider were based abroad and the question asked how to avoid conflicting national laws.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Suspending services during the dispute is the outcome the provision is meant to prevent; GARP wants the arrangement’s continuation addressed. B would be right only if the guidance treated suspension as the protective default.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** Mandatory litigation of every disagreement works against “expedite problem resolution” and says nothing about continuation. The guidance asks for a process, not a forum rule. C would be right only if the guidance required every dispute to be litigated.

d.reason: It states both limbs of GARP’s dispute resolution provision: a process to expedite problem resolution and to address continuation of the arrangement during the dispute resolution period.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q14
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of the U.S. operations of an Australian banking group, which reports to its parent in AUD, is reviewing a fund administration provider’s proposal to cap its contractual liability. The figures below have been converted into AUD.

| Item | AUD million |
|---|---|
| Annual fees payable to the provider | 0.9 |
| Proposed liability cap (12 months of fees) | 0.9 |
| Estimated loss to the institution if the provider fails to perform | 45.0 |

The provider employs about 1,200 staff across three countries. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The provider’s board should judge whether the cap is reasonable relative to the fees the provider earns, since the cap limits the provider’s own exposure.
The institution’s legal counsel alone should approve the cap, since a limitation on liability is a legal drafting matter rather than a risk decision.
The institution’s board of directors and senior management should determine whether the cap is reasonable when compared to the risks to the institution if the provider fails to perform.
The institution should reject the cap outright, since the guidance does not permit service providers to limit their liability contractually.

questions.solution:
CRO of an Australian group’s U.S. operations evaluating a provider’s proposed liability cap.

**Concept and theory**

Providers commonly seek to cap their exposure, typically at a multiple of fees. A low cap shifts the residual loss from a provider failure back onto the institution. The **limits on liability** provision does not forbid caps; it assigns the decision and sets the test. GARP: service providers may want to contractually limit their liability. The board of directors and senior management of the financial institution should determine whether the proposed limitations are reasonable when compared to the risks to the institution if a service provider fails to perform.

This fits the wider principle in Section 12.3: using service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility for outsourced activities, so a decision that leaves residual risk with the institution belongs at that level.

**Applying it to this question**

The comparison the guidance asks for can be expressed as a coverage ratio:

Coverage ratio $= \frac{\text{Liability cap}}{\text{Estimated loss if the provider fails to perform}}$

$= \frac{0.9}{45.0} =$ 0.02 = 2%

Residual loss retained = 45.0 − 0.9 = 44.1 AUD million

The cap equals 12 months of fees (AUD 0.9 million) but would cover only about 2% of the estimated loss, leaving about AUD 44.1 million with the institution. Whether that is acceptable is exactly the judgement the board and senior management must make. The headcount is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** The institution’s board and senior management decide; the benchmark is the risk to the institution if the provider fails, not the fees.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Limits on liability”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says providers may limit liability “subject to approval by the financial institution’s board of directors and management team” but omits GARP’s reasonableness criterion; GARP is used. Consistent on the actors.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q14 of 22.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The provider’s board is not the decision-maker, and fees earned are not the benchmark. The guidance compares the cap with the institution’s risk. A would be right only if the guidance sought to protect the provider’s exposure.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Legal counsel reviews contracts before execution, but the guidance assigns the reasonableness judgement on liability limits to the board and senior management, because it is a risk acceptance decision. B would be right only if the question asked who reviews the contract drafting.

c.reason: It names the correct actors (the institution’s board of directors and senior management) and the correct criterion (reasonableness compared with the risks to the institution if the provider fails to perform).

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP explicitly contemplates providers seeking to limit liability and asks the institution to assess reasonableness. There is no prohibition. D would be right only if the guidance banned limitation clauses.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q15
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing an agreement under which a provider runs the call centre that receives and resolves complaints from the bank’s credit card customers. Which of the following draft clauses is most consistent with the guidance?

options.text: The agreement specifies each party’s responsibilities for responding to complaints and, as the provider resolves them, requires it to give the bank summary reports tracking their status and resolution.
The agreement assigns all complaint handling to the bank, since the guidance does not allow a service provider to take responsibility for resolving customer complaints.
The agreement requires the provider, which resolves the complaints, to report to the bank only those complaints that have escalated into litigation or regulatory action.
The agreement requires the bank to send the provider summary reports tracking the status and resolution of complaints, since the provider is the party resolving them.

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst reviewing complaint-handling terms for an outsourced call centre.

**Concept and theory**

Customers experience the institution through whoever answers the phone. When a provider deals with customers, the institution still bears the reputational and regulatory consequences of how complaints are handled, so it needs both clarity of roles and visibility. The **customer** **complaints** provision supplies both. GARP: agreements should specify the responsibilities of financial institutions and service providers related to responding to customer complaints. If service providers are responsible for customer complaint resolution, agreements should provide for summary reports to the financial institutions that track the status and resolution of complaints.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider resolves complaints, so the conditional limb applies. The correct clause must (1) allocate responsibilities between both parties, (2) have reports flow from provider to bank, and (3) cover status and resolution of complaints in general, not a subset.

**Fragile fact.** If the provider resolves complaints, it reports to the institution, and the reports track both status and resolution.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Customer complaints”. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point (Schweser: state which party deals with complaints; if the provider, it reports the complaints and their status).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q15 of 22.

a.reason: It allocates responsibilities between the parties and, because the provider resolves complaints, requires the provider to give the bank summary reports tracking status and resolution.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP expressly contemplates providers being responsible for complaint resolution (“If service providers are responsible for customer complaint resolution. . . ”). There is no prohibition. B would be right only if the guidance barred providers from resolving complaints.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the reports to complaints that escalate into litigation or regulatory action, whereas GARP’s summary reports track the status and resolution of complaints generally. C would be right only if reporting were confined to escalated cases.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It reverses the flow: reports go from the provider that resolves complaints to the institution. D would be right only if the institution resolved complaints and the provider needed to monitor it.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q16
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a U.S. state member bank is reviewing the provision on the business resumption and contingency plan of the service provider in a draft core processing agreement. The draft provision contains the following items:

I. The continuation of the services provided by the provider in the event of operational failures.

II. The provider’s responsibility for backing up information and maintaining disaster recovery and contingency plans.

III. The provider’s responsibility for testing its plans and providing the testing results to the bank.

IV. An obligation on the provider to maintain a pool of comparable alternative service providers to which the bank can move if the provider is unable to perform.

Which of the items are appropriate for this provision?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst checking four items in the provider’s business resumption and contingency plan provision.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance deals with continuity at two levels, and confusing them is the trap here.

| Contract provision (part C): the provider’s plan | Programme element (part F): the institution’s plan |
|---|---|
| Continuation of services in the event of operational failures | Ensure a DR and BCP exists for the contracted services |
| Provider responsibility for backing up information and maintaining DR and contingency plans | Assess the provider’s plan and its alignment with the institution’s own plan |
| May include provider responsibility for testing plans and providing results to the institution | Document roles for maintaining and testing; test periodically Maintain an exit strategy, including a pool of comparable service providers |

The contract provision makes the provider responsible for keeping its own service running and proving it. The exit strategy, including a pool of comparable providers, is the institution’s contingency for the case where the provider cannot perform, so it cannot sensibly be the provider’s obligation.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I is the first sentence of GARP’s provision. Item II is the second. Item III is the optional third sentence (“may include”). Item IV takes the exit strategy from part F, which the institution maintains, and assigns it to the provider. Items I, II and III belong; IV does not.

**Fragile fact.** The contract provision covers the provider’s continuation, backups, DR plans and (optionally) testing; the institution keeps the exit strategy and pool of alternative providers.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Business resumption and contingency plan of the service provider”; contrast part F, Business Continuity and Contingency Considerations (LO 53.a). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser’s version adds that the focus should be on critical services and alternative arrangements, which GARP places in part F as the institution’s own contingency planning; GARP is used. This looks like Schweser merging two sections rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q16 of 22.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I and II only” excludes testing. GARP says agreements may include the provider’s responsibility for testing plans and providing results to the institution; optional does not mean inappropriate. A would be right only if the guidance excluded testing from the contract.

b.reason: I, II and III restate the three sentences of GARP’s “Business resumption and contingency plan of the service provider” provision. IV is an institution-side contingency measure.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It accepts IV, assigning the pool of comparable providers to the provider, and also drops II. The exit strategy is maintained by the institution (part F). C would be right only if IV were the provider’s duty and backups were not.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It accepts all four, including the misassigned IV. D would be right only if IV read “the institution maintains an exit strategy”, and even then it belongs in the institution’s contingency planning rather than this contract provision.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q17
questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a U.S. bank holding company that is negotiating an agreement with a provider based in São Paulo. Annual fees will be BRL 3.4 million, and the provider’s standard terms are governed by Brazilian law. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Including a choice-of-law clause will ensure that disputes are decided under U.S. law, since foreign courts are bound to apply the law named in the agreement.
The agreement should provide for disputes to be adjudicated under the laws of both countries at once, so that each party is protected in its home courts.
The institution may rely on the provider’s home-country supervisor to confirm that every aspect of the agreement will be enforceable in that country.
The institution should consider express choice-of-law and jurisdictional provisions placing all disputes under a single, specific jurisdiction, and seek legal advice on enforceability.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant advising on governing law for an agreement with a Brazil-based provider.

**Concept and theory**

Contracts are only as good as their enforceability. With a provider abroad, two legal systems may claim jurisdiction, and foreign law may treat contract enforcement differently from U.S. law. The **foreign-based service providers** provision addresses this. GARP:

- institutions should consider including express choice of law and jurisdictional provisions that would provide for the adjudication of all disputes between the two parties under the laws of a single, specific jurisdiction;
- such agreements may still be subject to the interpretation of foreign courts relying on local laws, and foreign law may differ from U.S. law in the enforcement of contracts;
- therefore institutions should seek legal advice regarding the enforceability of all aspects of proposed contracts with foreign-based providers and the other legal ramifications.

The clause reduces uncertainty but does not eliminate it, which is why legal advice is a companion requirement.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider’s terms are governed by Brazilian law, which is exactly the situation the provision anticipates. The annual fee of BRL 3.4 million is irrelevant. The right advice combines the single-jurisdiction clause with legal advice on enforceability; any option that promises certainty, splits jurisdiction or delegates the enforceability judgement is wrong.

**Fragile fact.** A single, specific jurisdiction is chosen, yet foreign courts may still apply local law, so the institution also seeks legal advice on enforceability.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Foreign-based service providers”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the contract could provide for the law of only one jurisdiction, specified as the financial institution’s; GARP says a single, specific jurisdiction without naming whose, and adds the foreign-courts caveat and the legal advice requirement. GARP is used; the stem and options avoid relying on whose jurisdiction is chosen.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q17 of 22.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP warns that such agreements may be subject to the interpretation of foreign courts relying on local laws, so a choice-of-law clause does not “ensure” a U.S. law outcome. A would be right only if foreign courts were bound to honour the clause.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Adjudication under both countries’ laws at once is the opposite of a single, specific jurisdiction and would multiply rather than reduce conflict. B would be right only if the guidance favoured parallel jurisdictions.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** GARP tells the institution to seek legal advice on enforceability; it does not delegate that assessment to the provider’s home-country supervisor. (Home-country supervisors appear in part G only in the context of access to customer information.) C would be right only if the guidance named the foreign supervisor as the source of enforceability assurance.

d.reason: It reproduces both limbs of GARP: consider express choice-of-law and jurisdictional provisions placing all disputes under a single, specific jurisdiction, and seek legal advice on enforceability.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q18
questions.question: An internal auditor at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing an incident at its document imaging provider. With the bank’s consent, the provider subcontracted the indexing of scanned files to a firm in another country, and that firm mishandled customer data. The provider argues that the subcontractor alone is responsible. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The primary provider has overall accountability for all services provided by it and its subcontractors, and the same contractual provisions should apply to the subcontractor.
Accountability for the subcontracted indexing passes to the subcontractor, since it performed the work and the institution consented to the subcontracting arrangement.
The subcontractor is bound only by those provisions that the primary provider chooses to pass on, provided the primary provider remains accountable to the institution.
The primary provider’s accountability extends only to domestic subcontractors, since a foreign subcontractor’s work is governed by its home jurisdiction’s standards.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor reviewing a data incident at a foreign subcontractor of the document imaging provider.

**Concept and theory**

Subcontracting creates a chain: institution, primary provider, subcontractor. The institution has a contract only with the primary provider, so without explicit terms the controls it negotiated could disappear one link down the chain. The **subcontracting** provision closes that gap with two core rules. GARP: if agreements allow for subcontracting, the same contractual provisions should apply to the subcontractor; and contract provisions should clearly state that the primary service provider has overall accountability for all services that the service provider and its subcontractors provide. GARP adds that institutions should pay special attention to foreign subcontractors, as information security and data privacy standards may differ in other jurisdictions.

The result is that the institution can always look to one accountable counterparty, and that the subcontractor is held to the institution’s standards.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider’s argument (“the subcontractor alone is responsible”) is exactly what the accountability rule prevents. The fact that the institution consented and that the subcontractor is foreign changes nothing about accountability; the foreign location is a reason for extra attention, not an exemption.

**Fragile fact.** The primary provider keeps overall accountability for subcontracted work, the same provisions flow down, and foreign subcontractors get extra scrutiny, not an exemption.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Subcontracting”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the subcontractor should be held to the same contract terms and the primary provider is ultimately responsible, but omits the special attention to foreign subcontractors; GARP is used. Consistent on the core rules. (Separately, Section 12.3 keeps ultimate responsibility for the outsourced activity with the institution’s board and senior management; the subcontracting rule allocates accountability between the providers in the contract.)

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q18 of 22.

a.reason: It states both GARP rules: the primary provider has overall accountability for all services provided by it and its subcontractors, and the same contractual provisions should apply to the subcontractor.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Accountability stays with the primary provider whatever the institution’s consent; the subcontractor does the work, but the primary provider answers for it. B would be right only if consent to subcontracting released the primary provider.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It keeps the primary provider’s accountability but lets the subcontractor be bound by a selection of terms. GARP requires the same contractual provisions to apply. C would be right only if the guidance allowed partial flow-down.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP singles out foreign subcontractors for special attention because data security and privacy standards may differ; it does not exempt them from the primary provider’s accountability. D would be right only if the guidance limited accountability to domestic subcontractors.

questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q19
questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a savings and loan holding company is reviewing the subcontracting provision of an agreement that permits subcontracting. The draft provision contains the following items:

I. The services that may be subcontracted.

II. The provider’s due diligence process for engaging and monitoring subcontractors.

III. A standing consent allowing the provider to change its subcontractors without notifying the institution, provided the services remain within the agreed scope.

IV. The provider’s process for assessing a subcontractor’s financial condition to fulfil the contractual obligations.

Which of the items should the agreement include?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Risk committee member checking four items in a subcontracting provision.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond the accountability and flow-down rules (Q18), the **subcontracting** provision specifies what the agreement should define. GARP: agreements should define (1) the services that may be subcontracted;

(2) the service provider’s due diligence process for engaging and monitoring subcontractors;

(3) the notification and approval requirements regarding changes to the service provider’s subcontractors;

and agreements should include (4) the service provider’s process for assessing the subcontractor’s financial condition to fulfil contractual obligations. Each item keeps the institution informed and in control of who actually performs its work. The notification and approval requirement matters most in practice: without it, the institution’s due diligence on the original subcontractor could become obsolete overnight.

**Applying it to this question**

Items I, II and IV are GARP’s items (1), (2) and (4). Item III, a standing consent to change subcontractors without notice, removes item (3), the notification and approval requirement. The answer is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Changes to subcontractors require notification and approval; the provider’s own process for assessing subcontractors’ financial condition goes into the agreement.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Subcontracting”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists acceptable tasks, how the primary provider supervises and reviews subcontractor work, and its method of financial due diligence, but omits the notification and approval of changes; GARP is used. Condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q19 of 22.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I and II only” omits IV, the provider’s process for assessing the subcontractor’s financial condition, which GARP says agreements should include. A reader who thinks subcontractor financial review is only a due diligence matter (LO 53.b) would drop it. A would be right only if the contract were silent on subcontractor financial condition.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts III, a no-notice standing consent, which reverses the requirement for notification and approval of changes, and drops the true items I and IV. B would be right only if the guidance allowed changes without notice.

c.reason: I, II and IV reproduce what GARP says agreements should define or include; III contradicts the notification and approval requirement regarding changes to subcontractors.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts all four, including III. D would be right only if III read “notification and approval requirements regarding changes to the provider’s subcontractors”.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q20
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a community bank is reviewing a proposed agreement under which a third-party sales agency will market the bank’s deposit products to new customers. The proposed compensation is shown below.

| Product sold by the agency | Commission (% of balance) |
|---|---|
| Standard savings account | 0.25 |
| Structured deposit (higher margin to the bank) | 1.50 |

In addition, the agency receives a fixed monthly retainer of USD 20,000. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?

options.text: Approve the schedule without further review, since the commissions are already set out in the cost and compensation provision as variable charges.

Review whether the commission gap could lead the agency to steer customers to the higher-margin product without regard to suitability, and ensure the incentives do not encourage imprudent risk-taking.
Leave the commission levels to the agency, since any reputational damage or litigation arising from unsuitable sales would fall on the agency rather than on the bank.
Replace all commissions with a fixed fee, since the guidance requires providers that sell on an institution’s behalf to receive fixed compensation only.

questions.solution:
CRO reviewing a sales agency’s commission schedule for deposit products.

**Concept and theory**

When a provider sells products on an institution’s behalf, it represents the institution to customers, and the way it is paid shapes what it sells. The guidance addresses this in two places. In the cost and compensation provision, institutions should ensure that any incentives in contracts (for example variable charges such as fees or commissions) do not create potential incentives to take imprudent risks on behalf of the institution. In part D (**incentive compensation review**), institutions should have an effective process to review and approve any incentive compensation embedded in provider contracts, including whether existing governance and controls are adequate. GARP’s example of an inappropriate incentive is one where variable fees or commissions encourage the provider to direct customers to products with higher profit margins without due consideration of whether they are suitable. Such incentives may cause reputational damage, increased litigation or other risks to the financial institution.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding feature is the differential, not the existence of commissions:

Commission multiple $= \frac{\text{1.50\%}}{\text{0.25\%}} =$ 6

The agency earns six times as much per unit of balance by selling the higher-margin structured deposit. That is the steering incentive GARP describes. The fixed retainer of USD 20,000 is irrelevant: it does not vary with product mix.

**Fragile fact.** The problem is the differential that steers customers to higher-margin, possibly unsuitable products; the reputational and litigation risk falls on the institution.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Cost and compensation”; also Section 12.4 part D, Incentive Compensation Review. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists “Incentive compensation” as a separate contract provision allowing the institution to review incentive compensation; GARP treats the contract aspect within cost and compensation and the review as a separate programme element (D). Content is consistent; the classification differs.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q20 of 22.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Disclosure of variable charges in the cost clause is necessary but not sufficient; GARP requires the institution to ensure those incentives do not encourage imprudent risks and to review and approve embedded incentive compensation. A would be right only if listing the charges discharged the review.

b.reason: It applies GARP’s test: review whether the variable commissions could direct customers to higher-margin products without regard to suitability, and ensure incentives do not encourage imprudent risk-taking on the institution’s behalf.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** GARP says inappropriately structured incentives may result in reputational damage, increased litigation or other risks to the financial institution. The bank, not the agency, bears these consequences. C would be right only if the agency were the party exposed.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The guidance does not prohibit variable compensation; it requires that incentives be reviewed so that they do not encourage imprudent risk-taking or unsuitable sales. D would be right only if the guidance mandated fixed fees.

questions.reading: ORR-12: Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q21
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing the draft agreement with a provider that internal assessments rate as higher risk following recent control weaknesses. Which of the following draft clauses best supports the bank’s ongoing oversight of this provider?

options.text: The provider must deliver its annual financial statements, give additional reporting in view of its higher risk, and accept increased monitoring if performance, control or viability concerns arise.
The frequency of the bank’s monitoring is fixed at signing and cannot be increased during the term, so as to give the provider certainty over its compliance costs.
The bank must deliver its own annual financial statements to the provider, so that the provider can monitor the bank’s ability to continue paying for the service.
The provider receives the same level of monitoring as the bank’s lower-risk providers, since its suitability was already established through due diligence before signing.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst choosing an oversight clause for a higher-risk provider.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser lists **oversight and monitoring** as a contract provision: the contract should require the provider to deliver annual financial statements (and annual report, if applicable) so that the institution can monitor its ability to continue as a going concern; it should allow the institution to increase monitoring and oversight when performance deficiencies, control weaknesses or viability concerns are noted; and for higher-risk providers it could stipulate extra reporting by the provider or additional monitoring by the institution. GARP covers the same content as a programme element (part E): the oversight process should be risk-focused; higher-risk providers may require more frequent assessment and monitoring and tailored risk mitigation plans, which may include additional reporting by the provider or heightened monitoring by the institution; more frequent and stringent monitoring is needed for providers with performance, financial, compliance or control concerns; institutions should monitor the financial condition of providers by reviewing their most recent financial statements and annual report; and risk management processes should include triggers to escalate oversight. Lower-risk providers can be monitored less.

Writing these rights into the contract matters because a provider is not otherwise obliged to hand over financial statements or accept extra scrutiny.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider is higher risk because of control weaknesses. The best clause must therefore deliver (1) financial information flowing from provider to institution, (2) extra reporting suited to its risk level, and (3) the ability to escalate monitoring when concerns arise.

**Fragile fact.** Monitoring is risk-focused and escalates with concerns; the provider supplies its financial statements to the institution.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” Schweser, LO 53.c, provision “Oversight and monitoring” (condensed source: GARP does not list oversight and monitoring among the contract provisions in part C, so the framing as a contract clause comes from Schweser, whose wording may compress GARP’s). Content cross-checked against GARP Chapter 12, Section 12.4, part E, Oversight and Monitoring of Service Providers (including “Financial condition” and “Escalation of oversight activities”). GARP vs Schweser: classification differs (contract provision in Schweser, programme element in GARP); substance consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q21 of 22.

a.reason: It combines annual financial statements, additional reporting for a higher-risk provider and the right to increase monitoring when performance, control or viability concerns arise, matching Schweser’s provision and GARP part E.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Freezing monitoring at the signing level contradicts the escalation principle: monitoring should increase when concerns arise. B would be right only if the guidance fixed monitoring intensity for the term.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It reverses the flow of financial statements. It is the institution that monitors the provider’s viability by reviewing the provider’s statements. C would be right only if the provider were monitoring the institution.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the risk-focus condition: higher-risk providers require more frequent and stringent monitoring than lower-risk ones, regardless of the due diligence performed at selection. D would be right only if monitoring did not depend on risk.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-12 c Q22
questions.question:
A junior analyst at a regional bank is filing four clauses from a draft agreement with a provider based in Singapore (annual fees SGD 2.1 million) under the provision headings used in the guidance.

| Clause | Text |
|---|---|
| 1 | The provider will give proof of its insurance and notify the bank of any material change in its coverage. |
| 2 | Because the provider is based outside the United States, all disputes will be adjudicated under the laws of a single, specific jurisdiction. |
| 3 | The provider will give the bank summary reports tracking the status and resolution of the complaints it handles. |
| 4 | The provider will have an opportunity to cure a contractual default before the bank exercises its termination rights. |

Which of the following assigns each clause to the correct provision heading?

options.text: 1: Insurance; 2: Dispute resolution; 3: Customer complaints; 4: Default and termination
1: Limits on liability; 2: Foreign-based service providers; 3: Customer complaints; 4: Default and termination
1: Insurance; 2: Foreign-based service providers; 3: Customer complaints; 4: Default and termination
1: Insurance; 2: Foreign-based service providers; 3: Customer complaints; 4: Dispute resolution

questions.solution:
Junior analyst assigning four clauses of a Singapore provider agreement to provision headings.

**Concept and theory**

Several provisions in the guidance sit close together and share vocabulary (disputes, termination, liability, cover), so the exam often tests whether a feature is attributed to the right heading. The four clauses here map to GARP as follows:

| Clause | Distinctive feature in GARP | Heading |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Proof of insurance; notify material change in coverage | Insurance |
| 2 | Express choice of law and jurisdiction; a single, specific jurisdiction for a provider abroad | Foreign-based service providers |
| 3 | Summary reports tracking status and resolution of complaints | Customer complaints |
| 4 | Opportunities for curing default; termination rights | Default and termination |

Near neighbours: limits on liability concerns a cap on the provider’s liability judged by the board and senior management; dispute resolution concerns expediting problem resolution and continuing the arrangement during a dispute.

**Applying it to this question**

Each wrong option differs from the correct one in exactly one clause, so the task is to find the one heading that is right for every clause. Clause 2 is the most tempting to misfile under dispute resolution, because it mentions disputes; but adjudication under a single jurisdiction is GARP’s foreign-based provider provision. Clause 4 mentions termination as well as cure, and cure opportunities belong to default and termination. The SGD fee is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** “Single, specific jurisdiction” belongs to foreign-based service providers, not dispute resolution; “opportunity to cure” belongs to default and termination.

**Reference**

LO 53.c: “Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.” GARP Chapter 12, Guidance on Managing Outsourcing Risk, Section 12.4 Service Provider Risk Management Programs, part C, Contract Provisions and Considerations, provision “Insurance”, and the provisions “Foreign-based service providers”, “Customer complaints” and “Default and termination” in the same part. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes the foreign-based provision as applying one jurisdiction “for the purposes of contract enforcement and resolution of disputes”, but keeps it under its own heading, as GARP does. No conflict on the headings.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-12 c, where it is Q22 of 22.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It files clause 2 under dispute resolution. Dispute resolution is about expediting resolution and continuation during a dispute; choice of law and jurisdiction for a foreign provider sit under foreign-based service providers. A would be right if clause 2 had read “a process to expedite resolution while services continue”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It files clause 1 under limits on liability. Proof of coverage and notice of material changes are the insurance provision; limits on liability concern a contractual cap. B would be right if clause 1 had described a cap on the provider’s liability.

c.reason: Insurance, foreign-based service providers, customer complaints, and default and termination are the GARP headings under which each clause’s distinctive wording appears.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It files clause 4 under dispute resolution. Opportunities to cure a default before termination are part of default and termination. D would be right if clause 4 had described keeping the arrangement running while a disagreement is resolved.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-13 a Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore private bank is drafting a glossary for the operational risk committee. The committee has asked for an entry that defines third-party risk management (TPRM) and explains how the term “third-party risk” relates to “outsourcing risk”. Which of the following entries is most accurate?

options.text: Third-party risk is the narrower term, covering only activities formally outsourced by the bank, while outsourcing risk covers all risks arising from external providers.
Outsourcing risk relates to activities outsourced to third parties, while third-party risk is the more general term covering all risks from third parties that can affect the bank.
Third parties are limited to providers of outsourced services under a formal contract, so suppliers of goods and business partners fall outside the scope of TPRM.
TPRM covers the identification, assessment and monitoring of third-party risks, while the mitigation of those risks passes to the provider under the contract.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Singapore private bank defining TPRM and relating “third-party risk” to “outsourcing risk”.

**Concept and theory**

Third-party risk management (TPRM) is the identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring, by an organisation, of the risks that arise from its use of third parties. A third party is any provider of goods or services that is not internal to the firm: vendors, suppliers, partners, contractors and service providers. The definition is deliberately wide. It is not limited to formal outsourcing of a business process; a supplier of goods or a business partner can expose the firm to loss just as an outsourced back office can.

Two labels are used for the same family of risks:

| Term | Scope |
|---|---|
| Outsourcing risk | Risks of activities that the firm has outsourced to third parties (the narrower term) |
| Third-party risk | All risks arising from third parties that can affect the client institution (the more general term) |

In practice the two are used quite interchangeably, but strictly third-party risk is the broader concept, because a firm can be exposed to a third party (a supplier, a partner) without having outsourced an activity to it. The “M” in TPRM matters: the framework is not only about spotting and watching risk, it includes mitigating it, and that duty stays with the client firm.

**Applying it to this question**

The glossary entry must do two things: define TPRM correctly and get the direction of the scope comparison right. The deciding fact is which term is the general one. Third-party risk covers all risks from third parties; outsourcing risk covers outsourced activities. Any entry that reverses this, narrows the set of third parties, or removes mitigation from the firm’s own TPRM is wrong.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of scope: third-party risk is the general term (all risks from third parties); outsourcing risk is the narrower one (outsourced activities). The terms are used interchangeably in practice, but they are not identical.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, Case Study: Third-Party Risk Management, section “Context and Scope: Nature of TPRM”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser defines TPRM as “identifying, monitoring, and assessing” and omits mitigation, and it does not discuss the outsourcing risk versus third-party risk distinction. Content here follows GARP; this looks like condensation in Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q1 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the scope comparison, making third-party risk the narrow term and outsourcing risk the broad one. The option would be correct only if the stem asked how a firm that defines third parties purely as outsourcing counterparties might (incorrectly) label the terms; on the source’s definitions the direction is the opposite.

b.reason: It states the relationship exactly as the source does: outsourcing risk relates to the risks of outsourced activities, while third-party risk is more general because it relates to all risks arising from third parties that can affect the client institution.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the definition of a third party to contracted outsourcing providers. The source lists vendors, suppliers, partners, contractors and service providers, so suppliers of goods and business partners are inside TPRM. The option would be correct only for a definition of outsourcing providers, not of third parties.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves mitigation to the provider. TPRM, as defined, is the firm’s own identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring of third-party risk. A contract can allocate tasks, but the client firm still mitigates its own exposure. The option would describe a provider’s internal control duties under an SLA, not the client’s TPRM.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-13 a Q2
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian credit union is preparing a business case for moving back-office reconciliations and cloud-based data management to a specialist provider. The projected saving is CAD 1.8 million a year. A board member asks how the move will affect the credit union’s operational risk. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The move transfers the operational risk of these activities to the provider, so the credit union’s operational risk exposure from them falls to zero.
The move may reduce costs, but because the work leaves the credit union it cannot reduce its process errors or its cybersecurity risk.
The move may reduce process errors, and the third-party risk it creates can be managed with the controls already used for the work in-house.
The move may reduce process errors or cybersecurity risk, but it does not fully mitigate operational risk and adds third-party risk with its own challenges.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a Canadian credit union asked how outsourcing back-office and cloud data work affects operational risk.

**Concept and theory**

Firms contract with third parties for two broad reasons. The first is cost: activities are outsourced to specialised firms that have a competitive advantage in particular systems, processes and knowledge. The second is risk: engaging a specialist can be an operational risk mitigation strategy, because back-office or cloud-based data management by an expert may reduce process errors or cybersecurity risk.

The catch is what outsourcing does to the risk profile overall. It does not fully mitigate operational risk. It also creates a new exposure, third-party risk, which has its own management challenges: the firm must now select, contract with, monitor and, if needed, exit the provider, and it depends on controls it does not run itself. So the net effect is a change in the shape of operational risk, not its removal.

| Effect | What outsourcing does |
|---|---|
| Cost | Can save costs through specialisation |
| Process and cyber risk | May be reduced by a specialist provider |
| Operational risk overall | Not fully mitigated |
| Third-party risk | Increased, with its own management challenges |

**Applying it to this question**

The CAD 1.8 million saving is irrelevant to the risk question. The board member asks about operational risk. The deciding fact is the two-sided statement in the source: the move may reduce process errors or cyber risk, but it does not fully mitigate operational risk and increases exposure to third-party risk, which needs its own management.

**Fragile fact.** Outsourcing can reduce some operational risks but never removes operational risk: it swaps part of it for third-party risk, which the client must manage.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Context and Scope: Nature of TPRM”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser gives the two reasons (cost saving and risk mitigation by contracting with experts) but omits GARP’s caveat that outsourcing does not fully mitigate operational risk and increases third-party risk. Content follows GARP; condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q2 of 20.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It promises that exposure falls to zero. The source states the opposite: outsourcing does not fully mitigate operational risk. The option would be correct only for a pure financial transfer of loss with no dependency at all, which does not describe outsourcing.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It denies that outsourcing can reduce process errors or cybersecurity risk. The source says outsourcing to a specialist has the potential to reduce exactly these risks, which is why it is sometimes a mitigation strategy. The option would be right only if the provider were less capable than the credit union.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the condition that third-party risk has its own management challenges, implying the existing in-house controls suffice. Once the work moves, the firm needs the TPRM life cycle (due diligence, contracts, monitoring, exit). The option would be correct only if the activity stayed in-house.

d.reason: It reproduces both halves of the source statement: a possible reduction in process errors or cybersecurity risk, together with incomplete mitigation of operational risk and a new third-party exposure that has its own management challenges.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-13 a Q3
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK general insurer is mapping the supply chain behind its outsourced policy-document printing. The insurer contracts directly with PrintCo. PrintCo has designated a central intermediary, StaffHub, to run the procurement support for the contract, and StaffHub in turn hires individual contractors who work on the insurer’s procurement function. The insurer has no contract with StaffHub or with the contractors. Which classification is most accurate?

options.text: PrintCo is a third party, StaffHub is a fourth party, and the contractors hired by StaffHub are fifth parties within the reach of TPRM.
PrintCo is a third party, and StaffHub and its contractors are both fourth parties, because they all work under the same provider.
PrintCo is a third party and StaffHub is a fourth party, but the contractors fall outside TPRM because the insurer has no contract with them.
StaffHub is a third party because its work supports the insurer’s own contract, and the contractors it hires are fourth parties.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst at a UK insurer classifying a printing provider, its designated intermediary and the intermediary’s contractors.

**Concept and theory**

A firm’s exposure does not stop at the providers it contracts with directly. Those providers use their own suppliers and subcontractors, who use theirs. The source names the layers:

| Layer | Who they are |
|---|---|
| Third party | The firm’s own provider (vendor, supplier, partner, contractor, service provider) |
| Fourth party | A third party of the third party: subcontractors of service providers, suppliers of suppliers |
| Fifth party | Less frequently, the suppliers of the suppliers of the suppliers |

The source’s own illustration of a fifth party is close to this stem: contractors of the service provider (the third party), hired by a central intermediary designated by the service provider (the fourth party), working in support of the procurement function of a large bank. The conclusion drawn is that TPRM rapidly touches the entire supply chain of the organisation. A missing direct contract does not take a party out of TPRM; it only changes the tools (for example, cascading standards through the third party’s contract).

**Applying it to this question**

Count the links from the insurer. PrintCo contracts with the insurer: third party. StaffHub is designated by PrintCo: one link further, fourth party. The contractors are hired by StaffHub: one more link, fifth party. The statement that the insurer has no contract with StaffHub or the contractors is a distraction: it is the normal position for fourth and fifth parties, and they remain within the reach of TPRM.

**Fragile fact.** Count links from the client: third (direct), fourth (third party’s third party), fifth (one step further). Lack of a direct contract does not remove a party from TPRM.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Context and Scope: Nature of TPRM”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes fifth parties as “third parties dealing with contractors who deal with other entities”, a looser wording of the same layering; GARP’s worked example is used here. No conflict on substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q3 of 20.

a.reason: It labels each layer by its distance from the insurer and keeps the fifth parties within TPRM, matching the source’s example of contractors hired by an intermediary designated by the service provider.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It applies the fourth-party label to the contractors, who are one link further away. Working under the same provider does not put two parties on the same layer. B would be correct only if PrintCo hired the contractors directly.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It adds a condition (a direct contract) for a party to fall within TPRM. Fourth and fifth parties, by definition, have no contract with the firm, and the source says TPRM touches the entire supply chain. C would be correct only for a narrow programme limited to direct counterparties, which the source rejects.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It treats StaffHub as the insurer’s own provider. StaffHub was designated by PrintCo and has no contract with the insurer, so it is PrintCo’s third party and the insurer’s fourth. D would be correct only if the insurer had appointed StaffHub itself.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian commercial bank is reviewing the risk identification section of a draft third-party risk policy. The section contains the following statements:

I. Nearly all operational risk types that can materialise in the bank can also materialise at one of its third parties.

II. Common third-party risks include service disruption, failings in service quality, fraud and compliance breaches.

III. A failing at a third party creates reputational damage for the vendor only, because the failing occurs outside the bank.

IV. A data privacy breach at a vendor counts as a third-party risk only when the leak is intentional rather than accidental.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
II and III only
I and II only
I, II and IV only

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” omits Statement II, which lists four of the source’s common third-party risks verbatim. A would be correct only if the policy had named a risk outside the list, such as market risk on the vendor’s own portfolio.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** “II and III only” accepts Statement III, which reverses who bears the damage. The source states that third-party failings are likely to impact the financial institution, reputational damage included. B would be correct only if III said the institution bears the damage.

c.reason: Statements I and II are correct and III and IV are not, so “I and II only” is the only consistent combination.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I, II and IV only” accepts Statement IV, which adds the condition that a breach must be intentional. The source lists accidental data privacy breaches alongside intentional leaks. D would be correct only if IV covered both accidental and intentional cases.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising an Australian asset manager that is redesigning its operational risk taxonomy. The head of operational risk wants to know where third-party risk sits in the main reference taxonomies. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Basel treats third-party failure as a level 1 event type in its own right, while the ORX taxonomy places it at level 2 under process management.
Basel treats third-party failure as a level 2 category under the event type Clients, Products and Business Practices.
The revised ORX taxonomy places third-party risk at level 2, so firms that treat TPRM as a level 1 category depart from industry practice.
Basel treats third-party failure as a level 2 category under Execution, Delivery and Process Management, while ORX and many firms treat it as level 1.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant advising an Australian asset manager on where third-party risk sits in the Basel and ORX taxonomies.

**Concept and theory**

Risk taxonomies arrange operational risk in levels: level 1 is the broad category, level 2 the subcategory beneath it. The Basel taxonomy has seven level 1 event types. The seventh is Execution, Delivery and Process Management (EDPM), and “third-party failure” is recorded as a level 2 category under it (together with other process-related sub-categories).

Third-party risk has grown so much in importance that, for many institutions, TPRM is now a level 1 category of operational risk, with specific risk management practices of its own. The industry body ORX, in its revised operational risk taxonomy, also places third-party risk at level 1.

| Taxonomy | Level | Parent |
|---|---|---|
| Basel event types | Level 2 (“third-party failure”) | EDPM, seventh event type |
| ORX revised taxonomy | Level 1 | None (own category) |
| Many institutions | Level 1 | None (own category) |

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts decide it: the Basel level (2), the Basel parent (EDPM), and the ORX and industry level (1). Only one option has all three right.

**Fragile fact.** Basel: level 2 “third-party failure” under EDPM (event type 7). ORX revised taxonomy and many firms: level 1.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Context and Scope: Evolution in Recent Years”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not state the taxonomy placement; this content is from GARP only. No conflict, but a reader of Schweser alone would not have it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q5 of 20.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It swaps the two taxonomies’ placements: Basel is given level 1 and ORX level 2. The source has Basel at level 2 under EDPM and ORX at level 1. A would be correct only with the names of the two taxonomies exchanged.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns the wrong parent event type. Clients, Products and Business Practices is a neighbouring Basel event type concerned with conduct towards clients; third-party failure sits under EDPM. B would be correct only for a conduct sub-category such as improper business practices.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It moves ORX down to level 2 and so concludes that level 1 treatment departs from practice. The source says the reverse: ORX places third-party risk at level 1 and many firms do the same. C would be correct only for the Basel taxonomy.

d.reason: It places third-party failure at level 2 under EDPM in the Basel taxonomy and records that ORX and many institutions treat third-party risk as a level 1 category, as the source states.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a US regional bank is reviewing a proposal to outsource customer call-centre work and account aggregation to a FinTech located in another country, whose local data privacy rules differ from US rules. Key terms of the proposal are shown below.

| Item | Proposal |
|---|---|
| Annual fee | USD 4.2 million |
| Expected cost saving | 18% of current in-house cost |
| Contract term | 5 years |
| Provider location | Outside the United States |

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: Because the work is done abroad, the provider’s local laws on record retention, sanctions and data privacy replace the US requirements for the outsourced activity.
The proposal adds country, compliance and legal risk, and the bank must still meet all US rules on record retention, sanctions, consumer protection and data privacy.
The proposal adds country risk, but compliance and legal risk are unchanged because the contract assigns all regulatory compliance to the provider.
The proposal adds compliance and legal risk only where local laws are stricter than US laws; where they are weaker, the bank faces country risk alone.

questions.solution:
CCO of a US regional bank assessing outsourcing of call-centre and account aggregation work to a foreign FinTech.

**Concept and theory**

Over recent decades financial firms have outsourced more and more core processes: loan and deposit processing, electronic funds transfer, payroll, merchant processing, mortgage servicing, treasury management and customer call centres. Many banks also use third parties, particularly FinTechs, to implement new business applications such as electronic bill payment, account aggregation and digital certification. These providers and their staff are often located in another country.

Outsourcing to a company in a different legal jurisdiction brings three risks at once:

| Risk | Why it arises |
|---|---|
| Country risk | The provider and its staff are located in another country |
| Compliance risk | The bank must still comply with all home-country laws and regulations |
| Legal risk | Home and host rules may interact and conflict |

The source’s example is a US bank using a foreign provider: it must still comply with all US laws and regulations, including record retention, national sanctions, consumer protection and data privacy laws, some of which may conflict with those in the provider’s location. Outsourcing moves the work, not the bank’s legal obligations.

**Applying it to this question**

The fee, the saving and the contract term are irrelevant to the risk classification. The deciding facts are that the provider is in a different jurisdiction (adding country, compliance and legal risk) and that US requirements continue to apply in full. The difference in local privacy rules is exactly the potential conflict the source warns of.

**Fragile fact.** Cross-border outsourcing adds country risk and also compliance and legal risk; the client’s home-country laws still apply in full.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Context and Scope: Evolution in Recent Years”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser states the added country, legal and compliance risk but not the list of US requirements that still apply; content follows GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q6 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses whose law governs: it lets host-country law replace US requirements. The source says the US bank must still comply with all US laws; local laws add to and may conflict with them. A would be correct only if the stem concerned the provider’s own obligations in its home market.

b.reason: It names all three added risks and states that the bank must still meet US requirements on record retention, sanctions, consumer protection and data privacy, as the source does for a US bank using a foreign-based provider.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves regulatory compliance to the provider through the contract. The bank remains subject to US law; a contract can require the vendor to understand and follow domestic laws, but it cannot transfer the bank’s obligation. C would be correct only for a description of what the bank should ask the provider to commit to, not of the bank’s risk.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It invents a condition (compliance and legal risk arise only where local laws are stricter). The source attaches compliance and legal risk to any outsourcing into a different jurisdiction, because home requirements continue and the two regimes may conflict either way. D would be correct only if conflict could arise in one direction alone.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a German savings bank is reviewing a briefing paper titled “Why third-party risk has grown”. The bank spends about EUR 95 million a year on outsourced services. Which of the following statements in the paper is NOT correct?

options.text: The COVID-19 pandemic increased reliance on outsourcing and brought the risks from international supply chain disruptions to the forefront.
Connected devices add complexity, because equipment linked to staff payment cards can serve as a backdoor to personal data, as in a vending-machine hack.
Survey evidence shows that most firms monitor their entire supply chain, so the main TPRM weakness lies in contract drafting rather than in visibility.
TPRM overlaps greatly with information security management, data privacy risks and business continuity management, and many firms report breaches caused by vendors.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at a German savings bank reviewing a briefing on why third-party risk has grown.

**Concept and theory**

The source explains the growth of third-party risk through a set of recent developments:

- **COVID-19.** The pandemic increased reliance on outsourcing even more and brought the risks from international supply chain disruptions to the forefront.
- **Internet of Things (IoT).** The spread of connected devices adds a layer of complexity to managing third-party risk and protecting sensitive data. Avanti Markets was hacked through its vending machines, which were connected to staff employee cards for payment; the hackers used the connected equipment as a backdoor to personal data.
- **Overlaps.** TPRM overlaps greatly with information security management, data privacy risks and business continuity management.
- **Evidence.** A 2018 Ponemon Institute study found almost 60% of companies surveyed had suffered a data breach caused by third parties or vendors in the past year. A 2020 survey of over 1,500 senior technology and procurement officers found:

| Finding (2020 survey) | Share |
|---|---|
| Limited visibility into third-party vendors | 77% |
| Suffered a third-party related breach in the past 12 months | 80% |
| Average number of such breaches in the past 12 months | more than two |
| Monitor their entire supply chain | 22.5% |

The message of the evidence is a visibility gap: most firms cannot see far into their supply chain, and only about one in five monitors all of it.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the statement that is NOT correct. Statements A, B and D restate the source. Statement C claims most firms monitor their whole supply chain and locates the weakness in contracts rather than visibility. The survey shows the opposite: only 22.5% monitor their entire supply chain and 77% have limited visibility. The EUR 95 million spend is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Survey direction: 77% have limited visibility and only 22.5% monitor their entire supply chain. The gap is visibility.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Context and Scope: Evolution in Recent Years”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser cites the 60%, 77% and 80% figures but omits the 22.5% figure and the overlap with information security and business continuity; the deciding fact is from GARP. No conflict on the figures both give.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q7 of 20.

a.reason: **Accurate statement, not the answer.** The source says COVID-19 increased reliance on outsourcing and brought international supply chain disruption risks to the forefront. Choosing A is a qualifier misread (treating “NOT correct” as “correct”). A would be the answer only if it said the pandemic reduced reliance on outsourcing.

b.reason: **Accurate statement, not the answer.** This is the Avanti Markets example: vending machines linked to staff employee cards for payment were used as a backdoor to personal data. B would be the answer only if it denied that connected devices add complexity.

c.reason: It is the inaccurate statement. It flips the survey finding (a minority, 22.5%, monitor the whole supply chain) and therefore draws the wrong conclusion about where the weakness lies.

d.reason: **Accurate statement, not the answer.** The source says TPRM overlaps greatly with information security, data privacy and business continuity management, and the Ponemon study found almost 60% of firms had suffered a breach caused by vendors. D would be the answer only if it claimed TPRM was separate from these disciplines.
