questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore payments firm is preparing a slide on the TPRM life cycle for newly hired analysts. Which of the following descriptions should she present?

options.text: Business model decision; evaluation, risk rating and due diligence; contracts, SLAs and contract management; continuous monitoring; remediation or termination, in a model from Shared Assessments, a US certifying body for TPRM professionals.

Evaluation, risk rating and due diligence; business model decision; contracts, SLAs and contract management; continuous monitoring; remediation or termination, in a model from Shared Assessments, a US certifying body for TPRM professionals.

Business model decision; evaluation, risk rating and due diligence; contracts, SLAs and contract management; continuous monitoring; remediation or termination, in a binding standard issued by the Basel Committee for all banks.

Business model decision; evaluation, risk rating and due diligence; contracts, SLAs and contract management; monitoring at scheduled end-of-contract reviews only; remediation or termination, in a model from Shared Assessments.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Singapore payments firm presenting the TPRM life cycle to new hires.

**Concept and theory**

Regulators have set standards on third-party risk for about 20 years, and growing complexity has brought a flurry of new and proposed rules. To organise the work, the source presents a TPRM life cycle in line with the approach of Shared Assessments, a US-based organisation that specialises in TPRM and certifies TPRM professionals (the CTPRP certification). Firms differ slightly in their approach, but the life cycle is described as a sound way of organising TPRM steps and tasks. It has five stages, drawn as a cycle:

| Stage | Name | Core content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Business model decision | Outsource or keep in-house; provider quality and price; risk appetite |
| 2 | Evaluation, risk rating, due diligence | Proportionate due diligence; risk rating of the vendor |
| 3 | Contracts, SLAs, contract management | Clear terms, measurable SLAs, fourth-party limits, audit rights |
| 4 | Continuous monitoring | Service, SLAs, compliance; trigger-based reassessment |
| 5 | Remediation or termination | Grievance procedure, exit strategy, orderly wind-down |

The logic of the order is simple: decide whether to outsource, then choose and vet the provider, then formalise the relationship, then watch it, then fix or end it.

**Applying it to this question**

Two features must both be right: the order of the five stages and the origin of the model. Monitoring must also be continuous, not limited to scheduled reviews.

**Fragile fact.** Order: business model decision, evaluation and due diligence, contracts, continuous monitoring, remediation or termination. Model source: Shared Assessments (CTPRP), not a regulator.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Third-Party Risk Management” and Figure 13.1 (TPRM life cycle). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser calls stage 4 “ongoing monitoring” where GARP uses “continuous monitoring”, and Schweser does not name Shared Assessments. Same content; terminology only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q8 of 20.

a.reason: It lists the five stages in the source’s order and attributes the model to Shared Assessments, the US body that certifies TPRM professionals.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It exchanges stages 1 and 2. Due diligence evaluates a provider, which presupposes that the firm has already decided to outsource. B would be correct only in a model where candidate providers are vetted before the firm decides whether to outsource at all, which is not the source’s model.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It credits the model to the Basel Committee as a binding standard. The source presents it as a model in line with Shared Assessments, a certifying organisation, and notes that firms’ approaches differ slightly. C would be correct only for a regulatory text, which the life cycle is not.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It limits monitoring to scheduled end-of-contract reviews. The fourth stage is continuous monitoring, with reassessment tied to trigger events as well as scheduled reviews. D would be correct only if the stage were renamed periodic review.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a Japanese regional bank is deciding whether to keep mortgage servicing in-house or outsource it, and is comparing two candidate providers.

| Provider | Annual price (JPY m) | Service quality score | Head office |
|---|---|---|---|
| Provider K | 640 | 82 | Osaka |
| Provider M | 575 | 71 | Fukuoka |

Which statement about how these determinations fit into the TPRM framework is most accurate?

options.text: They are operational choices rather than strategic ones, so they can be delegated to procurement without reference to the bank’s risk appetite.
The choice to outsource and the choice of a provider’s quality and price are strategic decisions that relate to the bank’s risk appetite.
They are made only after full due diligence on each provider, because the business model decision is the second stage of the life cycle.
They concern only whether to outsource; the trade-off between a provider’s quality and price is settled later, at the contract stage.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Japanese regional bank deciding whether to outsource mortgage servicing and comparing two providers.

**Concept and theory**

The first stage of the life cycle answers the most basic question: should the activity be done by a third party at all? The source frames two linked choices at this stage:

- the decision to outsource some activities or keep them in-house; and
- the choice about a provider’s quality and price.

Both are described as important strategic decisions that also relate to the risk appetite of the firm. They are strategic because they shape the firm’s operating model and its dependence on outside parties. They relate to risk appetite because outsourcing a process, or buying cheaper and lower-quality service, changes the amount and type of operational risk the firm accepts. Later stages (due diligence, contracting, monitoring) then manage the relationship the firm has chosen.

**Applying it to this question**

The table invites a cost comparison (JPY 640 million against JPY 575 million, quality 82 against 71) and the head office locations are irrelevant. The question, though, asks how the determinations fit into the framework. Whether to outsource and the quality versus price trade-off both belong to the business model decision, which is strategic and tied to risk appetite.

**Fragile fact.** Stage 1 covers both whether to outsource and the provider quality versus price choice, and is strategic and tied to risk appetite.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Business Model Decision”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes the stage as deciding “whether and which activities should be outsourced” and omits the provider quality and price choice. Content follows GARP; condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q9 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It calls the decisions operational and detaches them from risk appetite. The source calls them important strategic decisions that relate to risk appetite. A would be correct only for a routine purchase within an already approved outsourcing model.

b.reason: It states both elements of the first stage and their nature: strategic decisions that relate to the bank’s risk appetite.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It places the decision second, after full due diligence, borrowing the position of the evaluation stage. The business model decision is the first stage; due diligence on providers comes after. C would be correct only if the firm had already decided to outsource.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows the first stage to the outsourcing decision alone and moves the quality versus price choice to the contract stage. The source puts the choice about a provider’s quality and price in the business model decision. D would be correct only for the detailed SLA quality measures, which are set in contracts.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is reviewing a draft due diligence policy which states that “every new third party receives the same full due diligence and verification, to ensure consistency”. Three relationships are pending approval.

| Relationship | Profile | Fee (SGD 000) |
|---|---|---|
| External trainer | Two days of training; no dependency; no data sharing | 18 |
| Cloud hosting firm | Hosts sensitive customer data; multi-year dependency | 2400 |
| Events agency | Annual client events; uses public information only | 3100 |

Which recommendation should the analyst make?

options.text: Keep the uniform approach, because applying the same due diligence to every relationship is what proportionality requires.
Scale due diligence to the fee, so that the largest contract receives the deepest review whatever its data access or dependency.
Exempt the trainer from any evaluation, because low-risk relationships fall outside the scope of the TPRM life cycle.
Apply proportionality: light verification for the trainer, the deepest review for the cloud host, and intermediate levels between.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst at a Singapore bank reviewing a uniform due diligence policy across three pending relationships.

**Concept and theory**

Entering a relationship with a new party requires sound due diligence and evaluation of whom the firm will be doing business with. But due diligence is costly, and the risk posed by different third parties varies enormously. The source therefore applies the principle of proportionality: the depth of due diligence and verification should match the risk of the relationship.

The source’s two poles are an external consultant delivering two days of training (no dependency, no data sharing, low risk) and an IT cloud company hosting sensitive data. Between them sits a range of intermediate situations. The drivers of depth are risk features such as dependency and data sharing, not the size of the fee.

| Relationship | Dependency and data | Due diligence depth |
|---|---|---|
| Training consultant | None | Light |
| Intermediate vendors | Some | Intermediate |
| Cloud host of sensitive data | High | Most extensive |

**Applying it to this question**

The fee column is the deliberate trap: the events agency has the largest fee (SGD 3.1 million) but uses only public information, so its risk is modest. The cloud host has a smaller fee but holds sensitive customer data and creates dependency, so it needs the deepest review. The trainer is the source’s own low-risk pole. A uniform policy ignores proportionality.

**Fragile fact.** Proportionality scales due diligence to risk (dependency, data sharing), not to contract value; low risk means lighter review, not no review.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Evaluation, Risk Rating, and Due Diligence”. GARP vs Schweser: GARP’s low-risk example is a consultant delivering two days of training; Schweser’s is a one-day training course. The principle is identical; this looks like a paraphrase or version difference and is not decisive here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q10 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It defines proportionality as identical treatment, the opposite of its meaning. Proportionality means scaling effort to risk. A would be correct only as a description of a uniform (non-proportional) approach.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It replaces risk with fee as the driver. Ranking by fee would give the events agency the deepest review and the cloud host less, inverting the risk ranking. B would be correct only where fee and risk moved together, which they do not here.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** It removes low-risk relationships from TPRM entirely. The source says the due diligence is not the same for the trainer, not that there is none; the trainer still passes through evaluation, only at a lighter depth. C would be correct only if the stem asked which relationship needs the least verification.

d.reason: It applies proportionality as the source describes it: light verification at the low-risk pole, the deepest review for the sensitive-data cloud host, and intermediate depth for relationships between.

questions.subject: Operational Risk
questions.loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
questions.reading: ORR-13: Third-Party Risk Management
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-13 a Q11
questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Irish life insurer is testing the evaluation and due diligence procedures in the insurer’s third-party policy. The policy contains the following statements:

I. Third-party evaluation and due diligence play a role comparable to customer due diligence in anti-money laundering risk management.

II. To simplify and standardise due diligence, the insurer uses standard assessment questionnaires such as the SIG questionnaires.

III. Because standard questionnaires are used, every vendor receives the same depth of review and proportionality no longer applies.

IV. Due diligence on a new vendor is completed after the contract is signed, so that it covers the services actually being delivered.

Which of the statements reflect good practice?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at an Irish life insurer testing due diligence statements in the third-party policy.

**Concept and theory**

The second life-cycle stage is evaluation, risk rating and due diligence. The source makes three points about it:

1. **Analogy.** Just like customer due diligence in anti-money laundering (AML) risk management, third-party evaluation and due diligence is an essential step. In AML a bank must know its customer before doing business; in TPRM it must know its provider.
2. **Standardisation.** To simplify and standardise due diligence, more and more companies use standard assessment questionnaires. The SIG questionnaires provided by Shared Assessments are commonly used.
3. **Proportionality.** Depth still varies with risk: a low-risk trainer is not vetted like a cloud host of sensitive data.

Timing matters too. Due diligence is the gateway to a new relationship, and the next stage states that contracts should be signed only after the assessment and remediation of all remaining open items or issues. Due diligence therefore precedes signature. A standard questionnaire is a tool for consistent evidence gathering; it does not replace proportionate judgement about how deep to go.

**Applying it to this question**

I restates the AML analogy. II restates the use of standard questionnaires such as SIG. III wrongly treats standardisation as removing proportionality. IV puts due diligence after signing, reversing the order the source requires.

**Fragile fact.** Sequence: due diligence and remediation of open items before signing. Standard questionnaires (SIG, from Shared Assessments) standardise the work but do not remove proportionality.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, sections “Evaluation, Risk Rating, and Due Diligence” and “Contracts, SLAs, and Contract Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not mention the AML analogy or SIG questionnaires; these points are from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q11 of 20.

a.reason: Only Statements I and II are good practice, so “I and II only” is correct.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** “I, II and III only” accepts III, which claims every vendor now gets the same depth of review. Standard questionnaires simplify due diligence but proportionality remains good practice. B would be correct only if III said questionnaires are scaled (for example, a short form for low-risk vendors).

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “II and IV only” drops the true Statement I and accepts IV. The AML customer due diligence analogy is in the source. C would be correct only if Statement I were false and Statement IV described a practice the source endorses.

D would be correct only if IV described ongoing monitoring after signature rather than due diligence.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Canadian pension fund is applying a risk-based vendor rating scheme, in which each criterion is graded critical, high, medium or low. Four vendors are profiled below.

| Vendor | Process criticality | Data access | System access | Sector regulated | Substitut- ability | Fee (CAD m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| W | Operations halted without vendor | Highly confidential and sensitive | Critical systems, admin rights | Y | Very limited | 3.4 |
| X | Operations halted without vendor | Highly confidential and sensitive | Critical systems, admin rights | N | Immediate | 2.9 |
| Y | Operations halted without vendor | Highly confidential and sensitive | Critical systems, admin rights | N | Very limited | 0.6 |
| Z | Capacity to create major disruption | Sensitive and confidential | Sensitive systems | N | Limited | 5.1 |

Which vendor’s profile falls in the critical tier on every criterion?

options.text: Vendor W
Vendor X
Vendor Y
Vendor Z

questions.solution:
Risk consultant at a Canadian pension fund placing four vendors on a risk-based vendor rating scheme.

**Concept and theory**

Risk rating turns proportionality into a working tool. The source illustrates a risk-based vendor rating with five criteria and four tiers:

| Tier | Process criticality | Data access | System access | Regulated | Substitutability |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | Operations halted without vendor | Highly confidential and sensitive | Critical systems, admin rights | N | None or very limited |
| High | Capacity to create major disruption | Sensitive and confidential | Sensitive systems | N | Limited |
| Medium | Minor interruption | Internal | Non-sensitive systems | Y | Possible |
| Low | No interruption | Public | None | Y | Immediate |

Each criterion asks a risk question. How badly would the firm be hurt if the vendor failed (process criticality)? How sensitive is the data it sees (data access)? How deep into the firm’s systems does it reach (system access)? Is the vendor in a regulated sector (in the illustration “N” sits with the critical and high tiers and “Y” with the medium and low tiers; the source does not explain the column, and a natural reading is that sector regulation gives some outside assurance)? How quickly could it be replaced (substitutability: hard to replace means higher risk)? The tier then determines the due diligence and controls applied.

**Applying it to this question**

Read each vendor across the critical row. The fee column is irrelevant (and Vendor Y, the only all-critical profile, has the smallest fee).

| Vendor | Departure from the critical row |
|---|---|
| W | Sector regulated is Y (a lower-tier value) |
| X | Substitutability is immediate (the low-tier value) |
| Y | None: critical on all five criteria |
| Z | Every criterion matches the high row, not the critical row |

**Fragile fact.** Two directions trip readers: low substitutability means higher risk, and “sector regulated: N” goes with the critical and high tiers.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, risk-based vendor rating illustration within the section “Third-Party Risk Management” (the stages of the life cycle). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser names the risk rating stage but does not reproduce the rating criteria or tiers; this content is from GARP only. The in-text reference to the figure appears as “Figure 7.8” in the extraction, which looks like a cross-reference to the earlier chapter’s version of the same illustration.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q12 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Choosing W treats “sector regulated: Y” as a critical-tier value. In the illustration, critical and high vendors are “N” and medium and low vendors are “Y”. A would be correct if W’s regulated flag were N.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Choosing X treats easy replacement as high risk. Immediate substitutability is the low-tier value; critical vendors have none or very limited substitutability. B would be correct if X’s substitutability were very limited.

c.reason: Vendor Y matches the critical row on all five criteria: operations halted without it, highly confidential and sensitive data, critical systems with admin rights, not in a regulated sector, and very limited substitutability.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Choosing Z confuses the high tier with the critical tier. Capacity to create major disruption, sensitive and confidential data, sensitive systems and limited substitutability are the high-row values. D would be correct if the question asked which vendor sits in the high tier on every criterion.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese joint-stock bank is validating the bank’s vendor rating methodology, which governs third-party contracts worth about CNY 1.2 billion a year. Which of the following findings should the analyst include in the validation report as an accurate statement of good practice?

options.text: The rating criteria, thresholds, and the due diligence and controls attached to each tier must be consistent with the bank’s overall risk appetite.
A vendor that can be substituted immediately should be rated higher risk, because a vendor that is easy to replace is likely to be replaced at short notice.
Data access should be the sole rating criterion, with process criticality and system access left to be assessed during continuous monitoring.
Once a tier is assigned at onboarding it should stay fixed for the life of the contract, since reassessment would undermine comparability of ratings.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst at a Chinese joint-stock bank validating the vendor rating methodology.

**Concept and theory**

A vendor rating scheme is only useful if it is anchored to how much risk the firm is willing to take. The source states that the risk-rating criteria, the thresholds, and the corresponding due diligence and controls must be in line with the company’s overall risk appetite. This links stage 2 back to stage 1: the business model decision is itself tied to risk appetite, and the rating scheme translates that appetite into concrete thresholds (which vendors count as critical) and concrete responses (how much due diligence, which controls).

Three further features of a sound scheme follow from the source:

- it uses several criteria (process criticality, data access, system access, sector regulation, substitutability), not one;
- substitutability works inversely: the harder a vendor is to replace, the higher the risk;
- ratings are not frozen: continuous monitoring requires reassessment on trigger events (incidents, changes in business circumstances, legal or regulatory changes, changes in services, Acts of God, performance failures).

**Applying it to this question**

The validation report must contain a statement that matches good practice. The contract value of CNY 1.2 billion is irrelevant. The deciding fact is the explicit requirement that criteria, thresholds, due diligence and controls be in line with overall risk appetite.

**Fragile fact.** Criteria, thresholds, due diligence and controls are all set in line with the firm’s overall risk appetite; ratings can change on trigger events.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, sections on the risk-based vendor rating illustration and “Continuous Monitoring”, and the closing paragraph of “Remediation or Termination”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not state the risk appetite alignment of rating criteria (it ties risk appetite only to the business model decision); this point is from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q13 of 20.

a.reason: It restates the source requirement that rating criteria, thresholds and the associated due diligence and controls be in line with the company’s overall risk appetite.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction of substitutability. A vendor that can be replaced immediately is the low-risk case in the rating illustration; none or very limited substitutability marks the critical tier. B would be correct only if the criterion were reworded as lack of substitutability, so that a high score meant a vendor that is hard to replace.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It collapses the scheme to a single criterion and pushes the others to monitoring. The illustration rates on five criteria at the evaluation stage. C would be correct only for a data-privacy screen run alongside the full rating.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It freezes the rating for the life of the contract. Continuous monitoring requires reassessment on trigger events, not only at scheduled reviews, so a rating must be able to change. D would be correct only for a contract with no trigger events at all, which the source does not envisage.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a UK building society is reviewing the draft contract with an outsourced mortgage servicer, worth GBP 7.5 million over three years. The legal team proposes the following principles:

I. The contract should define clearly what can and cannot be done, by whom, when and where.

II. The SLA should include, wherever possible, clear and measurable quality measures.

III. Signing the contract before open due diligence issues are remediated is good practice, as the contract gives leverage to force remediation.

IV. Ambiguity in expectations by either party is one of the common reasons why third-party relationships fail.

Which of the principles are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I and II only” omits Statement IV, which is the source’s explanation of why contracts matter: ambiguity in expectations is a common cause of failure. A would be correct only if IV claimed ambiguity was rare.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** “I, II and III only” accepts Statement III, which reverses the order: the source says contracts should only be signed after open items are assessed and remediated. B would be correct only if III said open items must be closed before signing.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** “II, III and IV only” accepts III (signing before remediation) and drops I, the source’s core description of contract terms. C would be correct only if I were false and III reversed.

d.reason: “I, II and IV only” contains every true principle and excludes the false Statement III.

questions.question: The treasurer of an Australian superannuation fund oversees a contract under which a provider in the Philippines runs the fund’s member call centre. A sudden public-health lockdown in the Philippines prevents the provider’s staff from reaching its offices, and the contract requires all work to be performed on the provider’s premises. Which response is most consistent with good contract management?

options.text: Take no action, because the contract was signed by both parties and therefore remains enforceable whatever the circumstances.
Either move the activity back to Australia quickly or change the contracts and controls to allow the provider’s staff to work remotely.
Change the contract to allow remote working but leave the controls unchanged, because the place of work is a matter for the provider alone.
Defer any change until the scheduled end-of-contract renewal, because signed contract terms can be revisited only at that point.

questions.solution:
Treasurer of an Australian superannuation fund responding to a lockdown affecting an offshore call-centre provider.

**Concept and theory**

Contract management is not a one-off act at signature. The source adds that cross-country contract management brings another dimension to third-party management. Its example: when the COVID-19 shutdowns hit, US and European banks with call centres or other critical processes in countries such as India or the Philippines faced two choices:

1. rapidly move these activities back to their home countries; or
2. change contracts and controls to allow the offshore third-party employees to work remotely.

Two supporting features make this possible. A good practice is to set terms for periodic contract review and a remediation process to correct contract deficiencies, so contracts can be revisited when circumstances change. And continuous monitoring treats Acts of God (such as COVID-19) as triggers for reassessment, not events to wait out until renewal. Note the pairing of contracts with controls: remote working changes how and where the work is done, so the controls change together with the contract.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem reproduces the source’s scenario: a public-health lockdown at an offshore call centre whose contract requires on-site work. The response consistent with the source is to bring the work home quickly or to amend both the contract and the controls for remote working.

**Fragile fact.** The offshore COVID-19 response changed contracts and controls (or moved work home), not contracts alone.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, sections “Contracts, SLAs, and Contract Management” and “Continuous Monitoring”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says organisations “had to change their contracts to allow third-party employees to work fully remote” and omits both the option of moving work home and the change to controls. Content follows GARP; condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q15 of 20.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It treats enforceability as a guarantee of service. A signed contract is enforceable, but enforceability does not keep the call centre running, and the source expects contracts to be reviewed and deficiencies remediated. A would be correct only if the question asked when a contract becomes enforceable.

b.reason: It sets out exactly the two responses the source describes for offshore processes during the COVID-19 shutdowns, including the change to controls as well as contracts.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It leaves control changes to the provider alone. The source has the client firm changing contracts and controls together. C would be correct only if the provider’s working location had no bearing on the fund’s risk, which is not the case for member data.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It restricts contract changes to the scheduled renewal. The source sets periodic review and a remediation process for deficiencies, and Acts of God trigger reassessment outside scheduled reviews. D would be correct only for a contract with no review or remediation terms, which the source treats as poor practice.

questions.question: A supervisor at a central bank is reviewing how a commercial bank manages fourth-party risk. The bank’s cloud provider subcontracts data backup to another firm, and the bank has no contract with that firm. Which of the following practices by the bank best reflects good TPRM practice?

options.text: Leave the cloud provider to set its own subcontracting standards, because fourth parties fall outside the bank’s contractual reach.
Address fourth-party risk only at the remediation or termination stage, through a clause allowing exit if a subcontractor fails.
Use the contract to set standards or limits on the provider’s own outsourcing, largely replicating the bank’s vendor rules, backed by audit rights.
Set standards on the provider’s own outsourcing in the contract, but rely on the provider’s self-certification in place of audit rights.

questions.solution:
Central bank supervisor reviewing how a bank manages the fourth-party risk created by its cloud provider’s subcontractor.

**Concept and theory**

A fourth party (here, the firm doing backups for the cloud provider) has no contract with the bank, so how can the bank manage it? The source’s answer: contract terms with the third party are a good opportunity to address fourth-party risk management.

- **Standards or limits.** Good practice is for the contract to establish standards or limits on the outsourcing done by third-party vendors.
- **Cascading rules.** To a large extent, these standards can replicate the rules the firm applies to its own vendors, so that the vendors can apply them in turn to their own vendors and contractors.
- **Audit rights.** It is necessary for firms to have audit rights on their vendors, to be able to verify by themselves that the rules are applied. This is also part of the next stage, continuous monitoring.

The logic is that the firm’s control reaches the fourth party through the third party: rules are pushed down by contract and checked by audit.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank cannot contract directly with the backup firm, so the deciding facts are where fourth-party risk is addressed (the contract with the third party), what the contract does (standards or limits on outsourcing, replicating the bank’s rules) and how compliance is verified (audit rights, not self-certification).

**Fragile fact.** Fourth-party risk is handled through the third-party contract (standards or limits on its outsourcing), verified by the firm’s own audit rights.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Contracts, SLAs, and Contract Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser states that organisations should establish limits on outsourcing to vendors and fourth parties and have audit rights; it omits the replication of the firm’s own vendor rules. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q16 of 20.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It hands the standard-setting to the provider. The source has the client firm set standards or limits through its contract with the vendor. A would be correct only as a description of what happens when TPRM is absent.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves fourth-party management to the remediation or termination stage. The source places it in contract terms (stage 3), with verification in continuous monitoring. An exit clause is a stage 5 tool for ending a relationship. B would be correct only if the question asked how to end the relationship after a subcontractor failure.

c.reason: It describes the full good practice: contractual standards or limits on the provider’s outsourcing, modelled on the bank’s own vendor rules, with audit rights to verify them.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It keeps the standards but drops audit rights, the condition that lets the firm verify the rules by itself. The source calls audit rights necessary. D would be correct only if the question asked about the standards alone.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a French asset manager is testing whether the firm reassesses its fund-administration vendor between scheduled reviews. The following events occurred during the year:

I. The vendor was acquired by a larger financial group.

II. A regional flood closed the vendor’s main processing site for a week.

III. The vendor changed the services it provides to the firm by adding a new reporting module.

IV. The vendor missed its SLA accuracy targets for three consecutive months.

Which of these events should, on their own, trigger a reassessment of the relationship?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a French asset manager testing which in-year events should trigger reassessment of a fund-administration vendor.

**Concept and theory**

Continuous monitoring means more than a calendar. The source says it is good practice to define trigger events for reassessment, not just end-of-contract or scheduled period reviews. The triggers it lists are:

| Trigger | Example |
|---|---|
| Data breach or incident | A security breach at the vendor |
| Change in business circumstances of either firm | A merger or an acquisition |
| Legal or regulatory change | A new rule affecting the outsourced activity |
| Change in services provided | A new or altered service |
| Act of God | COVID-19, or any natural unavoidable circumstance |
| Breach of contract or performance failure | Missed SLA targets |

The point of triggers is speed: risk can change between scheduled reviews, and the firm needs to reassess when it does. Triggers also connect to the fifth stage: when things do not go as planned, the firm benefits from having an exit strategy.

**Applying it to this question**

Map each event: I is an acquisition, a change in the business circumstances of either firm. II is a flood, an Act of God. III is a change in services provided. IV is repeated SLA failure, a performance failure. All four are triggers.

**Fragile fact.** Six trigger types: breach or incident; change in business circumstances of either firm; legal or regulatory change; change in services; Act of God; breach of contract or performance failure.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Continuous Monitoring”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists data breaches and incidents, legal or regulatory changes, changes in business circumstances and Acts of God, but omits changes in services provided and breach of contract or performance failure. Events III and IV are therefore decided from GARP; condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q17 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I and III only” excludes the flood (an Act of God) and the SLA failures (performance failure), both listed triggers. A would be correct only if triggers were limited to deliberate business changes.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I, II and III only” excludes the SLA failures, treating performance problems as matters for scheduled review. The source lists a breach of contract or performance failure as a trigger. B would be correct only for a list limited to external events.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “II and IV only” excludes the acquisition and the service change. The source lists a change in the business circumstances of either firm and changes in services provided. C would be correct only if the trigger list covered disruptions and failures alone.

d.reason: Every event matches a trigger category in the source, so all four should trigger reassessment.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US asset manager is writing the continuous monitoring section of the firm’s TPRM standard. Which of the following statements should the analyst include?

options.text: Monitoring should cover service provision, quality SLAs, and compliance with regulation and with the contract terms, with reassessment tied to trigger events as well.
Monitoring should cover service provision and compliance with the contract terms, while the vendor’s compliance with regulation is left as the vendor’s own concern.
The more thorough the first four stages of the life cycle, the longer and more extensive the reassessment and reviewing cycle for the relationship needs to be.
Reassessment should take place only at scheduled period reviews and at the end of the contract, so that monitoring results remain comparable over time.

questions.solution:
Senior analyst at a US asset manager drafting the continuous monitoring section of a TPRM standard.

**Concept and theory**

The fourth stage keeps the relationship under review once it is live. The source describes its scope and its link to the earlier stages:

- **Scope.** Monitoring of service provision, quality SLAs, and compliance with regulation as well as with the terms of the contract are a natural component of third-party relationship management and TPRM.
- **Link to earlier stages.** The more thorough the implementation of the first four steps of the life cycle, the shorter the reassessment and reviewing cycle when the contract needs to be reviewed for continuation or change. Good groundwork makes later reviews lighter.
- **Triggers.** Reassessment should be tied to trigger events, not only to end-of-contract or scheduled period reviews.
- **Audit rights.** Rights negotiated in the contract are exercised here to verify the vendor’s compliance.

The vendor’s regulatory compliance is in scope because a regulatory failure at the vendor becomes the client’s problem.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the three-part scope (service provision and quality SLAs; compliance with regulation; compliance with the contract), the use of triggers alongside scheduled reviews, and the direction of the link between groundwork and reassessment effort.

**Fragile fact.** More thorough early stages lead to a shorter (lighter) reassessment cycle, not a longer one; monitoring includes the vendor’s regulatory compliance.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Continuous Monitoring”. GARP vs Schweser: GARP says thorough implementation of the first four steps gives a “shorter” reassessment and reviewing cycle; Schweser says the more robust the first few steps, the “less need there is for reassessment”. Both point the same way (less reassessment burden), which is all this question relies on; the wording difference looks like Schweser’s paraphrase.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q18 of 20.

a.reason: It states the full monitoring scope and ties reassessment to trigger events as well as scheduled reviews, as the source does.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It leaves the vendor’s regulatory compliance to the vendor. The source puts compliance with regulation inside the client’s monitoring. B would be correct only for an activity with no regulatory dimension.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the link between groundwork and reassessment. The source says the more thorough the first four steps, the shorter the reassessment and reviewing cycle. C would be correct only if the earlier stages had been done poorly, in which case reviews become heavier.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It confines reassessment to scheduled reviews and contract end. The source says reassessment should not be limited to these and should respond to trigger events. D would be correct only as a description of a calendar-only programme, which the source rejects.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a US property insurer must end its relationship with a claims-data vendor after a regulatory change. The vendor holds sensitive policyholder data and has built claims-triage tools under the contract, and the insurer plans to move the work to another provider. Which exit plan best reflects good practice?

options.text: End the relationship immediately and without a wind-down, because a regulatory change removes the need for fairness between the parties.
Rely on the vendor’s standard deletion policy for the data, and limit the plan to transferring the tools and appointing the new provider.
Plan a fair wind-down covering transmission of IP where necessary, transition to the new provider, and evidence of data transfer or destruction.
Treat the exit as a normal termination, because a regulatory change is the most common reason for ending a relationship, so no plan is needed.

questions.solution:
CCO of a US property insurer planning the exit from a claims-data vendor after a regulatory change.

**Concept and theory**

The fifth stage covers how relationships are repaired or ended. The source makes four points:

1. **Normal end.** Most commonly, relationships end as the provision of services ends; this is the normal cause for termination.
2. **Built-in tools.** In every contractual relationship it is good practice to have a grievance procedure as well as an exit strategy or termination clause if the situation deteriorates beyond repair.
3. **Other reasons.** Relationships can be terminated for convenience, for changes in regulations, or for other, possibly more abrupt reasons.
4. **Fair wind-down.** In these cases fairness matters, and both parties should plan a wind-down process that includes, when necessary:

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Transmission of IP | Retain intellectual property created under the contract |
| Transition plan | Move to in-house services or to another provider |
| Evidence of data transfer or destruction | Required if the vendor held sensitive data |

**Applying it to this question**

The trigger is a regulatory change, one of the listed reasons for termination other than the normal one. The vendor holds sensitive data (so evidence of transfer or destruction is needed), has built tools under the contract (so IP transmission is needed) and the work is moving to another provider (so a transition plan is needed). The plan must be fair and planned by both parties.

**Fragile fact.** Normal cause of termination: provision of services ends. Regulatory change is a different reason, and it still needs a fair wind-down with IP, transition and data evidence.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Remediation or Termination”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser mentions a “grievance period” (GARP: grievance procedure), an exit strategy or termination clause, and the transfer of IP to in-house; it omits fairness, transfer to another provider and evidence of data transfer or destruction. Content follows GARP; condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q19 of 20.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says a regulatory change removes the need for fairness. The source says that when relationships end for reasons such as regulatory change, fairness matters and both parties should plan a wind-down. No alternate stem makes the fairness claim correct under the source; the nearest case is a regulator ordering immediate cessation of the service, which shortens the wind-down but does not remove it.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the requirement for evidence of data transfer or destruction, relying instead on the vendor’s own deletion policy. The source requires evidence where sensitive data was held. B would be correct only if the vendor held no sensitive data.

c.reason: It contains all three wind-down elements the source lists and frames the process as fair and planned.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It treats regulatory change as the normal cause of termination. The normal cause is the end of the provision of services; regulatory change is one of the other reasons for which a wind-down plan matters. D would be correct only if the contract had simply reached its natural end with no data or IP to transfer.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Spanish bank is mapping TPRM practices to the stages of the life cycle. The draft mapping reads:

I. Using standard SIG questionnaires: evaluation, risk rating and due diligence.

II. Setting standards or limits on the vendor’s own outsourcing: contracts, SLAs and contract management.

III. Defining a grievance procedure and a termination clause: continuous monitoring.

IV. Deciding whether to keep an activity in-house, in light of provider quality, price and risk appetite: business model decision.

Which of the mappings are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Spanish bank checking a draft mapping of TPRM practices to life-cycle stages.

**Concept and theory**

Many TPRM practices sound alike, so exam questions often test which stage owns which practice. The source assigns them as follows:

| Stage | Practices |
|---|---|
| 1 Business model decision | Outsource or keep in-house; provider quality and price; risk appetite |
| 2 Evaluation, risk rating, due diligence | Proportionate due diligence; SIG questionnaires; vendor risk rating |
| 3 Contracts, SLAs, contract management | Clear terms; measurable SLAs; sign after remediation; periodic review; standards or limits on vendor outsourcing; audit rights |
| 4 Continuous monitoring | Service, SLAs, regulatory and contract compliance; trigger events; use of audit rights |
| 5 Remediation or termination | Grievance procedure; exit strategy or termination clause; fair wind-down |

Some items touch two stages: audit rights are agreed in the contract and exercised in monitoring, and the monitoring section notes the value of an exit strategy, which it says is addressed in the fifth stage. The grievance procedure and termination clause themselves belong to stage 5.

**Applying it to this question**

I: SIG questionnaires standardise due diligence, stage 2. Correct. II: standards or limits on the vendor’s own outsourcing are set in contract terms, stage 3. Correct. III: a grievance procedure and a termination clause are stage 5 tools, not continuous monitoring. Incorrect. IV: whether to keep an activity in-house, with provider quality, price and risk appetite, is stage 1. Correct.

**Fragile fact.** Grievance procedure and termination clause: stage 5. Limits on the vendor’s own outsourcing: stage 3 (contracts). SIG questionnaires: stage 2.

**Reference**

LO 54.a: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework. GARP Chapter 13, section “Third-Party Risk Management” (all five life-cycle subsections). GARP vs Schweser: the stage assignments agree; Schweser does not mention SIG questionnaires, so mapping I is decided from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 a, where it is Q20 of 20.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I and II only” omits IV, a correct mapping of the business model decision. A would be correct only if IV had placed the outsourcing decision in due diligence.

b.reason: “I, II and IV only” contains the three correct mappings and excludes the misplaced grievance procedure and termination clause.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** “II, III and IV only” accepts III, which assigns stage 5 tools to the neighbouring monitoring stage, and drops the correct I. C would be correct only if III read “remediation or termination” and I were wrong.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** “I, III and IV only” accepts III’s misplacement and drops II, the correct placement of outsourcing standards in contract terms. D would be correct only if II had placed outsourcing limits in the wrong stage and III had read “remediation or termination”.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-13 b Q1
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Swiss cantonal bank is preparing a briefing for newly hired analysts on the 2019 Capital One data breach. The auditor drafts the following statements about how the breach occurred:

I. The intruder was a former employee of the bank’s cloud services provider rather than of the bank itself.

II. The intruder exploited a misconfigured web application firewall to reach files stored in a database of the cloud services provider.

III. The data accessed related to about 100 million people in the United States and included roughly 140,000 bank account numbers and 80,000 Social Security numbers.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
II only
I, II and III

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Swiss cantonal bank briefing new analysts on how the 2019 Capital One breach occurred.

**Concept and theory**

The two case studies in this reading are not stories for their own sake: each is chosen because it shows a third-party relationship failing in a specific way, and the lessons only make sense if the facts are attached to the right case and the right actor. The Capital One case is the cloud case. Capital One is a US bank specialising in credit cards, auto loans, checking and savings accounts, and it hosted data with Amazon Web Services (AWS), its cloud services provider. In July 2019 the bank announced that data on about 100 million people in the United States had been illegally accessed. The mechanism has three parts that are easy to scramble:

| Element | What GARP reports |
|---|---|
| Actor | A former AWS cloud services employee, later arrested by federal authorities |
| Entry route | A weakness in a misconfigured web application firewall, exploited to reach files stored in an AWS database |
| Scale | About 100 million people in the US; charged with stealing 140,000 Social Security numbers and 80,000 bank account numbers |

The point for third-party risk management (TPRM) is that the attacker came from the vendor’s side of the relationship (a former employee of the third party), yet the data belonged to the bank’s customers and the consequences fell on the bank.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the three elements. Statement I identifies the actor: a former employee of the cloud provider, not of the bank. This matches GARP. Statement II identifies the entry route: a misconfigured web application firewall, used to reach files in an AWS database. This also matches.

Statement III gets the overall scale right (about 100 million people in the US) but swaps the two counts: GARP reports 140,000 Social Security numbers and 80,000 bank account numbers, whereas the statement says 140,000 bank account numbers and 80,000 Social Security numbers. One swapped attribution is enough to make the statement false, so only I and II are accurate.

**Fragile fact.** Former vendor employee (AWS), not a bank employee; 140,000 is the Social Security number count and 80,000 the bank account count.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, “Capital One Data Breach by Former Amazon Web Services (AWS) Employee”. GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes describe the scale as 100 million US bank customers “and many international” and the route as a weakness in “the system’s firewall”; GARP says about 100 million people in the United States and a misconfigured web application firewall. GARP is followed; this looks like condensation rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Choosing I only means rejecting statement II, typically because the reader replaces the firewall route with another breach mechanism (for example a stolen credential or an insider at the bank). The entry route in the source is the misconfigured web application firewall. I only would be correct if statement II had described a route not in the case, such as the attacker using an active bank administrator’s login.

b.reason: GARP states that federal authorities arrested a former AWS cloud services employee, who exploited a weakness in a misconfigured web application firewall to gain access to files stored in an AWS database, and who was charged with stealing 140,000 Social Security numbers and 80,000 bank account numbers. Statements I and II reproduce the first two facts; statement III inverts the third.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Choosing II only means rejecting statement I, which happens when the reader assumes the intruder was a bank insider. The source places the actor on the vendor side: a former AWS employee. II only would be correct if statement I had said the intruder was a former Capital One employee.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Choosing all three accepts statement III, in which the two data counts have been swapped with each other. The total of about 100 million people is right, which makes the swap easy to miss. D would be correct only if statement III read 140,000 Social Security numbers and 80,000 bank account numbers.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing a Singapore bank’s plan to move customer records to a public cloud platform under a SGD 40 million, five-year programme. To illustrate what went wrong at Capital One, the consultant prepares a slide on the role of encryption in that breach. Which of the following statements best describes the encryption point in the Capital One case?

options.text: The data was encrypted, but weakly, so the attacker could read it; the lesson is to impose stronger encryption standards on cloud vendors.
The data was left unencrypted by an improper configuration of the provider’s platform; the lesson is that encryption sits with the cloud provider.
Neither firm knew of the vulnerability before the attack; the lesson is that encryption offers no protection against unknown attack types.
Both firms knew of the vulnerability, and encryption would have made the data useless; it was unencrypted because of the bank’s own configuration.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant reviewing a Singapore bank’s cloud plan, explaining the encryption point in the Capital One case.

**Concept and theory**

Encryption is a compensating control: it does not stop an intruder getting in, but it makes what the intruder takes unreadable and therefore useless. That is why it matters most when a known vulnerability cannot be removed immediately. GARP’s account of Capital One builds the lesson in three steps:

1. Capital One and AWS knew their systems were vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks, of which this attack was one.
2. An effective response to that known vulnerability would have been to encrypt the data, making it useless to attackers.
3. The stolen data was not encrypted, and GARP attributes this to the improper configuration of Capital One’s systems.

After the breach the bank immediately addressed the bug, verified there were no other improper configurations in its environment, and altered its automated scanning to look regularly for the issue. The TPRM lesson is about actors: the vulnerability was known, the remedy was available, and the configuration failure sat with the client institution, not with the provider.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes two claims: a fact about the data and a lesson. Check the facts first. Was the data encrypted? No, which eliminates A. Did the firms know of the vulnerability? Yes, which eliminates C. Whose configuration left the data unencrypted? Capital One’s, which eliminates B. Only D has all three facts right: knowledge of the vulnerability, encryption as the effective response, and the bank’s own configuration as the cause. The SGD 40 million programme size is irrelevant to the answer.

**Fragile fact.** The vulnerability (SSRF) was known to both Capital One and AWS; the unencrypted data is attributed to the configuration of Capital One’s systems.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, “Capital One Data Breach by Former Amazon Web Services (AWS) Employee”. GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes say that both Capital One and AWS “continued to use unencrypted data”, which blurs the actor; GARP attributes the lack of encryption to the improper configuration of Capital One systems and names the SSRF vulnerability. GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A reverses “not encrypted” into “encrypted, but weakly”. Because the data was unencrypted, the attacker could use it at once; the case says nothing about the strength of an encryption that did not exist. A would be correct for a case in which data had been encrypted with an obsolete algorithm and then decrypted.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B gets the fact right (unencrypted because of an improper configuration) but gives the configuration to the provider and draws the lesson that encryption is the provider’s job. GARP places the improper configuration in Capital One’s systems and stresses that the business remains responsible. B would be correct only if the source had said the provider’s own platform settings caused the data to be stored unencrypted.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses “knew” into “neither firm knew”, turning a preventable failure into an unforeseeable zero-day attack, and then overreaches into the claim that encryption offers no protection. C would describe an attack using a genuinely unknown technique, which is not this case.

d.reason: GARP: “Capital One and AWS knew their systems were vulnerable to server side request forgery (SSRF) attacks” and “an effective response to this vulnerability would have been to encrypt the data in order to make it useless to attackers. Unfortunately, the stolen data was not encrypted, due to the improper configuration of Capital One systems.” Option D states exactly these three points.

questions.source: High quality paper ORR-13 b Q3
questions.question: The CRO of a Brazilian bank is presenting a public cloud migration to the board risk committee. One committee member argues that, because the chosen hyperscale provider has built strong security into its offering, monitoring, backups and maintenance of the hosted data become the provider’s job once the contract is signed. Which response by the CRO is most consistent with the lessons drawn from the Capital One case?

options.text: Providers build strong security and offer the needed controls, but risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance stay with the bank, which must use those controls.
Providers build strong security into their offerings, so responsibility for monitoring, backups and maintenance passes to the provider once clear service levels are signed.
Cloud breaches mainly reflect weaknesses in the providers’ own platforms, so the bank should select the provider with the strongest built-in controls and rely on them.
Cloud breaches are eliminated once the data is encrypted, so the bank’s remaining duty is limited to verifying that the provider encrypts all of the stored data.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Brazilian bank answering a board member who argues that cloud security duties pass to the provider.

**Concept and theory**

Cloud outsourcing is often treated as if buying a strong platform buys security. GARP uses the Capital One case to correct that view. Two statements carry the lesson. First: even though the major cloud service providers have built strong security into their offerings, it is still the business’s responsibility to handle risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance. Second, specialists attribute the rise in breaches involving cloud databases and services to poor security hygiene: all the major providers offer the controls needed to keep data in cloud storage private, but customers need to use them.

The division of labour is therefore:

| Cloud provider | Client institution (the bank) |
|---|---|
| Builds strong security into its platform | Keeps risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance |
| Offers privacy controls for stored data | Must configure and actually use those controls |

This is the cloud-specific form of the wider lesson that accountability for outsourced risk does not leave the client institution.

**Applying it to this question**

The board member’s argument has two parts: the provider’s security is strong (true) and therefore monitoring, backups and maintenance become the provider’s job (false). The correct response must accept the first part and reject the second. Option A does both and adds the hygiene point that the bank must use the controls on offer. Options B, C and D each fail at one specific point.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the business keeps risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance; the provider offers the controls, the customer must use them.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, “Capital One Data Breach by Former Amazon Web Services (AWS) Employee”. GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes do not include the cloud responsibility and security hygiene points; content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: It restates GARP’s two linked points: providers have built strong security and offer the controls needed, yet risk management, monitoring, backups and maintenance remain the business’s responsibility, and customers need to use the controls offered.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B keeps the true premise but moves monitoring, backups and maintenance to the provider once service levels are signed. GARP assigns these duties to the business regardless of the provider’s security. B would only be right if the source said the contract shifts those duties to the provider, which it does not.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses the cause of cloud breaches: specialists attribute them to poor security hygiene by customers, not to weaknesses in the providers’ platforms. C would be correct for a case where the provider’s own infrastructure had been compromised despite proper client configuration.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D promises that encryption eliminates cloud breaches and shrinks the bank’s duty to checking the provider. Encryption would have made the stolen data useless in this case, but nothing in the source says it removes the bank’s other responsibilities. D would need the qualifier “reduces the harm from” rather than “eliminates”, and would still be wrong on the narrowed duty.

questions.question: A compliance analyst at a Japanese trust bank is preparing a report for senior management on regulatory enforcement linked to cloud outsourcing. The analyst must include one sentence summarising why the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) fined Capital One USD 80 million. Which of the following sentences should the analyst include?

options.text: The OCC acted because the bank failed to notify affected customers promptly once it had detected the intrusion into its cloud environment.
The OCC acted because the cloud provider failed to vet the former employee who carried out the intrusion, and the bank was liable for the provider.
The OCC acted because the bank failed to establish effective risk assessment processes before migrating significant IT operations to the public cloud.
The OCC acted because the bank failed to remediate the misconfiguration after the breach, and the same weakness was later found elsewhere in its systems.

questions.solution:
Compliance analyst at a Japanese trust bank summarising why the OCC fined Capital One USD 80 million.

**Concept and theory**

Regulators fine banks for what the bank failed to do, and the timing of the failure matters. In the Capital One case the US banking regulator, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), fined the bank USD 80 million. In its released statement the OCC said the action was motivated by the bank’s “failure to establish effective risk assessment processes prior to migrating significant information technology operations to the public cloud environment.”

Three features of this finding are worth fixing:

- Who failed: the bank, not the cloud provider and not the individual attacker.
- What failed: risk assessment processes, a TPRM and governance failure rather than a single technical error.
- When: before the migration of significant IT operations to the public cloud, that is, well before the breach.

By contrast, the bank’s response after the breach was prompt: it immediately addressed the bug, verified there were no other instances of improper configuration, and altered its automated scanning to look for the issue regularly.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst needs the OCC’s stated basis. Ask: did the OCC act on the bank’s pre-migration risk assessment, on the vendor’s vetting, on customer notification, or on post-breach remediation? The source names only the first. Option C states it in the source’s own terms.

**Fragile fact.** Timing: the OCC faulted risk assessment before migrating to the public cloud, not the bank’s response after the breach, which was prompt.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, “Capital One Data Breach by Former Amazon Web Services (AWS) Employee”. GARP vs Schweser: the condensed notes phrase the basis as failing to adequately identify and manage risks before the breach related to vendor services, including moving data to the cloud with AWS; this is consistent with GARP’s wording, which is followed. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Customer notification is a feature of the Morgan Stanley case (notification of the 2016 incident at the OCC’s direction, the 2019 incident voluntarily), not the basis of the Capital One fine. A would fit a case in which the regulator penalised delayed breach disclosure.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B moves the failure to the cloud provider and makes the bank liable only by extension. The OCC’s stated failure was the bank’s own risk assessment. B would be correct only if the order had been directed at the provider’s hiring and vetting practices.

c.reason: It matches the OCC’s statement quoted in GARP: failure to establish effective risk assessment processes prior to migrating significant IT operations to the public cloud environment.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D reverses the remediation facts. GARP reports that the bank immediately addressed the bug, verified there were no other instances of improper configuration in its environment, and altered its automated scanning. D would be correct only if the bank had left the weakness in place after the breach.

questions.question: A supervisor at a UK prudential regulator is preparing a training case for supervisory staff on the OCC’s 2020 enforcement action against Morgan Stanley concerning the decommissioning of data-bearing hardware. Which of the following was NOT among the failures that the OCC concluded the bank had committed?

options.text: It did not adequately assess the risks of using third-party vendors, and this extended to the vendors’ subcontractors.
It did not maintain an appropriate inventory of the customer data stored on the devices that it was retiring.
It did not effectively assess or address the risks associated with the decommissioning of its hardware.
It did not encrypt the customer data on the devices before handing them to the vendors for disposal.

questions.solution:
UK supervisor identifying which failure the OCC did NOT cite against Morgan Stanley over hardware decommissioning.

**Concept and theory**

The Morgan Stanley case is the decommissioning case. Hardware that has reached the end of its life still carries data, and retiring it is usually outsourced to specialist vendors, who may in turn use subcontractors. If the bank does not know what data sits on each device and does not oversee who wipes and disposes of it, customer data can leave the building on equipment the bank no longer controls.

Through Morgan Stanley Bank and Morgan Stanley Private Bank, the firm received a USD 60 million fine from the OCC for failures in the risk management and oversight of vendors in decommissioning. In connection with the decommissioning, the OCC concluded that the bank failed to:

1. effectively assess or address the risks associated with the decommissioning of its hardware;
2. adequately assess the risk of using third-party vendors, including subcontractors; and
3. maintain an appropriate inventory of customer data stored on its devices.

The OCC also estimated that the bank did not exercise adequate due diligence in selecting the vendors and did not adequately monitor their performance. Encryption does not appear among these findings: it is the control GARP highlights in the Capital One case.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT, so three options must match the OCC’s list and one must come from elsewhere. Options A, B and C are paraphrases of findings 2, 3 and 1 respectively (note that A keeps the extension to subcontractors). Option D introduces encryption of the data on the devices, which belongs to the Capital One case. D is therefore the failure that was not cited.

**Fragile fact.** Morgan Stanley’s three failures: decommissioning risk, vendor risk including subcontractors, customer data inventory. Encryption is the Capital One lesson.

**Reference**

LO 54.b: “Describe the lessons learned from the presented case studies.” GARP Chapter 13, Case Studies, “OCC Fines Morgan Stanley for Weak Third-Party Controls Over Decommissioning of Data Centers”. GARP vs Schweser: both list the same three failures; the condensed notes fold the monitoring finding into the second failure. No conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-13 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A reader who picks A believes the OCC’s vendor finding stopped at the direct vendors. GARP explicitly extends it: the bank failed to adequately assess the risk of using third-party vendors, including subcontractors. A would be the answer only if the statement had said the finding covered subcontractors alone and not the vendors.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** A reader who picks B attaches the data inventory finding to the wrong case, but the inventory of customer data stored on devices is a Morgan Stanley finding and the key to why disposed hardware still held client data. B would be the answer only if the stem had asked about the Capital One order.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A reader who picks C narrows the case to vendor oversight and forgets that the OCC also faulted the bank’s assessment of the decommissioning itself. C would be the answer only if the OCC had found the decommissioning risks properly assessed and faulted only the vendors.

d.reason: GARP’s list of OCC conclusions for Morgan Stanley contains decommissioning risk, vendor and subcontractor risk, and the data inventory, plus inadequate vendor due diligence and monitoring. Encryption of device data is not among them; GARP raises encryption only in the Capital One case, where it would have made the stolen data useless.
