questions.question: A senior model validator at a US bank is reviewing a USD interest rate model whose developers assumed that the speed of mean reversion is constant. The validator would have chosen a time-varying speed, but accepts that both choices are defensible. Her replication of the code shows that the model does exactly what its documentation describes. Which of the following best describes the issue she has found?

options.text: A potential conceptual error, which is harder to identify because it may not be a matter of right or wrong and reasonable modelers can hold equally valid views.
A potential execution error, which is settled by replicating the code, because the disagreement concerns how the model has been implemented in the system.
A potential conceptual error, which is easier to identify than an execution error, because the assumption in question is recorded in the model documentation.
A confirmed conceptual error, which shows that the model is wrong in every context and that its use should therefore be discontinued with immediate effect.

questions.solution:
Senior validator at a US bank disagreeing with a defensible constant mean-reversion assumption in a model whose code is correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains that conceptual errors “are much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong”. An execution error has a reference point: the design. Code either matches it or does not, which is why replication is effective against execution errors. A conceptual question has no such reference point: “Different reasonable modelers can have different and equally valid opinions on an assumption.”

Because the answer may be a matter of judgment, GARP says the role of model risk management “in those situations” is to ensure transparency: understand the limitations of the model and communicate them clearly to users, who may not be quantitatively savvy. A model can be “right” in that it performs adequately in a particular context, but completely wrong if the context changes, so the aim is to tell users when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued, not to declare the model wrong everywhere.

**Applying it to this question**

The replication shows the model does exactly what its documentation says, so there is no execution error. The remaining issue is an assumption (constant mean reversion) on which the validator and the developers hold different but defensible views. That is the defining difficulty of a conceptual issue: it may not be a matter of right or wrong, which makes it harder, not easier, to identify and settle.

**Fragile fact.** Conceptual errors are the harder type to identify, precisely because they may not be a matter of right or wrong.

**Reference**

LO 57.a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. GARP Chapter 16, Definition and History, subsection 2. Model Risks. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point: Schweser states that conceptual errors are more difficult to identify; GARP supplies the reason (no clear right or wrong, equally valid views).

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 a, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: It restates GARP’s two facts: conceptual errors are harder to identify than execution errors, and the reason is that they may not be a matter of right or wrong because reasonable modelers can hold equally valid views.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It classifies an assumption choice as an execution issue. The replication has already shown that implementation matches the design, which is what an execution check tests. Option B would be correct if the replication had shown the code using a different mean-reversion speed from the documented one.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses GARP’s comparison: conceptual errors are harder, not easier, to identify than execution errors. Documenting an assumption does not make it right or wrong. Option C would be correct with the two error types swapped: execution errors are easier to identify because the documented design provides a reference point.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It upgrades a defensible disagreement into a confirmed error “in every context”. GARP says a model can be right in one context and wrong in another, and the response is transparency about when it can be safely used. Option D would be closer to correct if evidence showed that the constant-speed assumption had stopped holding in the conditions in which the model is used; discontinuing use in those conditions could then be warranted, but not in every context.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Shanghai asset manager uses a risk model for a CNY equity portfolio. The model’s correlation inputs were estimated over a calm three-year window, and the model documentation lists this calibration choice as a limitation.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Average pairwise correlation, calm estimation window | 0.25 |
| Average pairwise correlation, recent stress episode | 0.70 |
| Number of holdings | 40 |

She considers the following statements:

I. The model may perform adequately in calm markets yet be wrong when the context changes, which is a conceptual rather than an execution issue.

II. Correlations estimated in normal times tend to overstate correlations in volatile markets, so the model overstates risk in a stress episode.

III. Because the developers documented the calibration window as a limitation, the users of the model can be taken to be aware of it.

IV. The limitation should be communicated to users in a way that shows when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I and IV only

questions.solution:
Portfolio manager at a Shanghai asset manager weighing statements on a CNY risk model calibrated to calm-period correlations.

**Concept and theory**

Conceptual errors are often not errors when the model is built. An assumption can be a good description of reality in one environment and a poor one in another. GARP puts it as: a model can be “right” in that it performs adequately in a particular context, but it could be completely wrong if the context were to change. Schweser gives the standard example: risk models often rely on correlations as an input, and correlation estimates from normal times often underestimate correlations during more volatile market conditions.

GARP’s illustration inside its discussion of model risks is the Gaussian copula: the assumption was valid and gave accurate values in normal conditions, but when correlations spiked it no longer held, and many users kept using the pricing tools without realizing the size of the errors.

The second point is about who knows what. Modelers are usually aware of their model’s limitations and may discuss them in the documentation, but GARP warns that “this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them”. The assumptions must therefore be communicated in a way that helps users understand “when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued”.

**Applying it to this question**

The table shows an average correlation of 0.25 in the calm estimation window against 0.70 in the stress episode, so calm-period estimates understate stressed correlations, as the source states. Higher correlation means less diversification, so the model understates risk in stress (this link is standard portfolio reasoning; the chapter itself states only the direction of the correlation bias). The number of holdings is irrelevant.

- Statement I: correct. The model can be right in calm markets and wrong when the context changes; that is a conceptual issue, since the model is doing what it was designed to do.
- Statement II: incorrect. It reverses the direction: normal-time correlations understate, not overstate, volatile-market correlations.
- Statement III: incorrect. Documentation by developers does not establish that users are aware of, or understand, the limitation.
- Statement IV: correct. It restates GARP’s requirement on how the limitation should be communicated.

**Fragile fact.** Correlations estimated in normal times understate stressed correlations; and the developer documenting a limitation is not the same as the user understanding it.

**Reference**

LO 57.a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. GARP Chapter 16, Definition and History, subsection 2. Model Risks. Boundary call: Statement IV touches the role of model risk management (LO 57.b), but GARP places this requirement inside its discussion of conceptual errors, so it is tested here only as a property of conceptual errors. No GARP vs Schweser conflict: the correlation example is Schweser’s and is consistent with GARP’s Gaussian copula illustration; both say limitations must be communicated to users.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 a, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts Statement II, which reverses the source’s direction (normal-time correlations underestimate volatile-market correlations), and drops the communication requirement in Statement IV. Option A would be correct only if Statement II said “understate” and “understates risk” and Statement IV were false.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Its decisive error is the same reversed correlation direction in Statement II, compounded by accepting Statement III and rejecting the two true statements. It would be correct only if normal-time correlations overstated stressed correlations and documentation alone guaranteed user awareness, and the source states neither.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It accepts Statement III, attributing the developers’ knowledge of the limitation to the users. GARP says the modelers’ awareness, even in writing, does not mean users are aware. Option C would be correct if the stem said the limitation had been explained to the users and they had confirmed that they understood when the model should and should not be used.

d.reason: Statements I and IV restate the source; Statement II reverses the direction of the correlation bias and Statement III equates documentation with user awareness.

questions.question: A supervisor at an insurance regulator is reviewing the INR valuation model that an Indian life insurer uses for a savings product with guaranteed returns and embedded options. The model estimates the liability by a linear regression on interest rates, although the product’s payoff is strongly non-linear in rates. The insurer has verified that the code and the input data match the model specification exactly. Which of the following best describes the insurer’s exposure to model risk?

options.text: Execution risk, because the model’s output is wrong and so the model does not do what it is intended to do.
A conceptual error, because an unsuitable modeling technique was chosen even though the model executes as designed.
Execution risk, because implementation errors include any mismatch between a model’s design and the product it values.
Neither type of model risk, because the code and the input data were verified against the model specification exactly.

questions.solution:
Supervisor reviewing an Indian life insurer’s INR valuation model that applies a linear regression to a strongly non-linear payoff.

**Concept and theory**

A model sits between three layers: reality, the design (the chosen theory, technique and assumptions), and the implementation (code and data). Each type of model risk is a gap between two of these layers:

| Gap | Type | Source wording |
|---|---|---|
| Implementation vs design | Execution risk | The model does not do what it is intended and designed to do (coding, implementation, wrong data) |
| Design vs reality | Conceptual error | Wrong assumptions or modeling techniques are used |

Conceptual errors therefore come in two forms: an assumption that does not represent reality, and a modeling technique that is unsuitable for the problem. Both GARP (“wrong assumptions or modeling techniques”) and Schweser (“incorrect modeling techniques are used”) name the second form explicitly. A model can be implemented perfectly and still be conceptually wrong.

**Applying it to this question**

The insurer has verified that code and data match the specification exactly: the implementation-versus-design gap is closed, so there is no execution error. The specification itself, however, applies a linear technique to a payoff that the stem states is strongly non-linear: a design-versus-reality gap created by the choice of technique. That is a conceptual error.

**Fragile fact.** An unsuitable technique is a conceptual error even when the code matches the specification perfectly; execution risk is about implementation departing from design.

**Reference**

LO 57.a: Define a model and describe different ways that financial institutions can become exposed to model risk. GARP Chapter 16, Definition and History, subsection 2. Model Risks. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point: both list incorrect modeling techniques, as well as invalid assumptions, as conceptual errors.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It equates “the output is wrong” with “the model does not do what it is intended to do”. Execution risk is a departure from the intended design; here the model follows its design exactly, and the design is the problem. Option A would be correct if the specification had called for a non-linear valuation method and the code had implemented a linear one instead.

b.reason: Conceptual errors “occur when the wrong assumptions or modeling techniques are used in the model”; here an unsuitable technique was chosen while the model does exactly what it was designed to do.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It stretches implementation errors to cover a mismatch between the design and the product. Implementation errors are departures of the implementation from the design. Option C would be correct if the mismatch were between the model as specified and the model as coded or deployed.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It treats verified code and data as proof that no model risk remains. Those checks address execution risk only; conceptual errors survive them. Option D would be correct only if the technique and assumptions were also suitable for the product, and even then the output would remain an estimate subject to error.

questions.reading: ORR-16: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.topic: Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation
questions.source: High quality paper ORR-16 b Q1
questions.question: A board risk committee member at a UK building society is reviewing a proposal to replace the society’s current practice, under which each model is tested only by the team that built it, with a dedicated model risk management (MRM) function. The proposal must state where the function sits, who staffs it and what its remit is. Which of the following designs best reflects the typical MRM function?

options.text: It sits in the first line of defence, is staffed by experienced model developers, and its responsibilities cover all aspects of a model throughout its life cycle.
It sits in the second line of defence, is staffed by experts independent of model development, and its responsibilities cover all aspects of a model throughout its life cycle.
It sits in the second line of defence, is staffed by experts independent of model development, and its responsibilities are limited to validating each model before deployment.
It sits in the third line of defence, is staffed by internal auditors independent of model development, and its responsibilities cover all aspects of a model throughout its life cycle.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member at a UK building society specifying the placement, staffing and remit of a new MRM function.

**Concept and theory**

Model risk is inherent to modelling, and the stakes in finance are such that relying on the best-faith efforts of the development team to handle it is not sufficient. Modelling errors can cause large and sometimes catastrophic losses, so regulators have steadily raised their expectations for a professional, independent model risk management function.

GARP describes the typical MRM function along three dimensions:

| Dimension | Typical MRM function |
|---|---|
| Placement | Sits in the second line of defence. |
| Staffing | Experts who are independent of model development. |
| Remit | All aspects of a model throughout its life cycle (development, deployment, use, monitoring, review, retirement). |

Independence matters because the people who built a model are poorly placed to challenge their own choices. The second line exists to give an objective, independent view and to act as a backstop for errors the first line has missed. The life-cycle remit matters because model risk does not end at approval: a model that was right in one environment can become wrong when the environment changes, which is why MRM also runs annual reviews and monitors performance between validations.

**Applying it to this question**

The building society currently relies on the builders testing their own models, which is exactly the arrangement GARP calls insufficient. The proposal has to fix three things: the line of defence, the staffing and the remit. All three must match: second line, independent experts, whole life cycle. Each wrong option gets exactly one of the three wrong.

**Fragile fact.** MRM is the second line, not the first (developers and owners) and not the third (internal audit); its remit is the whole life cycle, not just the initial validation.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”; context on why best-faith efforts are not enough from “Definition and History”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says the MRM team consists of experts independent of the original developers but does not name the second line or the life-cycle remit; GARP is the source for both. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q1 of 16.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** Model developers are the first line: they generate and own the risk. Placing MRM in the first line and staffing it with developers destroys the independence that is the reason for having the function. The description would be correct for a first-line QA/QC team at a mature institution, not for MRM.

b.reason: GARP states that “a typical model risk management (MRM) function sits in the second line of defense and is staffed with experts who are independent of model development” and that its “responsibilities cover all aspects of a model throughout its lifecycle.” Option B reproduces all three elements.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Placement and staffing are right, but the remit is cut down to pre-deployment validation. GARP gives MRM responsibility for all aspects of a model throughout its life cycle, including annual reviews and the review of monitoring reports after deployment. The option would be correct only if the question asked about the initial validation step alone.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Internal audit is the third line. It is independent, but it is not the MRM function, which GARP places in the second line. The option would describe internal audit’s assurance role if the stem asked who reviews the MRM function itself.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is drafting the charter of its newly created MRM function and lists the following responsibilities:

I. Setting model documentation standards.

II. Setting data quality expectations and versioning criteria for models.

III. Taking over ownership of a model’s risk from the model owner once the model has been validated.

IV. Reviewing and challenging models to minimise model risk.

Which of the listed items are consistent with the role of a typical MRM function?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
CRO of a Singapore bank listing responsibilities for the charter of a new MRM function.

**Concept and theory**

GARP lists the core standard-setting duties of MRM: it “sets, among other things, model documentation standards, data quality expectations, and versioning criteria.” These standards give every model a common baseline: documentation makes a model reviewable, data quality expectations protect the inputs, and versioning criteria make it clear which version of a model is in use and has been validated.

Beyond setting standards, “one of its more visible and important responsibilities is that of reviewing and challenging models to minimize the risks” of execution and conceptual errors.

What MRM does not do is take ownership of model risk. In the three lines of defence model, model developers and model owners are the first line: they generate the risk, own it and must mitigate it to the greatest extent possible. The second line independently assesses the risk and the first line’s risk management practices.

| Activity | Who |
|---|---|
| Set documentation, data quality and versioning standards | MRM (second line) |
| Review and challenge models | MRM (second line) |
| Own and mitigate model risk | Developers and owners (first line) |

**Applying it to this question**

Statements I and II are the standard-setting duties GARP names. Statement IV is the review and challenge duty. Statement III moves ownership of risk from the first line to the second line after validation, which contradicts the ownership rule: the first line keeps owning the risk whether or not MRM has validated the model.

**Fragile fact.** MRM sets the standards and challenges the models; the first line (developers and owners) owns the model risk before and after validation.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says MRM teams set standards for model documentation, data quality and model version control, consistent with GARP. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q2 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** I and II are correct, but the option omits IV, reviewing and challenging models, which GARP calls one of MRM’s more visible and important responsibilities. It would be correct only if the charter were limited to standard setting.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It includes III, which hands ownership of model risk to MRM. GARP is explicit that developers and owners own the risk; MRM’s existence must not lead the first line to abdicate its responsibilities. It also omits I and IV.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** It again includes III and drops II (data quality and versioning criteria), a standard GARP assigns to MRM. It would be correct only if ownership of risk transferred on validation, which it does not.

d.reason: I, II and IV each paraphrase a responsibility GARP assigns to MRM; III is a role misassignment. Only D selects exactly I, II and IV.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising an Australian bank that currently validates all 240 of its AUD models with the same depth and on the same schedule. She recommends that the MRM function tier the models instead. Which of the following best describes the characteristics usually used to tier models and what the tier then determines?

options.text: Materiality of output, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use; the tier dictates both the thoroughness and the frequency of validation.
Materiality of output, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use; the tier dictates the frequency of validation, while its thoroughness is the same for all models.
Materiality of output, complexity, client-facing use and vendor provenance; the tier dictates both the thoroughness and the frequency of validation.
Materiality of output, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use; the tier dictates whether a model is reviewed at all, with low-tier models exempt from review.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant at an Australian bank recommending model tiering: which criteria, and what the tier decides.

**Concept and theory**

Not all models pose the same risk, and validating every model to the same depth on the same schedule is either too costly (if every model gets top-tier treatment) or too thin (if the high-risk models get the treatment suited to trivial ones). GARP explains that “to balance the cost and burden of model validation with the need to ensure that model risk is adequately addressed, MRM functions assign models to different tiers according to the risk they pose.”

The usual tiering characteristics are:

| Characteristic | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Materiality of output | How big a financial loss could the firm face from an error in the model’s forecast? |
| Complexity | How complex is the model, and so how likely are errors? |
| Client-facing use | Is the model’s use client facing? |
| Regulatory use | Is the model used for regulatory purposes? |

The consequence is stated directly: “The model tier dictates the thoroughness and the frequency of its validation.” Tiering never removes a model from review: all models, whatever their tier, receive an annual review.

**Applying it to this question**

The question has two parts: the criteria, and what the tier determines. The correct option must list all four criteria and say that the tier fixes both depth (thoroughness) and frequency. Option A is the only one with both parts right; the 240-model count is context only.

**Fragile fact.** The tier dictates both thoroughness and frequency; no tier is exempt from the annual review. The four criteria are materiality, complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser lists the same four tier drivers and frames tiering as a cost-benefit choice. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q3 of 16.

a.reason: It lists the four characteristics GARP gives (materiality, complexity, client-facing use, regulatory use) and states that the tier dictates both thoroughness and frequency, as in the sentence quoted above.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The criteria are right, but the effect of the tier is narrowed to frequency only. GARP says the tier dictates thoroughness and frequency; for example, top-tier models are reviewed in detail with comprehensive back-testing, while lower tiers have depth tailored to the tier. It would be correct only if the stem asked solely about scheduling.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** “Vendor provenance” replaces regulatory use. Whether a model was bought or built is not one of the tiering characteristics in the source. The option would be correct if “vendor provenance” were replaced with “regulatory use”.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It says low-tier models are exempt from review. GARP states that all models, independently of their tier, undergo an annual review. It would be correct only if “whether a model is reviewed at all” were replaced with “the thoroughness and frequency of validation”.

questions.question:
A senior model validator at a Japanese bank is proposing tiers for three models in the inventory: M1, an IRB mortgage PD model; M2, a marketing campaign optimiser; and M3, a robo-adviser allocation engine. Loss on failure is the MRM function’s estimate of the financial loss the bank could face from an error in the model’s output.

| Model | Client facing | Regulatory use | Loss on failure (JPY bn) | Complexity | Years in use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | No | Yes | 40.0 | High | 9 |
| M2 | No | No | 0.3 | Low | 2 |
| M3 | Yes | No | 6.0 | Medium | 1 |

Which proposed treatment is most consistent with good model risk management practice?

options.text: Rank the models by years in use and place M3 in the highest tier, since the newest model has the shortest performance record.
Place all three models in the same tier, since only identical scrutiny of every model ensures that model risk is adequately addressed.
Place M1 in the highest tier, M3 in an intermediate tier and M2 in the lowest tier, tailoring validation depth and frequency to each tier.
Place M1 in the highest tier, M3 in an intermediate tier and M2 in the lowest tier, and exempt M2 from all review until it is redeployed.

questions.solution:
Senior model validator at a Japanese bank assigning tiers to an IRB PD model, a marketing optimiser and a robo-adviser engine.

**Concept and theory**

Tiering ranks models by the risk they pose, using four characteristics: materiality of output (the size of the loss an error could cause), complexity, client-facing use and regulatory use. The higher the tier, the more thorough and frequent the validation: top-tier models are reviewed in detail with comprehensive back-testing and replicability checks and receive full-scope validations usually every 2 to 3 years; mid-tier models perhaps every 4 or 5 years; low-tier models more rarely still. Whatever the tier, every model receives an annual review of its environment, data and other important elements.

Model age is not a tiering characteristic. A new model may need careful monitoring, but tiering is driven by the risk the model poses.

**Applying it to this question**

Score each model on the four characteristics and ignore “years in use”, which is not a tiering criterion:

| Model | Materiality | Complexity | Client facing | Regulatory | Resulting tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | High (JPY 40.0 bn) | High | No | Yes | Highest |
| M3 | Medium (JPY 6.0 bn) | Medium | Yes | No | Intermediate |
| M2 | Low (JPY 0.3 bn) | Low | No | No | Lowest |

M1 ranks highest on materiality, complexity and regulatory use. M3 is client facing with moderate materiality and complexity. M2 is low on every criterion. The ranking is therefore M1, then M3, then M2, with depth and frequency tailored to each tier and every model still subject to the annual review.

**Fragile fact.** Low tier means less frequent and less deep validation, never no review: the annual review applies to every model.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: same four tier drivers in both. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q4 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It tiers by years in use, the deliberately irrelevant input. Age is not one of the tiering characteristics. The option would be correct only if the bank had chosen to tier by length of performance record, which the source does not describe.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It asserts that only identical scrutiny of every model ensures model risk is addressed. GARP says the opposite: tiering exists to balance the cost and burden of validation against the need to address model risk. It would be correct only for an inventory in which every model posed the same risk.

c.reason: It ranks the models on the four characteristics GARP lists and tailors validation depth and frequency to the tier, as GARP requires (“the model tier dictates the thoroughness and the frequency of its validation”).

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The ranking is right, but exempting M2 from all review breaks the rule that all models, independently of their tier, undergo an annual review. It would be correct if “exempt M2 from all review” read “validate M2 least often, subject to the annual review”.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Chinese bank is reviewing four candidate validation policies for the bank’s CNY credit and market risk models. Each policy sets the interval between full-scope validations for each tier and states which tiers also receive an annual review. Which policy is most consistent with the practice of a typical MRM function?

options.text: High tier: full scope every year, with comprehensive back-testing; mid tier: every 2 to 3 years; low tier: every 4 or 5 years; annual review: all tiers.
High tier: full scope every 4 or 5 years, with comprehensive back-testing; mid tier: every 2 to 3 years; low tier: more rarely; annual review: all tiers.
High tier: full scope every 2 to 3 years, with comprehensive back-testing; mid tier: every 4 or 5 years; low tier: more rarely; annual review: high and mid tiers.
High tier: full scope every 2 to 3 years, with comprehensive back-testing; mid tier: every 4 or 5 years; low tier: more rarely; annual review: all tiers.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Chinese bank choosing between four tiered validation policies.

**Concept and theory**

Tiering turns into a concrete validation calendar. GARP describes the typical pattern:

| Tier | Full-scope validation | Depth |
|---|---|---|
| Highest | Usually every 2 to 3 years | Reviewed in detail; comprehensive back-testing; replicability of output assessed |
| Mid | Perhaps every 4 or 5 years | Similar process, depth tailored to tier |
| Low | Even more rarely | Similar process, depth tailored to tier |
| All tiers | Annual review of environment, data and other important elements | Confirms no material change since the last full-scope validation |

Two different activities are easily confused. A full-scope validation is the complete, in-depth review whose frequency depends on the tier. The annual review is a lighter check, applied to every model, that asks whether anything material has changed since the last full-scope validation. Between both, MRM also monitors performance through monitoring reports.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each policy against three tests: (1) highest tier every 2 to 3 years, (2) mid tier every 4 or 5 years and low tier more rarely, so the interval lengthens as the tier falls, and (3) an annual review for every tier. Only D passes all three.

**Fragile fact.** Highest tier: full scope every 2 to 3 years; mid: 4 or 5; low: more rarely. “Annual” belongs to the review of every model, not to the full-scope validation.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser gives only the top-tier interval (usually every 2 to 3 years) and the annual review of all models; the mid-tier (4 or 5 years) and low-tier intervals are from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q5 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It turns the annual review into an annual full-scope validation for the top tier and shifts every other interval down one step (mid 2 to 3 years, low 4 or 5 years). The yearly activity GARP describes is the annual review, not a full-scope validation. The option would be correct only if “full scope every year” read “annual review every year”.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the high and mid intervals, so the riskiest models are validated less often than mid-tier ones. Frequency rises with the tier. It would be correct if the high and mid intervals were swapped back.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The intervals are right, but the annual review is restricted to high and mid tiers. GARP applies it to all models, independently of their tier. It would be correct if the last item read “all tiers”.

d.reason: It gives the highest tier full scope every 2 to 3 years with comprehensive back-testing, mid tier every 4 or 5 years, low tier more rarely, and the annual review for all tiers, exactly as GARP describes (“All models, independently of their tier, undergo an annual review”).

questions.question: The head of validation at a Brazilian bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on how the bank’s highest-tier models, which include its BRL interest rate risk and capital models, are validated. Which of the following statements should she include as the most accurate?

options.text: They undergo full-scope validations less frequently than mid-tier models, because their detailed reviews take longer to complete.
They are reviewed in detail, with the validation team performing comprehensive back-testing and assessing the model for replicability of output.
They are reviewed in detail, with the model development team performing comprehensive back-testing and certifying the replicability of output.
They are reviewed in detail and, once validated, need no further review or monitoring until the next full-scope validation falls due.

questions.solution:
Head of validation at a Brazilian bank describing to new analysts how highest-tier models are validated.

**Concept and theory**

The tier dictates the thoroughness and frequency of validation. For the highest tier, GARP states that models “will be reviewed in detail, with the validation team performing comprehensive backtesting and assessing the model for replicability of output. These high-tier models also undergo more frequent full scope validations, usually every 2 to 3 years.”

Three features define top-tier treatment:

- Depth: a detailed review.
- Specific tests performed by the validation team: comprehensive back-testing (comparing forecasts with realised outcomes) and an assessment of replicability (can the output be independently reproduced?).
- Frequency: more frequent full-scope validations than lower tiers.

The validation is performed by MRM, which is independent of development. On top of the scheduled validation, every model receives an annual review and its performance is monitored through monitoring reports produced by model owners.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the actor (the validation team, not the developers), the direction of frequency (higher tier means more frequent) and the continuity of oversight (annual review and monitoring continue between validations). Only B gets all three right.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the validation team performs back-testing and replicability checks. Direction: the higher the tier, the more frequent the full-scope validation.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser describes top-tier validation as “comprehensive backtesting for reliability of model output”; GARP says comprehensive back-testing and assessing “replicability of output”. The difference looks like condensation wording; GARP is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q6 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says top-tier models are validated less often than mid-tier ones. GARP says they undergo more frequent full-scope validations, usually every 2 to 3 years, against 4 or 5 years for mid-tier models. It would be correct if “less frequently” read “more frequently”.

b.reason: It reproduces the GARP description: detailed review, with the validation team performing comprehensive back-testing and assessing replicability of output.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** The tests are right, but the actor is wrong: GARP gives backtesting and replicability assessment to the validation team, which is independent of development. Developers are the first line and cannot provide the independent challenge. It would be correct if “model development team” read “validation team”.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the annual review (applied to all models regardless of tier) and the ongoing monitoring through owners’ reports. GARP also stresses that MRM should be continuous rather than a point-in-time exercise. It would be correct only for the narrow question of when the next full-scope validation falls due.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German bank is preparing a note on the status of a mid-tier EUR deposit behaviour model. The table summarises the model’s record.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Model tier | Mid |
| Last full-scope validation | November 2024 |
| Annual review (November 2026) | No material changes in the environment, the data or other important elements |
| Development cost | EUR 0.8 million |

Which conclusion should the note record?

options.text: A full-scope validation must be carried out now, because each annual review is itself a full-scope validation.
The last full-scope validation results still hold, and the annual review cancels the next scheduled full-scope validation.
The last full-scope validation results still hold, and the continued use of the model is approved.
The model must be suspended until its next full-scope validation, because two years have passed since the last one.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a German bank recording the outcome of a clean annual review for a mid-tier EUR model.

**Concept and theory**

Between full-scope validations, GARP requires a lighter check on every model: “All models, independently of their tier, undergo an annual review of the environment, the data, and other important elements to ensure that no material changes have been observed since the last full scope validation. If no changes are observed, the last full scope validation results still hold, and the continued use of the model is approved.”

The logic is conditional:

| Annual review finding | Consequence |
|---|---|
| No material change | Last full-scope results still hold; continued use approved |
| Material change | Last validation can no longer be relied on as it stands; further action is needed |

The annual review does not replace the tier’s full-scope schedule; it confirms that the last full-scope validation remains valid until the next one falls due.

**Applying it to this question**

The model is mid tier, so its next full-scope validation is roughly 4 or 5 years after November 2024. The November 2026 annual review found no material changes in the environment, data or other important elements. The condition in GARP’s rule is met, so the last full-scope results still hold and continued use is approved. The development cost of EUR 0.8 million is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Annual review with no material change: last full-scope results still hold and continued use is approved; the full-scope schedule is neither brought forward nor cancelled.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser states that all models should be reviewed annually regarding changes in the environment, input data quality and other important elements, but does not state the “results still hold, continued use approved” consequence; that comes from GARP. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q7 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It treats the annual review as a full-scope validation. They are different activities: the annual review checks for material change; full-scope validation is the in-depth review scheduled by tier. It would be correct only if the annual review had found a material change requiring a fresh validation.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The first half is right, but the annual review does not cancel the next full-scope validation. GARP says the results “still hold” and continued use is approved; the tier still dictates the frequency of full-scope validation. It would be correct if the second half read “the next full-scope validation remains on schedule”.

c.reason: It states the exact consequence GARP attaches to an annual review that finds no material changes.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns a clean review into a suspension. Two years without a full-scope validation is normal for a mid-tier model (interval 4 or 5 years), and a clean annual review approves continued use. It would be correct only if the review had found material changes and the model could not be relied on.

questions.question: A risk consultant reviewing the MRM framework of a US bank is asked to describe how the performance of models is monitored between scheduled validations and reviews. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

options.text: Model owners produce monitoring reports, usually as per MRM standards, at intervals suited to how often each model is used, and MRM monitors performance through them.
MRM produces monitoring reports, as per its own standards, at intervals suited to how often each model is used, and model owners monitor performance through them.
Model owners produce monitoring reports, usually as per MRM standards, once a year for every model to match the annual review, and MRM monitors performance through them.
Model owners produce monitoring reports, usually as per MRM standards, at intervals suited to how often each model is used, but only for models in the highest tier.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant describing how model performance is monitored between scheduled validations at a US bank.

**Concept and theory**

Scheduled validations and annual reviews leave gaps in which a model can drift. GARP closes the gap with ongoing monitoring: “Beyond these regularly scheduled validations and reviews, MRM groups monitor the performance of models through the monitoring reports produced by model owners (usually as per MRM standards). These monitoring reports are produced at intervals that are appropriate given the frequency at which models are used.”

The division of labour:

| Task | Actor |
|---|---|
| Produce monitoring reports | Model owners (first line) |
| Set the standards the reports follow | MRM, usually |
| Monitor performance through the reports | MRM (second line) |
| Set report frequency | According to how often the model is used |

This fits the three lines of defence: the first line, which owns the risk, measures its own models’ performance; the second line reviews that evidence independently.

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts decide the answer: who produces the reports (owners), who uses them to monitor performance (MRM), and what sets the frequency (how often the model is used). Option A gets all three right; each other option breaks one.

**Fragile fact.** Owners produce the monitoring reports; MRM monitors performance through them. Frequency follows how often the model is used, not its tier.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says MRM teams review the periodic model performance reports prepared by model owners, consistent with GARP; the frequency guidance is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q8 of 16.

a.reason: It restates GARP: owners produce reports, usually per MRM standards, at intervals appropriate to the frequency of use, and MRM monitors model performance through them.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It swaps the actors: MRM produces the reports and owners review them. In GARP the owners produce them and MRM monitors through them. It would be correct if the two actors were swapped back.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It ties monitoring frequency to the annual review cycle. The annual review is a separate activity; monitoring frequency depends on how often the model is used (some models annual or quarterly, others monthly or even weekly). It would be correct only for a model, such as some capital models, whose use justifies annual monitoring.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It restricts monitoring to the highest tier. GARP states no such restriction; the interval is driven by frequency of use. It would be correct only if the stem had asked which models receive comprehensive back-testing.

questions.question:
A model risk analyst at a Canadian bank must propose how often the owners of three models should produce monitoring reports.

| Model | How the model is used | Tier | Annual run cost (CAD 000) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Economic capital model | Run at each quarter end | High | 450 |
| Card fraud detection model | Scores transactions in real time | Mid | 320 |
| Retail loan pricing model | Prices new loans daily | Mid | 120 |

Which proposal is most consistent with good monitoring practice?

options.text: Capital model: weekly; card fraud model: quarterly; loan pricing model: monthly.
Capital model: quarterly; card fraud model: quarterly; loan pricing model: quarterly.
Capital model: quarterly; card fraud model: weekly; loan pricing model: monthly.
Capital model: quarterly; card fraud model: weekly; loan pricing model: not monitored.

questions.solution:
Model risk analyst at a Canadian bank setting monitoring frequencies for capital, card fraud and loan pricing models.

**Concept and theory**

Monitoring reports are produced by model owners “at intervals that are appropriate given the frequency at which models are used.” GARP gives the range:

| Type of model | Typical monitoring frequency |
|---|---|
| Capital models | Annual or quarterly |
| Other models | Monthly |
| Fraud monitoring models (very dynamic) | Increasingly higher frequency, such as weekly |

The principle is simple: a model run once a quarter cannot produce new performance evidence every week, while a model scoring transactions continuously in a fast-changing environment, such as fraud, can drift within days, so monthly or quarterly monitoring would leave it unchecked for too long.

**Applying it to this question**

Match each model’s frequency of use to a monitoring interval:

- Economic capital model, run at each quarter end: a capital model, so quarterly (or annual) monitoring.
- Card fraud model, scoring in real time in a very dynamic area: weekly monitoring.
- Retail loan pricing model, used daily: an “other” model, so monthly monitoring.

The tier and the annual run cost are distractors; neither drives the monitoring interval in the source.

**Fragile fact.** Capital models: annual or quarterly; other models: monthly; fraud models: weekly. The driver is how often the model is used, not its tier or cost.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not give monitoring frequencies; this content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q9 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the capital and fraud intervals: weekly monitoring for a model run quarterly and quarterly monitoring for the most dynamic model. It would be correct if the two frequencies were swapped back.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** One quarterly interval for every model ignores the rule that intervals depend on how often each model is used. It would be correct only if all three models were used at the same, quarterly frequency.

c.reason: Quarterly for the capital model, weekly for the fraud model and monthly for the pricing model matches GARP’s guidance that frequency follows the frequency of use, with fraud monitoring the leading example of weekly monitoring.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops monitoring for the pricing model. GARP describes monitoring through owners’ reports for models generally, with “other models” typically monthly. It would be correct if “not monitored” read “monthly”.

questions.question: A risk committee member at a Japanese bank notes that, although MRM is meant to be a continuous effort, the bank’s MRM function still works almost entirely through scheduled, point-in-time validations and reviews. Which of the following best explains why many institutions still operate in this way?

options.text: A periodic model is predictable, so staffing needs are predictable and much smaller validation teams can move from one scheduled task to the next.
A periodic model eliminates the risk that a model continues in use after it has stopped producing reliable forecasts between two validations.
A periodic model suits dynamic environments better, because models that need frequent recalibration are best reviewed at fixed dates.
A periodic model is unavoidable, because model owners are not expected to produce any monitoring reports between scheduled validations.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member at a Japanese bank asking why MRM remains point in time rather than continuous.

**Concept and theory**

GARP sets a clear best practice: “Model risk management should be seen as a continuous effort rather than a point-in-time exercise revolving around validations and reviews.” It adds that this “is still one of the biggest challenges faced by many institutions.”

Why do institutions cling to the periodic model? GARP gives the operating reason: “Focusing on periodic rather than continuous validations is a more manageable operating model, a model that is predictable, which makes staffing needs predictable. It allows banks to operate much smaller teams of validators because once validators are done with a validation or review, they can move on to the next scheduled task.”

| Feature | Point in time (periodic) | Continuous |
|---|---|---|
| Workload | Predictable, scheduled | Ongoing, less predictable |
| Team size | Much smaller teams | Larger capacity needed |
| Fit with environment | Long-cycle regulatory models | Dynamic environments, frequent recalibration |
| Status | Historical default | Best practice; still a major challenge |

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks why the periodic model persists, not whether it is best practice. The answer must be the operating advantage GARP names: predictability of workload and staffing, allowing smaller teams.

**Fragile fact.** Point-in-time MRM is chosen for predictability and small teams; continuous MRM is the best practice and remains one of the biggest challenges.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says MRM should be continuous rather than periodic, to limit damage from models that no longer produce reliable forecasts, but does not give the staffing reasons; those are from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q10 of 16.

a.reason: It paraphrases GARP’s explanation: a predictable model, predictable staffing, and much smaller validation teams that move on to the next scheduled task.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It credits the periodic model with eliminating the risk that a model keeps running after it has stopped working. That risk is exactly what periodic validation leaves open between validations, and is why continuous MRM is preferred. It would be closer to true as a description of the aim of continuous MRM, though even that limits rather than eliminates the risk.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction: GARP says growing reliance on models, dynamic environments and the need for more frequent recalibration require a move to continuous MRM. It would be correct if “periodic” read “continuous”.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It denies the monitoring role of model owners. GARP says owners produce monitoring reports between scheduled validations and reviews, which MRM uses to monitor performance. It would be correct only at an institution with no monitoring framework, contrary to the source.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Swiss bank is preparing a report on how the MRM operating model has evolved. She drafts four statements:

I. Many institutions first adopted point-in-time MRM because most of their material models were regulatory models with very long development and deployment cycles.

II. The US Basel II implementation called for a four-quarter parallel run, during which old and new capital models were in use simultaneously.

III. A continuous MRM approach is now favoured mainly because it allows banks to operate much smaller teams of validators.

IV. Growing reliance on models, increasingly dynamic environments and a rising need for frequent recalibration are pushing MRM towards a continuous approach.

Which statements should she include in the report?

options.text: I and III only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Swiss bank auditing four statements on the history of the MRM operating model.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains why point-in-time MRM arose and why it is giving way. “In the early days of model risk management, many institutions adopted some variation of this point-in-time model. This choice was driven by the fact that most material models in use at banks were regulatory models with very long development and deployment cycles.” Two examples are given: the US Basel II implementation “called for a four-quarter, so-called, parallel run during which both old and new capital models were in use simultaneously”, and stress-testing models, “which are used only once a year”.

The change of direction: “As the reliance on models grows and the environment models are deployed in becomes increasingly dynamic and the potential need for more frequent recalibrations rises, MRM functions must adapt and move to a more continuous risk management approach.”

The staffing advantage belongs to the periodic model: it is predictable and lets banks run much smaller validation teams.

**Applying it to this question**

| Statement | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| I | True | GARP’s stated reason for the early point-in-time model |
| II | True | GARP’s Basel II example |
| III | False | Smaller teams are the advantage of the periodic model, not of continuous MRM |
| IV | True | GARP’s stated drivers of the move to continuous MRM |

**Fragile fact.** Smaller, predictable validation teams belong to the point-in-time model. The push to continuous MRM comes from growing reliance on models, dynamic environments and the need for frequent recalibration.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management”. GARP vs Schweser: the historical origin (regulatory models, Basel II parallel run, annual stress tests) is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q11 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It includes III, which gives the continuous approach the staffing advantage of the periodic approach, and omits the true statements II and IV. It would be correct only if III described the point-in-time model and II and IV were false.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It again includes III and omits the true statements I and IV. Statement III is the sibling-swap corruption of GARP’s sentence on periodic validation.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It contains the true statements I and IV but also III, and leaves out the true Basel II example in II. It would be correct if III read “A point-in-time MRM approach allows banks to operate much smaller teams of validators” and II were false.

d.reason: I, II and IV are each supported by GARP; III attributes a property of the periodic model to the continuous one. Only D selects I, II and IV.

questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank finds that, after the MRM function doubled the size of its highly regarded validation team, the bank’s credit modelling team stopped running its own pre-release testing. options.text: Acceptable: once MRM, as the independent second line, has validated a model, ownership of the model’s risk passes from the modelling team to MRM.
Not acceptable: MRM is an independent backstop for errors the first line misses, but the first line owns the risk and must not abdicate its responsibilities.
Not acceptable: the modelling team should instead have passed its pre-release testing to internal audit, the third line, which independently validates models.
Acceptable: provided the validation team is large and competent enough, it will catch all of the errors that the modelling team might make before release.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at an Australian bank finds the modelling team dropped its own testing after MRM expanded.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes its discussion of MRM with the three lines of defence and a warning: “The existence of large and competent validation teams can result in modeling teams becoming more complacent with regard to their risk management practices.”

The roles are:

- First line: model developers and model owners. They “generate the risk to which the institution is exposed. As such, they own the risk and should take the appropriate measures to mitigate it to the greatest extent possible.”
- Second line: MRM, which “exists as an independent backstop to ‘catch’ errors that the first line might have missed”, and does an independent assessment of the risk and of the first line’s risk management practices.

The key sentence: the second line’s “existence however should not result in an abdication by the first line of its own responsibilities.” A backstop catches what the first line misses; it is not a substitute for the first line’s own controls.

**Applying it to this question**

The modelling team cut its own testing because MRM became bigger and better. That is the complacency GARP warns about, and the head of modelling’s remark is an abdication of first-line responsibility. The practice is not acceptable, and the reason is first-line ownership of risk, not a need to hand the work to another line.

**Fragile fact.** Actor check: the first line (developers and owners) generates and owns the risk; the second line (MRM) is the backstop. A stronger MRM team is a complacency risk, not a reason for the first line to do less.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management” (three lines of defence paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser names “model users and developers” as the first line; GARP names “model developers and model owners”. GARP is used here; the difference looks like condensation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q12 of 16.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It moves ownership of the risk to MRM after validation. GARP is explicit that developers and owners own the risk; the second line assesses it independently. It would be correct only if the first and second lines’ roles were reversed.

b.reason: It identifies MRM as an independent backstop, states that the first line owns the risk, and rejects abdication, all as in GARP.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason, swapping in internal audit (third line) as the validator. Model validation is a second-line MRM activity, and the fix is for the first line to resume its own testing. It would be correct only if the third line were the validation function, which it is not in the source.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It assumes a large, competent validation team will catch all errors. GARP warns that such teams can breed complacency, and a backstop catches errors the first line “might have missed”, not every possible error. It would be correct only if a second line could guarantee zero errors, which no source supports.

questions.question: A regulator examining a Brazilian bank asks its CRO to map the parties involved in model risk to the three lines of defence. Which of the following mappings is most accurate?

options.text: Model developers and model owners are the first line and generate and own the risk; MRM is the second line and independently assesses the risk and the first line’s risk management practices.
Model developers and model owners are the first line and generate and own the risk; MRM is the second line and independently assesses the risk, but not the first line’s risk management practices.
MRM is the first line and generates and owns the risk; model developers and model owners are the second line and independently assess the risk and MRM’s risk management practices.
Model developers and model owners are the first line and generate the risk; MRM is the second line and owns the risk, mitigating it to the greatest extent possible.

questions.solution:
Regulator asks a Brazilian bank’s CRO to map developers, owners and MRM to the three lines of defence.

**Concept and theory**

In the three lines of defence model applied to model risk, GARP assigns the roles as follows:

| Line | Who | Role |
|---|---|---|
| First | Model developers and model owners | Generate the risk, own it, and mitigate it to the greatest extent possible |
| Second | MRM | Independent backstop; independent assessment of the risk and of the first line’s risk management practices |

GARP’s wording: developers and owners “are, in the context of model risk, the first line and thus the actors that generate the risk to which the institution is exposed. As such, they own the risk and should take the appropriate measures to mitigate it to the greatest extent possible, with the second line doing an independent assessment of the risk and of the risk management practices of the first line.”

The logic: whoever creates a risk is best placed, and most accountable, to control it. The second line assesses both the risk itself and how well the first line manages it.

**Applying it to this question**

Four facts must all be right: developers and owners are the first line; they generate and own the risk; MRM is the second line; MRM assesses both the risk and the first line’s practices. Option A states all four.

**Fragile fact.** Owners are first line, not second line. The second line assesses two things: the risk and the first line’s risk management practices.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management” (three lines of defence paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser names “model users and developers” as the first line, whereas GARP names “model developers and model owners”. GARP is used here; the difference looks like condensation in Schweser rather than a change of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q13 of 16.

a.reason: It matches GARP’s allocation of generation and ownership to the first line and of a two-part independent assessment (risk and first-line practices) to the second line.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the second half of MRM’s assessment remit. GARP says the second line assesses the risk and the risk management practices of the first line. It would be correct if “but not” read “and”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It inverts the two lines, making MRM the risk generator and owner and developers the independent assessors. It would be correct only if the labels “first” and “second” were swapped back.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives ownership and mitigation of the risk to MRM. GARP gives ownership and mitigation to the first line, with MRM assessing independently. It would be correct if “MRM is the second line and owns the risk” read “developers and owners own the risk”.

questions.question: At a mature UK insurer, the modelling teams have formed their own quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC) team. A newly appointed chief compliance officer asks how this team fits into model risk management. Which of the following best describes its role?

options.text: It is part of the second line, acting as MRM’s own quality team, and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.
It is the first line’s risk team and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly the risk of conceptual errors.
It is the first line’s risk team and plays a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.
It is the first line’s risk team and, by mitigating execution risk, removes the need for independent validation by the second line.

questions.solution:
Chief compliance officer at a mature UK insurer asks how the first-line QA/QC team fits into model risk management.

**Concept and theory**

The first line does not discharge its ownership of model risk only through individual developers’ diligence. GARP notes: “At more mature institutions, the modeling teams will form a quality control/quality assurance team. These QA/QC teams are the first line’s risk team and play a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.”

Why execution risk in particular? Execution risk arises when a model does not do what it is intended and designed to do, through coding errors, implementation errors, use of the wrong data and so on. These are checkable errors that a team close to the code and data is well placed to catch before release. Conceptual errors (wrong assumptions or techniques) are harder to identify and are not simply right or wrong; there MRM’s role of ensuring transparency is central.

| Team | Line | Main contribution |
|---|---|---|
| QA/QC team | First | Mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk |
| MRM | Second | Independent review and challenge; backstop |

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the line (first, because it is formed by the modelling teams) and the risk it mainly targets (execution risk). The QA/QC team supplements, but does not replace, second-line validation.

**Fragile fact.** QA/QC: first line (formed by the modelling teams), particularly execution risk. Not second line, not conceptual errors, not a substitute for MRM.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “3. Model Risk Management” (three lines of defence paragraph). GARP vs Schweser: Schweser does not mention QA/QC teams; this content is from GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The risk focus is right, but the team is placed in the second line as MRM’s quality team. GARP says it is formed by the modelling teams and is the first line’s risk team. It would be correct if “part of the second line, acting as MRM’s own quality team” read “the first line’s risk team”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps execution risk for its sibling, conceptual errors. GARP singles out execution risk; conceptual errors call for MRM’s transparency and challenge role. It would be correct if “conceptual errors” read “execution risk”.

c.reason: It restates GARP: QA/QC teams are the first line’s risk team and play a critical role in mitigating model risk, particularly execution risk.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It says the QA/QC team removes the need for second-line validation. GARP keeps the second line as an independent backstop to catch what the first line misses. It would be correct only if first-line controls could guarantee error-free models.

questions.question: A validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing an SGD mortgage prepayment model. She and the developer hold different views on a key prepayment assumption, and both views are reasonable and equally valid. The developer has noted the assumption’s limitations in the model documentation. Which course of action best reflects the role of MRM in this situation?

options.text: Decide which view of the assumption is correct and require the developer to adopt it, since conceptual questions of this kind are ultimately a matter of right or wrong.
Ensure transparency, making sure the assumption and its limitations are communicated to users so that they understand when the model can be safely used and when to stop.
Accept the assumption without further action, since limitations that are discussed in the model documentation can be relied on to be understood by all users.
Remove the conceptual risk entirely by requiring the developer to recalibrate the model until it is shown to be valid in every possible market environment.

questions.solution:
Validator at a Singapore bank and a developer hold equally reasonable but different views on a prepayment assumption.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two sources of model risk. Execution errors are errors in doing what the model is designed to do; they are matters of right or wrong. Conceptual errors arise from wrong assumptions or techniques and are “much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong. Different reasonable modelers can have different and equally valid opinions on an assumption.”

MRM cannot “correct” such a disagreement by decree. GARP states: “In those situations, the role of model risk management is to ensure transparency.” Understanding the limitations of a model and communicating them clearly to users, who might not be quantitatively savvy, is crucial. Modelers may discuss limitations in the documentation, “but this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them.” MRM should therefore ensure the assumptions are communicated “in a manner that is useful to their understanding of when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued.” A model can be right in one context and wrong if the context changes.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem builds the exact condition GARP describes: two reasonable, equally valid views on an assumption. That points to a conceptual question with no single right answer, so MRM’s role is transparency. The fact that the limitation is in the documentation is a trap: documentation alone does not ensure users understand it.

**Fragile fact.** Conceptual errors: MRM’s role is transparency and clear communication to users. Documentation by the modeler is not the same as users understanding the limitation.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “2. Model Risks”. Boundary call: the execution versus conceptual taxonomy belongs to LO 57.a; this question tests only MRM’s role when a conceptual question arises, which falls under the role of the MRM function. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser says assumptions and limitations should be documented and effectively communicated to users (under LO 57.a). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q15 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It treats the conceptual question as a matter of right or wrong. GARP says conceptual errors may not be a matter of right or wrong, which is why MRM’s role is transparency. It would be correct for an execution error, such as a coding mistake, where one answer is right.

b.reason: It states the GARP role (ensure transparency) and the GARP purpose of communication (so users understand when the model can be safely used and when its use should be discontinued).

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It treats mention in the documentation as enough. GARP says documented limitations do not mean users are aware of them or understand them; MRM must ensure clear communication. It would be correct only if every user were known to have read and understood the documentation.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It promises to remove conceptual risk and to make the model valid in every environment. GARP says a model can be right in one context and wrong if the context changes; the risk is managed through transparency, not eliminated. It would be correct only if a model could be valid in all environments, which the source rules out.
