questions.question: The head of MRM at a US asset manager is training validators on the priorities of the function when reviewing a complex USD pricing model used by portfolio managers with little quantitative background. Which of the following statements is least accurate?

options.text: MRM should replicate the model to confirm that no coding errors exist and that the outputs generated are the intended ones.
MRM’s more critical responsibility, beyond replication, is challenging the assumptions upon which the model relies.
MRM should help users understand in non-technical terms what the model’s limitations are, so as to minimise its misuse.
MRM’s most important skill is technical modelling depth, since it is the modelers’ responsibility alone to ensure that the model works.

questions.solution:
Head of MRM at a US asset manager training validators on MRM priorities for a complex pricing model with non-quantitative users.

**Concept and theory**

GARP sets out what a risk management function contributes when a complex model is used by people who cannot see inside it. Its role is “primarily one of improving transparency by shedding light in the so-called black box.” The priorities are ranked:

| Priority | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Always required | Replicate the model to ensure no coding errors exist and that the prices generated are the intended ones |
| More critical | Challenge the assumptions on which the model relies and ensure users understand its limitations |
| Most important skill | Effective communication |
| Purpose | Help users understand in non-technical terms what the limitations are, to minimise misuse |

GARP explains why communication is the key skill: most model users at financial institutions do not have a quantitative background, and “it is easy for them to deflect responsibility by simply relying on the argument that they cannot understand the model and that it is the modelers’ responsibility to ensure that it works.” A good MRM function prevents that deflection by making the limitations understandable.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least accurate statement. A, B and C each restate a GARP point (replication, the more critical challenge of assumptions, non-technical explanation of limitations). D names the wrong skill and endorses the very deflection of responsibility GARP warns against.

**Fragile fact.** Replication is always needed, but challenging assumptions is the more critical responsibility, and effective communication is the most important skill.

**Reference**

LO 57.b: “Describe the role of the model risk management function and explain best practices in the model risk management and validation processes.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Study: Model Risk and Model Validation, section “Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing” (paragraph on the role of the risk management function). Boundary call: the case’s facts and lessons belong to LO 57.c; this question tests only the general MRM priorities and skill stated there, which describe the role of the MRM function. GARP vs Schweser: Schweser places the transparency and effective communication point under its LO 57.c case summary and does not rank replication against challenge; GARP is used. No conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 b, where it is Q16 of 16.

a.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP says MRM always needs to replicate the model to ensure that no coding errors exist and that the outputs are the intended ones. Because it is true, it cannot be the least accurate statement. It would become the answer only if it claimed replication were MRM’s most critical responsibility.

b.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP says that MRM’s more critical responsibility, beyond replication, is challenging the assumptions on which the model relies. It would be the answer only under a polarity flip that ranked replication above challenge.

c.reason: **Accurate statement.** GARP says a good MRM function helps users understand in non-technical terms what the limitations are, to minimise misuse. It would be the answer only if it said MRM should explain the model in technical terms or leave users to rely on the modelers.

d.reason: D is the inaccurate statement, so it is the answer. It is a sibling swap: GARP names effective communication, not technical modelling depth, as the most important skill, and it describes “it is the modelers’ responsibility” as an excuse users use to deflect responsibility, not as a principle.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on the Gaussian copula approach to CDO pricing that David X. Li published in the early 2000s. The slide must state how the approach obtained the correlations among the assets in a pool. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: It estimated the correlations from historical mortgage default data, since long default histories were available and could be observed directly for each pool.
It inferred the correlations from CDS prices, on the premise that efficient market prices should reflect them, so pools could be priced without observing the correlations.
It inferred the correlations from traded CDO tranche prices, on the premise that a deep and long-established tranche market already reflected the pool correlations.
It inferred the correlations from CDS prices, a premise that was robust because CDS markets had several decades of data spanning a number of housing cycles.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Japanese bank writing a slide on how Li’s Gaussian copula approach obtained pool correlations.

**Concept and theory**

A collateralised debt obligation (CDO) is backed by a pool of assets, such as the mortgages in the GARP case. Pricing it requires the correlation between the default probabilities of the assets in the pool, that is, how likely they are to default together. The practical problem in the early 2000s was that these correlations could not be observed or calculated directly for a given pool.

David X. Li’s paper offered a way round this. The concept at the centre of his approach was the Gaussian copula, used to model the correlations between default probabilities of the assets in the pool. The key modelling choice was where that correlation came from:

| Element | Li’s choice (GARP, Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing) |
|---|---|
| Correlation source | Prices of credit default swaps (CDSs), rather than observed historical correlations |
| Justification | If markets are efficient, market prices should already reflect the correlation |
| Benefit | Pools could be priced without being able to observe and calculate their correlations |
| Weakness | CDSs had existed for only about a decade, a short and relatively benign sample |

The CDO market took off on the back of this approach. The lesson of the case starts here: the model’s output was only as good as an assumption (that CDS prices over a benign decade told you the true correlation) whose validity depended on the environment.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must state how the correlations were obtained. Two facts decide it: the source (CDS prices, not history and not tranche prices) and the stated premise (efficient markets). A third fact, the length of the CDS sample, rules out the option that gets the source right but overstates the data.

**Fragile fact.** Source direction: Li used CDS prices instead of historical correlations, and the CDS sample was short (about a decade) and benign.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing. Schweser additionally calls the inferred correlation the “Gaussian constant” and notes that historical mortgage default correlations tended to be low; GARP does not use the term. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the CDS-implied source for its sibling, historical correlations. GARP says explicitly that Li’s formula used CDS prices “rather than observed historical correlations”, and the whole point was that correlations could not be observed directly for each pool. This option would be correct for a stem describing a traditional historical-estimation approach to default correlation, not Li’s.

b.reason: GARP states that the approach was about “how to price pools of assets without being able to observe and calculate their correlations”, and that it used “CDS prices to infer the correlation of assets (assuming market prices should reflect the correlation if they are efficient)”. Option B states exactly this.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin.** It names the wrong market instrument: CDO tranche prices instead of CDS prices. The CDO is the product being priced, so it cannot be the source of its own correlation input, and the CDO market only “took off” after the approach was published, so it was not deep or long established. It would be right only for a stem about a later practice of backing out correlations from quoted tranche prices, which is not this case.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The source and premise are right, but it overextends the data condition. GARP says CDSs had been in existence “for only about a decade”, a “very short and relatively benign sample” in which house prices rose consistently and defaults were at all-time lows. This option would be correct only if the CDS history had covered several housing downturns, which is precisely what it lacked.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Singapore bank is reviewing a draft board paper on why CDO pricing based on the Gaussian copula broke down in 2008. Which of the following statements in the draft is most accurate?

options.text: The Gaussian copula assumption was invalid even in normal markets, so the CDO values it generated were inaccurate throughout the years before the crisis.
Correlations implied by CDS prices were high during the benign period and fell sharply once house prices reversed, which destabilised CDO prices.
The CDS data covered a long sample that included stress periods, so the breakdown must have come from coding errors in the banks’ pricing tools.
Correlations implied by CDS prices over a short, benign sample were very low and sensitive to house prices, and they shot up once house prices reversed.

questions.solution:
Singapore CRO reviewing a board paper on why Gaussian copula CDO pricing broke down in 2008.

**Concept and theory**

The copula case is GARP’s illustration of a conceptual error: a model that is “right” in one context and “completely wrong” if the context changes. Nothing in the code needs to be broken for this to happen. The chain of cause and effect in the case runs as follows:

1. The correlation input came from CDS prices, and CDSs had only about a decade of history.
2. That decade was benign: house prices rose consistently and defaults were at all-time lows.
3. CDS-implied correlations were therefore very low and extremely sensitive to the trajectory of house prices.
4. In normal markets the Gaussian copula assumption was “perfectly valid and generated accurate values”.
5. The moment house prices reversed, implied correlations “shot up”, with dramatic consequences for CDO prices; the assumption was no longer valid, yet many kept using tools built on it.

The lesson is that validity is conditional on the environment, and that a model calibrated on a short, calm sample hides how fragile its key input is.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes a claim about (i) whether the assumption worked in normal markets, (ii) the level and direction of implied correlations, and (iii) the nature of the error. Only one option gets all three right: low correlations in the benign sample, high sensitivity to house prices, and a spike on reversal.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: CDS-implied correlations were low in the benign period and shot up when house prices fell. The assumption was valid in normal markets; it failed when the context changed.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; also Model Risks (paragraph on conceptual errors, which cites the CDO case). Schweser describes the model as incorporating changing correlations “with a lag”; GARP frames it as banks failing to update the model. This is a difference of framing, not of substance, and does not affect the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It extends the failure to all conditions. GARP says the Gaussian copula assumption was “perfectly valid and generated accurate values in normal market conditions”; it became invalid only when correlations spiked. This option would be correct for a model whose assumption was wrong from the outset, which is not what the case describes.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses both directions: implied correlations were low in the benign period and rose sharply when house prices reversed. It would be correct only for an imaginary market in which a housing downturn made defaults less likely to cluster.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the conceptual error for its sibling, an execution (coding) error, and it reverses the data condition: the sample was short and benign, not long and stressed. It would describe a different case, in which the model’s concept was sound and the implementation was faulty.

d.reason: GARP: “Correlations implied by CDS prices in this environment were very low and extremely sensitive to the trajectory of house prices. The moment house prices reversed course, correlations implied by CDS prices shot up with dramatic consequences to CDO prices.” The “short, benign sample” is GARP’s own description of the decade of CDS data.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a German asset manager is reviewing a lessons-learned note on the Gaussian copula case. The note records that the pricing approach was adopted by bond investors, banks, rating agencies and regulators, and became so entrenched that warnings about its limitations were largely ignored. Which of the following best describes where the case places the blame for the losses?

options.text: With those who used the formula blindly: the quants, who should have known better and warned users, and the users, who relied on black-box prices they did not understand.
With the formula itself, because its mathematics was flawed and would have produced wrong CDO prices under any market conditions, however carefully it was used.
With the users alone, because the quants had documented the model’s limitations, and documenting the limitations ensures that users are aware of and understand them.
With the rating agencies and regulators, because their adoption of the approach entitled the quants and users at banks to rely on its prices without further challenge.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a German asset manager reviewing where the copula case places the blame for losses.

**Concept and theory**

A tempting reading of the CDO collapse is “the formula was wrong”. GARP rejects this. It quotes the Wired account that Li’s method “was adopted by everybody from bond investors and Wall Street banks to ratings agencies and regulators”, and that it became “so deeply entrenched, and was making people so much money, that warnings about its limitations were largely ignored”. GARP then states: “While it might be easy to simply blame the formula, the reality is that the blame falls with those who used it blindly.” It names two groups:

| Actor | Failing identified by GARP |
|---|---|
| Quants at the financial institutions | Should have known better and warned users |
| Users of the model | Should not have relied blindly on prices “spat out of a black box” they did not understand |

GARP adds that “the problem was not with the formula itself” but with the failure to update it. The broader point from the Model Risks section is that modellers may be aware of limitations, and may even document them, but “this does not mean that the users of the model will necessarily be aware of them or understand them”.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives the entrenchment facts and asks where the blame lies. The deciding fact is GARP’s attribution to both quants and users, for blind use, and its explicit refusal to blame the formula.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the blame falls on both the quants (who should have warned) and the users (who relied blindly), not on the formula and not on the regulators or rating agencies.

questions.question: A model validation lead at a US bank is asked by the risk committee what the model risk management function’s most critical responsibility would have been in a context like the Gaussian copula and CDO pricing case. Which of the following answers is most accurate?

options.text: Replicating the model to confirm that no coding errors exist and that the prices generated are the intended ones, since this is the core defence against such failures.
Taking ownership of CDO pricing decisions away from model users, since users without a quantitative background cannot be expected to use such models appropriately.
Challenging the assumptions on which the model relies and ensuring that users understand its limitations, so that the model is not misused when conditions change.

|---|---|

| More critical | Challenge the assumptions upon which the model relies and ensure that users understand its limitations |
| Key skill | Effective communication, because most users do not have a quantitative background |

|---|---|
| File sent by Barclays | Excel file of 1,000 rows and 24,000 cells, sent at 7.50 p.m. on 18 September |
| Submission deadline | Midnight on 18 September, to the bankruptcy court’s website |
| Contracts not wanted | 179 trading contracts listed in the file |
| Discovery of the problem | 1 October |

Which of the following best describes how the error arose and was dealt with?

The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted; a junior law associate at Cleary Gottlieb, reformatting the file to PDF, was unaware of them, and they became visible in the PDF.
The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted; a court clerk converting the file to PDF for the court’s website made them visible, and the court later excluded them itself.
The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted and became visible in the PDF, but the error was caught before the deal was approved, so no legal motion was needed.

| Submission | Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton, Barclays’ law firm, had to file the offer on the bankruptcy court’s website by midnight on 18 September |
| The file | Barclays sent an Excel file at 7.50 p.m. on 18 September: 1,000 rows, 24,000 cells, including 179 contracts it did not want to buy |
| The flaw | The 179 rows were hidden rather than deleted |
| The trigger | A junior law associate at Cleary Gottlieb, on a tight schedule, reformatted the file to PDF; unaware of the hidden rows, he produced a PDF in which they were visible again |
| Discovery | 1 October, after the deal had been approved |

It is a model, because the contract values it contains may carry estimation errors, which makes the spreadsheet itself the source of model risk for those values.
It is not a model, because there is no uncertainty around its contents; any estimation error in the values belongs to the models used to value the contracts.

1. There is no uncertainty around the information it contains.
2. The list of assets is known, and their values are known or at least agreed upon.

There is no valid view in which two teams can use different unit systems for the same operation. The option would describe a genuine conceptual disagreement, such as the choice of default correlation for a new loan pool.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the copula case’s feature, an assumption valid in normal conditions that fails when the environment changes, to the orbiter. The unit mismatch was wrong from the start; no change in conditions made it wrong. This would be the right characterisation of the Gaussian copula case.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The classification is correct but the actors are swapped. GARP says Lockheed Martin’s engineering team used English units, while the agency (NASA) used the metric system. The option would be right only if the roles were reversed.

questions.question: A board member of a UK bank questions the cost of the model risk management function. Its annual budget is GBP 18 million, and it reported 312 model errors last year, almost all of which would have caused small losses, if any. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the lessons of the model risk case studies?

options.text: The function should review only the models whose errors have caused catastrophic losses in the past, because the other errors it catches are benign.
The function can identify in advance which mistakes will be catastrophic, so its reviews can be restricted to those mistakes and its budget reduced.
Most caught mistakes would cause benign losses, but a small subset could be catastrophic, and since these cannot be identified in advance, all models need review.
The board’s concern is unfounded, because most of the mistakes caught by the function would have caused catastrophic losses had they not been caught.

questions.solution:
UK board member questioning the cost of MRM when almost all caught errors would have caused small losses.

**Concept and theory**

The Mars orbiter section closes with GARP’s general argument for comprehensive model risk management. It anticipates exactly the objection a board might raise:

1. The cost of an MRM function that “reviews all models and double checks all the work often upsets executives because of the perceived benign nature of some of the mistakes that are caught”.
2. It is “undeniable that in most instances these benign mistakes would have resulted in benign losses, if any”.
3. It is “equally undeniable that a small subset of these mistakes could result in catastrophic losses, such as the loss of the Mars orbiter”.
4. “Unfortunately, it is impossible to determine which mistakes will lead to catastrophic losses and which ones will not!”

The logic is that of a tail risk. GARP’s Model Risks section explains that model risk is often underestimated because of its tail nature: most errors are benign, which leaves institutions with misplaced confidence, and the rarity of severe events makes the cost of MRM “seem disproportionate relative to the risk”. Since the catastrophic few cannot be singled out in advance, the only defence is to review everything. Schweser puts the same point as MRM being “sometimes viewed as a bureaucratic obstacle” whose importance “cannot be overstated”.

**Applying it to this question**

The budget (GBP 18 million) and the number of errors (312) are irrelevant inputs; the argument does not depend on them. The board member’s premise (almost all caught errors are benign) is true. The question is what follows from it. The deciding fact is that catastrophic mistakes cannot be identified in advance.

**Fragile fact.** Frequency: most caught mistakes are benign; a small subset could be catastrophic, and which ones cannot be determined in advance.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: NASA Mars Orbiter (closing paragraph); Definition and History (tail nature of model risk). Schweser: “Oftentimes, small mistakes result in losses; some of those losses, however, can be quite large.” No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It narrows review to models with a history of catastrophic loss. The orbiter’s error had no such history; it was a simple convention nobody thought to check. Because catastrophic mistakes cannot be predicted, past catastrophes are not a usable filter. The option would hold only if catastrophic errors recurred in the same models.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It asserts that MRM can tell in advance which mistakes will be catastrophic. GARP says the opposite: “it is impossible to determine which mistakes will lead to catastrophic losses and which ones will not”. If that foresight existed, targeted review would indeed be efficient, which is why the option is tempting.

c.reason: It accepts the true premise, adds GARP’s “small subset” that could be catastrophic, and draws GARP’s conclusion from the impossibility of telling them apart in advance: all models need review.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the frequency: GARP says most caught mistakes would have caused benign losses, if any, and only a small subset could be catastrophic. Defending MRM on a false premise would be wrong even though the conclusion (keep MRM) is right. The option would be correct only in an institution where most errors were severe.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at a French bank is reviewing four statements in a paper on what the Barclays and NASA Mars orbiter cases teach about model risk.

I. Trivial-seeming execution errors, paired with bad luck and a confluence of events, have resulted in catastrophic losses.

II. Because most errors are benign or caught early, a record of few model-related losses shows that an institution manages model risk well.

III. Errors of the kind seen in the Barclays case are also found in tools that are not considered models.

IV. Both cases show that conceptual errors are easier to identify than execution errors, because conceptual errors are a matter of right or wrong.

Which of the statements are consistent with the case study reading?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
French risk committee member auditing four statements on what the Barclays and Mars orbiter cases teach.

**Concept and theory**

GARP uses the Barclays and Mars orbiter cases to make a point about execution errors in its Model Risks section:

- “Execution errors often seem like trivial errors that cannot result in a material loss. Yet over and over such trivial seeming errors, paired with bad luck and a confluence of events that set the right conditions for a ‘perfect storm,’ have resulted in catastrophic losses. The Barclays’ acquisition of Lehman Brothers and the NASA Mars orbiter case studies below are prime examples.”
- Such errors can be coding errors, implementation errors, use of the wrong data and so forth, and “such errors are also found in tools that are not considered models”; the Barclays spreadsheet is itself such a tool.
- Conceptual errors, by contrast, “are much more difficult to identify because, unlike execution errors, they may not be a matter of right or wrong”.

GARP adds that model risk is underestimated because most errors are benign and are either caught early or do not lead to material losses, which “often leaves institutions with misplaced confidence in their ability to manage the risk”.

**Applying it to this question**

| Statement | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| I | True | GARP’s own statement, with Barclays and NASA as prime examples |
| II | False | Polarity flip: a record of few losses creates misplaced confidence; it is not evidence of good management |
| III | True | Execution-type errors are also found in tools that are not models; the Barclays spreadsheet is one |
| IV | False | Polarity flip: conceptual errors are harder to identify, because they may not be a matter of right or wrong |

**Fragile fact.** Direction: execution errors seem trivial but can be catastrophic; conceptual errors are the harder ones to identify. Few past losses breed misplaced confidence.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Model Risks (execution errors and the two case studies); Definition and History (tail nature and misplaced confidence); Case Studies: Barclays’ Acquisition of Lehman Brothers. Boundary note: the passages are in the section serving LO 57.a, but they state what these two cases teach, so they are tested here only as case lessons. No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “I only” omits statement III. A reader who thinks the case lesson is confined to models will reject III, but GARP says expressly that such errors are also found in tools that are not considered models, and the Barclays spreadsheet “does not fit the definition of a model”. This option would be right only if III were limited to models.

b.reason: Only statements I and III are consistent with the reading: I is GARP’s description of what the two cases exemplify, and III is GARP’s statement that such errors also occur in tools not considered models, of which the Barclays spreadsheet is the case example.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts statement II, which reverses GARP’s point. A record of few losses is what produces “misplaced confidence”; the tail risks materialise under extreme conditions. II would be correct only if a short loss record were a reliable measure of tail exposure.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It accepts statements II and IV, both of which reverse GARP, and drops the true statement I. IV inverts GARP’s comparison: conceptual errors are harder to identify than execution errors. This combination would be correct only if both directions were reversed in the source.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is training new hires on the three model risk case studies. She asks them to choose the row that correctly matches each case with the nature of the error.

| Row | Gaussian copula and CDO pricing | Barclays spreadsheet | NASA Mars orbiter |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Assumption valid in normal markets became invalid as conditions changed | Simple implementation error in a tool that is not a model | Simple assumption taken for granted (choice of unit) |
| B | Coding error in the copula pricing routine | Simple implementation error in a tool that is not a model | Simple assumption taken for granted (choice of unit) |
| C | Assumption valid in normal markets became invalid as conditions changed | Invalid assumption in the spreadsheet’s estimated asset values | Simple assumption taken for granted (choice of unit) |
| D | Assumption valid in normal markets became invalid as conditions changed | Simple implementation error in a tool that is not a model | Debatable modelling judgment on which reasonable engineers could differ |

Which row is correct?

options.text: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.solution:
Singapore senior analyst training new hires to match each case study with the nature of its error.

**Concept and theory**

The three cases illustrate three different ways in which a model, or a tool, can fail. Schweser’s key concepts summarise them as the risk of using models given “(1) the invalidity of assumptions, (2) implementation error, or (3) input measurement error”. GARP’s text supports the following matrix:

| Case | Nature of the error | Key GARP wording |
|---|---|---|
| Gaussian copula | Conceptual: an assumption valid in normal markets that became invalid when correlations spiked | “perfectly valid . . . in normal market conditions”; “no longer valid” |
| Barclays | Simple implementation error, in a tool that does not fit the definition of a model | “a perfect example of a simple implementation error” |
| Mars orbiter | Error in a simple assumption taken for granted, the choice of unit; execution-type | “an error in the ‘assumptions’ of the model, the choice of the unit” |

**Applying it to this question**

Each wrong row corrupts exactly one cell of Row A. The reader has to check every cell, not only the first column.

**Fragile fact.** Classification: copula = assumption that ceased to be valid (conceptual); Barclays = implementation error in a non-model tool; Mars = simple unit “assumption” (execution-type).

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies (all three sections); Model Risks. GARP vs Schweser difference: Schweser’s key concepts call the Mars orbiter case “input measurement error”, while GARP calls it an error in the “assumptions” of the model (the choice of unit). The matrix uses GARP’s wording, and no row turns on the input versus assumption label.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: Row A matches each case to GARP’s classification: the copula assumption valid in normal markets but invalid when conditions changed; the Barclays simple implementation error in a non-model tool; and the Mars orbiter error in the choice of unit, a simple assumption taken for granted.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Row B makes the copula case a coding error. GARP says MRM must always replicate a model to exclude coding errors, but the copula problem was “not with the formula itself”; it was the failure to update an assumption that was no longer valid. Row B would be correct for a case in which a correctly conceived model was coded wrongly.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Row C turns the Barclays case into an invalid assumption in estimated asset values. GARP says there is no uncertainty in the spreadsheet, the asset values are known or agreed, and any estimation error would belong to the valuation models. Row C would fit a case in which the spreadsheet was itself a valuation model.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Row D gives the Mars orbiter case the property of a conceptual error, a debatable judgment on which reasonable experts could differ. GARP says the error “sounds too obvious to not have been caught” and groups it with Barclays as an execution error. Row D would fit a genuine disagreement between experts about an assumption.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is checking a training handout that pairs each model risk case study with a lesson for model risk management. Which of the following pairings is NOT correct?

options.text: Gaussian copula: challenge the model’s assumptions and explain its limitations to users in non-technical terms, so that the model is not used blindly.
Barclays spreadsheet: even seemingly simplistic tools need the right review, challenge and controls, because simple errors can nearly cost millions.
Mars orbiter: check simple assumptions that are often taken for granted, such as the currency or the discount factor used in a financial model.
Barclays spreadsheet: replicate the spreadsheet’s valuation of the 179 contracts, because the error arose from estimation error in the spreadsheet’s values.

questions.solution:
Brazilian internal auditor finding the incorrect case-to-lesson pairing in a training handout.

**Concept and theory**

Each case carries its own lesson for model risk management:

| Case | MRM lesson (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Gaussian copula | Improve transparency; challenge assumptions; ensure users understand limitations, explained in non-technical terms, to minimise misuse |
| Barclays | Even seemingly simplistic tools or models need the right review, challenge and controls; the error nearly cost Barclays millions |
| Mars orbiter | Check simple assumptions taken for granted (in finance: currency, discount factor); review all models because catastrophic mistakes cannot be identified in advance |

In the Barclays case the risk lay in the handling of the file (rows hidden rather than deleted and then exposed by conversion), not in the values. GARP says the asset values were known or agreed, and that any estimation error in them would be model risk of the valuation models, not of the spreadsheet.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT correct, so three pairings are true and one misstates a lesson. The deciding fact is the location of the Barclays error: in implementation, not in estimation.

Here each of the remaining options is a correct pairing, so choosing it is the error.

**Fragile fact.** Location of the Barclays error: in implementation (hidden rows), not in the values; valuation estimation error belongs to the valuation models.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies (all three sections). No GARP vs Schweser conflict on the point tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: **Qualifier misread.** This pairing is correct: in the copula case MRM’s critical responsibility is challenging assumptions and ensuring users understand limitations, communicated in non-technical terms to minimise misuse. A reader who picks A has probably been distracted by “blindly”, which is GARP’s own word for how the formula was used. This option would be the answer only if it paired the copula case with replicating the code to remove coding errors, which GARP ranks below challenging assumptions.

b.reason: **Qualifier misread.** This pairing is correct: GARP calls the Barclays case “an excellent example of why even seemingly simplistic tools or models still need the right review, challenge and controls”, and says the error “nearly cost Barclays millions of dollars”. Choosing B usually reflects the belief that a non-model tool needs no review, which the case refutes. This option would be the answer only if it said that a tool outside the model definition needs no review.

c.reason: **Qualifier misread.** This pairing is correct: GARP’s financial parallel for the unit error is “the use of the wrong currency, discount factor, or other simple assumptions that are often taken for granted”. A reader who rejects C may be thinking only of physical units and not of their financial equivalents. This option would be the answer only if it described the unit choice as a debatable modelling judgment.

d.reason: This pairing is the incorrect one, which makes D the answer. It attributes the Barclays error to estimation error in the spreadsheet’s values, which GARP rules out: there was “no uncertainty around the information contained in the spreadsheet”, and estimation errors in values “would be model risks related to the models used to value them not the spreadsheet”. Replicating a valuation would not have caught a hidden row.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing a US bank’s internal post-mortem on its CDO pricing losses in 2008. The bank had priced its CDOs with a Gaussian copula model that drew its correlations from CDS prices. As house prices fell, CDS prices rose sharply. Which of the following best explains what went wrong, according to the case study?

options.text: Banks updated the copula model promptly with the higher CDS-implied correlations, and the losses arose because the formula cannot produce valid prices at high correlations.
Banks switched from CDS-implied correlations to historical correlations once CDS prices rose, and the low historical correlations then understated the risk in their CDOs.
Banks failed to update the copula model with the new, higher correlation estimates implied by CDS prices, and they continued to price CDOs using the old assumptions.
Banks’ pricing tools contained coding errors that went unnoticed in benign markets, and the losses arose because these errors were magnified once CDS prices rose.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant reviewing a US bank’s post-mortem on its 2008 Gaussian copula CDO pricing losses.

**Concept and theory**

Having said that the blame falls on those who used the formula blindly, GARP pins down the mechanism of failure: “In actuality, the problem was not with the formula itself, but with the fact that banks failed to update the copula model with the new correlation estimates implied by the higher CDS prices, and instead continued to price CDOs using the old assumptions.”

The sequence is:

1. The model’s correlation input was meant to come from CDS prices.
2. As house prices fell in 2008, CDS prices rose, implying much higher correlations.
3. Banks did not feed these higher correlations back into the model; they kept the low correlations from the benign period.
4. CDO prices therefore rested on stale assumptions, until “the correlations implied by the CDSs, and consequently the CDO prices, swung dramatically, resulting in a collapse of the market”.

GARP’s conceptual-error paragraph says the same: many continued to use CDO pricing tools that relied on the assumption “without realizing the magnitude of the pricing errors that were resulting”. The lesson is that an assumption must be monitored and updated as the environment changes, and that users must know when a model should no longer be used.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks what went wrong. The deciding fact is the direction of the banks’ action: they did not update the model with the new CDS-implied correlations. Options that have banks updating promptly, switching to another data source, or suffering from code defects all contradict the source.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of action: banks failed to update the model with the higher CDS-implied correlations and kept the old assumptions; the formula itself was not the problem.

**Reference**

LO 57.c: “Describe lessons learned from the three case studies involving model risk.” GARP Chapter 16, Case Studies: Gaussian Copula and CDO Pricing; Model Risks (conceptual errors paragraph). Schweser says the model “incorporated changing correlations with a lag”. That is compatible with GARP’s statement that banks failed to update the model and kept the old assumptions; GARP’s wording is used. No substantive conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Operational Risk and Resilience: the paper for ORR-16 c, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the banks’ action (they did not update promptly) and then blames the formula, which GARP says was not the problem. It would be correct only for a model that was kept current but could not handle high correlations, which is not what GARP describes.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin.** It replaces the CDS-implied input with its twin, historical correlations. The case says nothing about a switch to historical data; GARP says banks kept the old CDS-implied assumptions. This option would describe a different failure, in which a bank replaced a market-implied input with a backward-looking one.

c.reason: It restates GARP’s diagnosis: banks “failed to update the copula model with the new correlation estimates implied by the higher CDS prices, and instead continued to price CDOs using the old assumptions”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the conceptual failure for an execution failure (coding errors). GARP says the problem was not with the formula, and its conceptual-error paragraph cites this case as one where a valid assumption ceased to hold. It would be the right explanation for a case in which a correctly conceived model was implemented wrongly.
